The project

Second Brain — what you are building

One application, built in nineteen milestones across eleven parts. Not eleven disconnected demos: the same codebase, growing one layer per part, from a script that talks to a local model into a containerised product a stranger can run with one command.

The project in brief

What it does

Second Brain is a research assistant over your own documents. You drop PDFs, markdown or text files into it; it indexes them; you ask questions in plain language and get an answer with citations you can check. When a question needs more than a lookup — a calculation, a multi-step search, writing a file — an agent decides what to do, and asks your permission before anything irreversible.

The reason for this particular project: it is the smallest system that forces you to confront every real problem in the field. Retrieval quality, hallucination, prompt injection through untrusted documents, streaming, cancellation, cost, evaluation, permissions. A weather-lookup chatbot avoids all of them.

What it looks like when finished

CapabilityWhy it is in the project
Answers stream token by token, with a Stop button that genuinely halts the model rather than just hiding the output.Perceived latency drops from about 4.9 seconds to 0.4 — the single largest improvement to how the product feels.
Citations are verified against the retrieved text before you see them. Fabricated quotes are dropped, not displayed.Language models produce plausible text by construction. This is the engineering answer to that fact rather than a prompt asking nicely.
It says "not in the documents" when the answer is not there.Abstention is a feature. Most systems will confidently answer anything.
Hybrid retrieval: keyword search and semantic search, fused, then reranked.Exact identifiers and paraphrased questions fail in opposite ways. You will implement both and see each one rescue the other.
An agent trace you can open, showing every step, tool call and error.Debugging a non-deterministic system is impossible without it.
An approval dialog that shows the full arguments of any risky action.Prompt injection has no complete fix, so the defence is limiting what a compromised model can do.
An evaluation suite with committed baselines that fails your build on a quality regression.The skill employers most often say they cannot find, and the only way to know a change helped.
One command to run the whole stack: docker compose up.The difference between a project and a portfolio piece.

The stack, and why

LayerChoiceIn one line
Model runtimeOllama, running a small local modelFree, private, no credit card, and it makes token costs and memory limits tangible instead of abstract.
BackendPython + FastAPIWhere the ecosystem lives, and Pydantic makes the model's output validate itself.
FrontendAngular + TypeScript + SCSSTaught from zero in Part 9. Streaming, citations and consent are where trust in an AI product is won or lost.
RetrievalNumPy first, then a real vector storeYou implement cosine similarity and BM25 by hand before using a library that hides them.
PackagingDocker Compose + nginxFour containers, one command, no setup instructions longer than a line.

Everything is free — not trial-free, actually free. No API key is required at any point. If you have a key for a hosted provider, Part 4 makes swapping to it a one-line configuration change, and Part 10 shows that the same one line is how you deploy.

How it grows

By the end of…You have
Part 1A chat loop with history that reports its own tokens per second. (M1)
Part 3Streaming answers validated against a schema, with a repair loop and an abstention path. (M2)
Part 5The full RAG pipeline: ingestion, chunking, hybrid retrieval, reranking, verified citations, and an eval harness. (M3–M6)
Part 6An agent — tools, a hand-written loop, memory, a supervisor, guardrails, and an MCP server. (M7–M13)
Part 9A real Angular frontend: streaming with cancel, safe markdown, citations panel, trace viewer, approval dialog. (M16–M18)
Part 10Production: SSE endpoints, tracing, a CI regression gate, security, and the whole thing in containers. (M14, M15, M19)

The complete milestone map — every one of the nineteen, the files it produces and what each demonstrates in an interview — is in section 11.7.

What you need

  • A machine with 8 GB of RAM. No GPU required. The default model is small enough to run on a CPU; section 0.4 gives four hardware tiers and the model choice for each.
  • Some programming experience. Python is taught where it matters and Angular is taught from nothing, but this assumes you have written software before.
  • No maths beyond arithmetic. You will implement gradient descent and attention by hand, but every number is worked through explicitly.

The one thing to know before you start. This is not a machine-learning course with software attached. It is a software engineering course for a dependency that fails plausibly — one that cannot be unit-tested in the usual way and changes underneath you when a vendor ships. Almost everything unusual about the discipline follows from that single property, and almost every technique in this course exists to manage it.

Part 0

How to use this, and how to set your machine up

Everything here runs on hardware you already own, with software that is free as in you never enter a credit card. Where a hosted service is used, its free tier is stated exactly. Where a model is used, its licence is stated.

0.1 How this course is built

This is one HTML file. It works offline (syntax colours need the internet on first load; without it the code is still readable, just grey). Progress is saved in your browser, so you can close it and come back.

The one rule that shapes everything

Every code block in this course follows the same eight-step shape, so you never have to guess what a line does:

#What you get
1A one-sentence goal before the code.
2The complete file. No ..., no "rest of the code here".
3A line-by-line table: Line(s) / What it does / Why we need it.
4An explanation of every new import, why it beat the alternatives, and the exact install command.
5Expected output, so you can tell success from silence.
6What breaks here — the 2–3 errors you are most likely to hit, and the fix.
7A Try this yourself variation.
8The file tree, so you always know where the file goes.

TypeScript, HTML templates and SCSS get the identical treatment in Part 9. An Angular component is explained line by line exactly like a Python function.

Three things I will keep doing

  • Define every acronym once. LLM = Large Language Model. RAG = Retrieval Augmented Generation. You will get each one at first use.
  • Say when something is hype. A lot of GenAI content sells you a technique that buys you nothing on a small project. I will say so.
  • Flag anything I am not sure is current. Library APIs move monthly. Where I am not certain a function signature is still right, I say "verify this" and link the docs rather than inventing a plausible-looking API.

Version honesty. This material was written against: Python 3.12/3.13, Node.js 24 LTS, Angular 22 (the stable line as of mid-2026), Ollama's current release, and the library versions pinned in each install command. Angular ships a major every six months and Python ships a major every October — if ng version or python --version shows something newer, that is expected, and I flag the places where the difference matters.

Deeper dive: why one HTML file and not a website

A course you can grep, print, and diff is a course you actually finish. A single file has no link rot inside itself, no dependency on a server, and survives being emailed to yourself. The only external dependency is the syntax-highlighting stylesheet and script from a CDN (Content Delivery Network — a public file host). If those fail to load, the page degrades to plain monospace code, which is why the code blocks are readable without colour.

0.4 Hardware reality check — pick your tier now

Everything in this course runs locally by default. What changes with your hardware is which model you run, not which techniques you learn. Find your row and remember the model names; I refer back to these tiers constantly.

TierYour machineDefault chat modelEmbedding modelRealistic speed
A — light8 GB RAM, no GPU (or Apple M1 8 GB)qwen3:1.7b or llama3.2:1ball-MiniLM-L6-v2 (CPU, 22 MB)5–15 tokens/sec. Usable, occasionally dumb.
B — normal16 GB RAM, no GPU / integratedqwen3:4b or llama3.2:3ball-MiniLM-L6-v2 or bge-small-en-v1.510–25 tokens/sec.
C — comfortable16 GB+ RAM with 8 GB+ VRAM GPU, or Apple silicon 16 GB+qwen3:8b or llama3.1:8bbge-base-en-v1.5 or nomic-embed-text30–80 tokens/sec. Genuinely pleasant.
D — escape hatchAnything, plus internetGroq or Google AI Studio free tierlocal MiniLM (embeddings stay local — they are cheap)200–1000 tokens/sec, rate limited.

If you have 8 GB RAM, read this twice. A 7–8 billion parameter model quantised to 4 bits needs roughly 5–6 GB of RAM plus room for your OS, your browser, and the context window. On an 8 GB machine that means swapping to disk, which turns 20 tokens/sec into 1 token/sec. Stay at 1B–4B parameters locally, and use the Tier D free API when you need a smarter answer. Nothing in this course requires a big local model — the capstone is designed to work at 1.7B.

What the model names mean

  • qwen3:1.7b — family Qwen 3 (Alibaba), 1.7 billion parameters. Apache-2.0 licence for most sizes.
  • llama3.2:3b — Meta's Llama 3.2, 3 billion parameters. Llama Community Licence: free for you, with restrictions above 700 M monthly users (not your problem).
  • The tag after the colon is the size or the quantisation. qwen3:8b-q4_K_M means 8 B parameters compressed to roughly 4 bits per weight. Part 2 explains quantisation properly; for now, more parameters = smarter and slower, fewer bits = smaller and slightly dumber.
Deeper dive: the one number that decides everything (RAM/VRAM)

Rough working figure: bytes needed ≈ parameters × bits-per-weight ÷ 8, then add 20–30% for the KV cache (the model's short-term memory of your conversation) and runtime overhead.

  • 8 B params at 4 bits ≈ 8e9 × 0.5 bytes = 4 GB, → ~5.5 GB in practice.
  • 3 B params at 4 bits ≈ 1.5 GB → ~2.2 GB in practice.
  • 1.7 B params at 4 bits ≈ 0.85 GB → ~1.3 GB in practice.

If the model fits entirely in GPU VRAM it runs fast. If it half-fits, the runtime splits layers between GPU and CPU and you get maybe 30% of the speed. If it does not fit in RAM at all, your OS swaps and speed collapses by 10–50×. There is no gentle degradation here; it is a cliff. Section 0.8 shows how to check which side of the cliff you are on.

0.5 Python and uv

Get a Python 3.12 or 3.13 interpreter and a fast, reproducible way to make isolated environments.

Which Python version

Use 3.12 or 3.13. Python 3.14 is out and fine for pure-Python work, but the machine-learning ecosystem (PyTorch, some vector DB clients, some tokenizer builds) lags a few months behind each new release, and hitting "no wheel available for your Python version" in week one is a miserable way to start. 3.11 is also fine. Anything below 3.10 will break the type-hint syntax used throughout.

OSInstall Python
WindowsDownload from python.org/downloads. Tick "Add python.exe to PATH" on the first installer screen. Do not use the Microsoft Store build.
macOSbrew install python@3.13, or the python.org installer. Do not use the /usr/bin/python3 that ships with macOS.
Linuxsudo apt install python3.13 python3.13-venv (Ubuntu 24.04+), or use uv below to install Python for you.

Why uv instead of plain venv + pip

uv is a Python package manager written in Rust by Astral (MIT/Apache-2.0, free, runs locally). It does what pip, venv, pip-tools and pyenv do, roughly 10–50× faster, and it can install Python itself. You can do this entire course with python -m venv and pip — I give both — but installing PyTorch with pip takes minutes and with uv takes seconds, and you will do it more than once.

Install uv, create the project folder, and make an isolated environment.

# 1. install uv (one line, no admin rights needed)
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# 2. restart your shell, then confirm
uv --version

# 3. make the project
mkdir second-brain
cd second-brain

# 4. create a virtual environment pinned to Python 3.13
uv venv --python 3.13

# 5. activate it
source .venv/bin/activate

# 6. prove you are inside it
which python
python --version
# 1. install uv
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

# 2. restart PowerShell, then confirm
uv --version

# 3. make the project
mkdir second-brain
cd second-brain

# 4. create a virtual environment pinned to Python 3.13
uv venv --python 3.13

# 5. activate it
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# 6. prove you are inside it
Get-Command python
python --version
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
1–2Downloads the uv installer script and runs it. Installs a single binary into ~/.local/bin (or %USERPROFILE%\.local\bin).No admin rights, no system Python touched. If this ever goes wrong you delete one file.
uv --versionConfirms the binary is on your PATH.If this fails, your shell has not picked up the new PATH — restart the terminal. This is the single most common first-hour problem.
mkdir second-brainCreates the capstone project folder.Every milestone M1–M19 lives in here. Make it somewhere without spaces or OneDrive sync if you can — sync clients corrupt virtual environments.
uv venv --python 3.13Creates .venv/, downloading Python 3.13 first if you do not have it.A virtual environment is a private copy of Python's package folder. Without it, every project's dependencies fight each other globally.
source .venv/bin/activatePoints your shell's python and pip at the environment.Without activating, pip install writes to your system Python and the imports fail in confusing ways.
which python / Get-Command pythonPrints the full path of the interpreter now in use.The path must contain .venv. This is the check that saves you an hour later.

Expected output

uv 0.9.x (or newer)
/Users/you/second-brain/.venv/bin/python
Python 3.13.x

The important part is that the path contains .venv, and that your prompt now starts with (second-brain) or (.venv).

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
uv: command not foundPATH not reloaded.Close and reopen the terminal. On macOS/Linux, source ~/.zshrc or source ~/.bashrc.
PowerShell: cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabledWindows execution policy blocks the activate script.Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned, answer Y, then activate again.
which python shows /usr/bin/pythonYou are not in the environment.Re-run the activate line from inside the project folder. Every new terminal window needs activating again.
Try this yourself. Run uv pip install requests, then uv pip list. Now deactivate and run python -c "import requests". It should fail with ModuleNotFoundError unless you happen to have requests globally. That failure is the whole point of virtual environments — the package exists in one place and not the other.
Deeper dive: doing this without uv 
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # Windows: .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install --upgrade pip

Then use pip install X everywhere I write uv pip install X. Everything else in the course is identical. The only real cost is speed and the lack of a lockfile.

0.6 Git and VS Code

Get version control and an editor that will catch your mistakes before you run them.

Git

Install from git-scm.com (free, open source, local). Then, once:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

cd second-brain
git init
printf '.venv/\n__pycache__/\n.env\nnode_modules/\ndata/\n*.gguf\n' > .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "chore: initial commit"
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
git config --global …Sets the name and email stamped on every commit you make.Git refuses to commit without them. Doing it globally means you do it once, ever.
git initCreates a .git folder — the repository.You are about to write 19 milestones into one codebase. You will want to go back.
printf … > .gitignoreLists paths git must never track: the virtual environment, Python bytecode caches, your secrets file, Node modules, ingested documents, downloaded model weights.These are large, machine-specific, or secret. A committed .env is the classic way people leak an API key.
git add / git commitStages the file and records the first snapshot.Gives you a clean baseline to diff against.

VS Code and the extensions worth having

Download from code.visualstudio.com (free, MIT-licensed core, runs locally). Install these from the Extensions panel (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+X):

ExtensionPublisherWhy
PythonMicrosoftInterpreter selection, debugging, test running. Pulls in Pylance.
PylanceMicrosoftType checking as you type. This is what makes the type hints in Part 1 actually pay off.
RuffAstralLinting and formatting for Python, instantly. Replaces flake8 + isort + black.
Angular Language ServiceAngularAutocomplete and type checking inside HTML templates. Without it, template typos are silent until runtime. Essential for Part 9.
ESLintMicrosoftTypeScript linting for the Angular side.
PrettierPrettierFormats TS/HTML/SCSS. Stops you arguing with yourself about quotes.
DockerMicrosoftSyntax and container management for Part 10.
REST Client or Thunder ClientHuachao Mao / Ranga VadhineniFire HTTP requests at your FastAPI backend from inside the editor. Both have free tiers; REST Client is fully free and file-based.

Point VS Code at the right Python. Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P → "Python: Select Interpreter" → pick the one inside ./.venv. If you skip this, VS Code will underline every import in red while the code runs fine in the terminal, and you will lose twenty minutes to a lie.

0.7 Ollama and your first local model

Ollama is a free, MIT-licensed program that downloads open-weight models and serves them over a local HTTP API. It runs entirely on your machine — no account, no key, no network after the download. It is the backbone of this whole course.

OSInstall
Windows / macOSDownload the installer from ollama.com/download and run it. It installs a background service and a menu-bar/tray icon.
Linuxcurl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

Download a small model, talk to it in the terminal, then talk to it over HTTP the way your Python code will.

# 1. confirm the service is up (should print a version)
ollama --version

# 2. pull a model. Pick ONE line based on your tier from 0.4:
ollama pull qwen3:1.7b        # Tier A — 8 GB RAM, ~1.4 GB download
ollama pull qwen3:4b          # Tier B — 16 GB RAM, ~2.6 GB download
ollama pull qwen3:8b          # Tier C — GPU or 16 GB+, ~5.2 GB download

# 3. also pull an embedding model — tiny, everyone needs it in Part 5
ollama pull nomic-embed-text  # ~275 MB

# 4. see what you have
ollama list

# 5. chat with it interactively (type /bye to exit)
ollama run qwen3:1.7b
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
ollama --versionChecks the CLI can reach the background server on 127.0.0.1:11434.If the server is not running, every later step fails with "connection refused".
ollama pull qwen3:1.7bDownloads the model weights (quantised GGUF format) into ~/.ollama/models.This is the actual brain. It is a file on your disk; you own it and it works offline forever.
ollama pull nomic-embed-textDownloads an embedding model, which turns text into vectors rather than generating text.Part 5 (RAG) needs it. Pulling now saves a download later.
ollama listPrints installed models with sizes.Your inventory, and a quick way to spot a half-finished download.
ollama run qwen3:1.7bLoads the model into memory and opens a chat prompt.The fastest possible sanity check that your machine can do this at all.

Expected output

$ ollama list
NAME                  ID            SIZE      MODIFIED
qwen3:1.7b            8f3a1b2c4d5e  1.4 GB    2 minutes ago
nomic-embed-text      0a109f422b47  274 MB    1 minute ago

$ ollama run qwen3:1.7b
>>> say hello in exactly five words
Hello there, nice to meet you.
>>> /bye

Note that it got the five-word instruction wrong (that is six words). Small models do this constantly. Part 3 is about making that failure rarer; Part 2 explains why it happens at all.

Now the same thing over HTTP

See the raw request and response your Python code will send, before any library hides it from you.

curl http://localhost:11434/api/chat -d '{
  "model": "qwen3:1.7b",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with the single word: pong"}],
  "stream": false
}'
{
  "model": "qwen3:1.7b",
  "created_at": "2026-09-01T10:12:03.51Z",
  "message": { "role": "assistant", "content": "pong" },
  "done": true,
  "total_duration": 843112000,
  "eval_count": 4,
  "eval_duration": 121000000
}

Remember three fields — you will use them for the rest of the course: message.content is the answer, eval_count is how many tokens the model generated, and eval_duration is how long generation took in nanoseconds. Tokens ÷ seconds = your tokens-per-second, the number that tells you whether your setup is healthy.

Windows users: that curl line uses single quotes, which PowerShell handles differently. Either run it in Git Bash / WSL, or use Invoke-RestMethod, or just skip it — the Python version in section 1.10 does the same thing and works everywhere.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
Error: could not connect to ollama appBackground service is not running.macOS/Windows: launch the Ollama app from Applications/Start Menu. Linux: sudo systemctl start ollama, or run ollama serve in a spare terminal.
model requires more system memory than is availableYou pulled a model too large for your tier.ollama rm <model> and pull the tier-A model instead. Close Chrome; it is probably holding 3 GB.
Download stalls at 99%Ollama is verifying the layer digest, not stuck.Wait. If it truly hangs, Ctrl+C and re-run the pull — it resumes.
Answers are gibberish or endless repetitionVery small model plus a vague prompt.Expected at 1B. Give it a shorter, more concrete instruction. Part 3 fixes most of this.
Try this yourself. Ask the same question twice in ollama run. You will usually get two different answers. Then quit and re-run with ollama run qwen3:1.7b --verbose and read the timing block it prints after each reply. Write down your tokens-per-second — that number decides how much patience the rest of this course will require.

0.8 Are you on GPU or CPU? (and does it matter)

A GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) does thousands of multiplications at once, which is exactly what running a model is. A CPU does a few dozen at once, very cleverly. For LLM inference the GPU is typically 5–20× faster — but only if the whole model fits in its VRAM (the GPU's own dedicated memory).

Find out, in one command, whether your model is actually using the GPU.

# load the model first (ask it anything), then in a second terminal:
ollama ps
NAME          ID            SIZE     PROCESSOR          UNTIL
qwen3:4b      2f4d9c1a       3.4 GB   100% GPU           4 minutes from now

# or, on a CPU-only machine:
qwen3:1.7b    8f3a1b2c       1.9 GB   100% CPU           4 minutes from now

# or, the bad case — a split:
qwen3:8b      7c2e5a91       6.1 GB   62%/38% CPU/GPU    4 minutes from now
What PROCESSOR saysWhat it meansWhat to do
100% GPUThe model fits in VRAM. Best case.Nothing. Consider a bigger model.
100% CPUNo usable GPU, or a GPU too small to bother with. Normal on laptops and Apple silicon reports differently.Nothing, if speed is acceptable. Otherwise drop a model size.
A split like 62%/38%Half the layers are on the GPU, half on the CPU, and every token crosses the bus. Often slower than pure CPU on small GPUs.Drop to the next model size down, or reduce context length. Do not accept a split as "half-fast" — it usually is not.

Extra checks by platform

PlatformCommandWhat you are looking for
NVIDIA (Win/Linux)nvidia-smiThe Memory-Usage column climbing while the model answers. If the command is missing, your driver or CUDA toolkit is not installed.
Apple siliconollama ps + Activity Monitor → GPU HistoryApple's unified memory means RAM is VRAM. Ollama uses Metal automatically; you rarely need to configure anything.
AMD (Linux)rocm-smiROCm support exists but is patchier than CUDA. If it does not work, CPU mode is a legitimate answer.
Anyollama run <model> --verboseThe eval rate line, in tokens/sec. This is the number that matters, whatever the hardware is called.

Be honest with yourself about speed. Below roughly 8 tokens/sec, iterating on prompts becomes miserable and you will start skipping experiments — which is where the actual learning is. If that is you, do the local work with a 1B model to prove the code runs, and switch the same code to a Tier D free API (one config line, taught in Part 4) whenever you want quality. That is not cheating; it is exactly what production teams do with routing.

0.9 Node.js, npm and the Angular CLI

You need Node.js only as a build tool for the frontend. No JavaScript runs on your server in this course — the backend is Python. Node compiles TypeScript to browser JavaScript and runs the dev server.

Install Node

Get the LTS (Long Term Support) line from nodejs.org/en/download. As of writing that is Node 24 "Krypton", supported into 2028. Node 26 is the "Current" line — newer, shorter-lived; avoid it for this. npm (Node Package Manager) comes bundled.

node --version     # expect v24.x
npm --version      # expect 11.x

# install the Angular CLI globally
npm install -g @angular/cli

ng version
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
node --versionConfirms the runtime.Angular refuses to build on unsupported Node majors, with a clear error. Better to see it now.
npm install -g @angular/cliInstalls the ng command system-wide.ng scaffolds projects, generates components with the right boilerplate, runs the dev server, and builds for production. Doing all that by hand is possible and pointless.
ng versionPrints the CLI version, the Angular packages, and the Node version it sees.The CLI major and the framework major must match. Write down the number it prints — that is the version all Part 9 examples must be checked against.

Which Angular version this course targets. Examples in Part 9 are written for Angular 22 (stable line as of mid-2026; v20 and v21 will run nearly all of it). Version-sensitive things I will flag as they come up:

  • @if / @for built-in control flow — v17+. Older tutorials use *ngIf / *ngFor; both still work.
  • Standalone components as the default (no NgModule) — v17+, enforced by default from v19.
  • Signals (signal, computed, effect) — stable from v17; input()/output() functions from v17.1/17.3; resource() and friends later.
  • Zoneless change detection by default in new projects — v21+. If you are on v20 or below your app still ships zone.js and everything here still works.
  • File naming without the .component suffix (app.ts, not app.component.ts) — v20+ CLI default. If your generated files carry the old suffix, you are on an older CLI; just adjust the paths I give you.
  • Signal Forms — v22. We do not depend on them.

Anything in Part 9 that I am not certain is still current, I will mark and point you at angular.dev.

Create the frontend project

Scaffold the Angular app that will become the Second Brain chat UI.

ng new frontend --style=scss --routing=true --ssr=false --skip-git
FlagWhat it doesWhy we need it
frontendProject name and folder name.Matches the repo layout in 0.10: /backend and /frontend side by side.
--style=scssUses SCSS instead of plain CSS for component styles.Variables and nesting, which the chat UI benefits from. SCSS is a superset of CSS — plain CSS is valid SCSS, so this costs you nothing to learn.
--routing=trueAdds the router with an app.routes.ts file.We need at least two views (chat, documents) by M18.
--ssr=falseNo Server-Side Rendering.SSR needs a Node server in production. Our production server is nginx serving static files, with Python doing the thinking. Adding SSR here would double the deployment complexity for zero benefit on a logged-in app.
--skip-gitDoes not create a second git repo inside our repo.We already ran git init at the project root. Nested repos cause confusing "changes not staged" behaviour.

The CLI will also ask a couple of interactive questions (analytics opt-in, sometimes zoneless or AI-tooling config, depending on version). Decline analytics; accept the defaults for the rest.

What it generated

frontend/
├── angular.json          # build + serve configuration for the whole workspace
├── package.json          # dependencies and the npm scripts (start, build, test)
├── tsconfig.json         # TypeScript compiler options
├── public/               # static assets copied verbatim into the build
│   └── favicon.ico
└── src/
    ├── index.html        # the ONE html page the browser loads
    ├── main.ts           # entry point: bootstraps the root component
    ├── styles.scss       # global styles
    └── app/
        ├── app.ts        # root component class (v20+ naming; older CLIs: app.component.ts)
        ├── app.html      # root component template
        ├── app.scss      # root component styles
        ├── app.config.ts # application-wide providers (HttpClient goes here in Part 9)
        └── app.routes.ts # route table
FileWhat it is for
src/index.htmlThe only HTML the server ever sends. It contains one custom tag, <app-root>, which Angular replaces with your whole application. This is what "Single Page Application" means.
src/main.tsRuns bootstrapApplication(App, appConfig). The first line of your code that executes in the browser.
src/app/app.tsThe root component: a TypeScript class with a decorator that ties it to a template and some styles. Everything else hangs off it.
src/app/app.config.tsWhere you register application-wide services — provideHttpClient(), the router, and later our AI service configuration.
angular.jsonBuild targets, output paths, budgets (bundle-size limits that fail the build), and the dev-server proxy config we will need for CORS in Part 9.

Run it

cd frontend
npm start        # equivalent to: ng serve
Watch mode enabled. Watching for file changes...
  ➜  Local:   http://localhost:4200/
Application bundle generation complete. [2.145 seconds]

Open http://localhost:4200. You will see Angular's placeholder page. We delete it in Part 9 and never speak of it again.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
ng: command not foundnpm's global bin folder is not on PATH.Run npm config get prefix and add its /bin to PATH. On Windows, reopen the terminal after install.
The Angular CLI requires a minimum Node.js version of …Node too old (or an odd-numbered Current release the CLI rejects).Install Node 24 LTS. If you juggle versions, use nvm (macOS/Linux) or nvm-windows.
EACCES: permission denied during npm install -gnpm trying to write into a system folder.Do not use sudo. Set a user-level prefix: npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global and add ~/.npm-global/bin to PATH.
Port 4200 already in useAnother ng serve is running.ng serve --port 4300, or kill the old process.
Try this yourself. Open src/app/app.html, delete everything, and type <h1>Second Brain</h1>. Save. The browser updates without a reload. That instant feedback loop is the main reason the frontend has a build step at all.
Deeper dive: why Angular here, and what you give up

Most GenAI tutorials use Streamlit or Gradio (Python UI libraries) or React. We are not, because you asked for Angular and because Angular is what a lot of enterprise teams already run. The honest trade:

  • Streamlit/Gradio (both free, Apache-2.0) get you a working chat UI in 15 lines of Python. They hide token streaming, cancellation, markdown rendering and citation display behind one function call. They are excellent for a demo and a poor fit for a product: no real routing, awkward multi-user state, limited control over the DOM.
  • Angular costs you a build step, a second language, and a week of learning. It buys you full control over streaming, cancellation, sanitisation, virtual scrolling and component testing — which are exactly the four things AI chat UIs actually need.

Part 7 puts this in a table with the other UI options, and Part 9 shows you what you have to write yourself because you left the prototype tools behind.

0.10 The repo layout we will use

One repository, two services, one compose file to run them together. This is the shape most Python-backend + SPA-frontend teams converge on, and it is the shape recruiters expect to see.

DecisionWhy
One repo, not twoThe Pydantic schema and the TypeScript interface must change together. Splitting the repo means every change is two pull requests that can be merged out of order.
backend/app/ as a packageLets you write from app.llm import chat from anywhere, instead of fragile relative imports. The __init__.py is what makes it a package.
Feature folders in the frontendAngular scales badly when organised by file type (all services in one folder). Organise by feature and lazy loading becomes trivial later.
.env.example committedDocuments which variables exist without leaking values. First thing a new contributor copies.
data/ gitignoredVector stores are binary, large, and regenerable. Committing them is how a 4 MB repo becomes 2 GB.

A first, working docker-compose.yml

Run Ollama and Chroma as containers so the whole stack is reproducible — even though our own code is not containerised yet.

Install Docker Desktop (free for personal use and for companies under 250 employees / $10 M revenue — check the current terms, they have changed before) or Docker Engine on Linux (Apache-2.0, entirely free).

services:
  ollama:
    image: ollama/ollama:latest
    container_name: sb-ollama
    ports:
      - "11434:11434"
    volumes:
      - ollama-models:/root/.ollama
    restart: unless-stopped

  chroma:
    image: chromadb/chroma:latest
    container_name: sb-chroma
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    volumes:
      - ./data/chroma:/data
    environment:
      - IS_PERSISTENT=TRUE
      - ANONYMIZED_TELEMETRY=FALSE
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  ollama-models:
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
services:Declares the containers to run.Compose starts them together with one command and puts them on a shared network where they can reach each other by name.
image: ollama/ollama:latestPulls the official Ollama container.Optional — if you already installed Ollama natively in 0.7, skip this service. Native is faster on macOS because Docker cannot pass through Apple's GPU.
ports: "11434:11434"Maps container port 11434 to the same port on your machine.Your Python code talks to http://localhost:11434 either way, so nothing else changes.
volumes: ollama-models:/root/.ollamaStores downloaded weights in a named Docker volume.Without it, every docker compose down deletes several gigabytes of model that you then re-download.
./data/chroma:/dataBind-mounts a host folder into the container.Your vector index survives container restarts and you can inspect the files.
ANONYMIZED_TELEMETRY=FALSETurns off Chroma's usage reporting.Local-first means local-first.
restart: unless-stoppedRestarts the container after a crash or reboot.Stops you debugging a "connection refused" that is really just a dead container.
 
docker compose up -d      # start in the background
docker compose ps         # what is running
docker compose logs -f    # follow the logs
docker compose down       # stop (volumes survive)

Two version caveats, stated plainly. (1) I have used the :latest tag for both images. In real work you pin an exact tag — chromadb/chroma:1.2.3 — so a surprise upgrade cannot break your index format. Check the current tags on Docker Hub and pin what you actually pulled. (2) Chroma's client API and its server config keys have changed across majors; when you get to Part 5, follow docs.trychroma.com for the exact client call rather than trusting any tutorial, including this one.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
Cannot connect to the Docker daemonDocker Desktop is not running.Start it. On Linux: sudo systemctl start docker, and add yourself to the docker group to avoid sudo.
port is already allocatedYou installed Ollama natively and in Docker; both want 11434.Pick one. Comment out the ollama service, or change the host port to 11435:11434.
Ollama in Docker is slow on macOSDocker on macOS runs a Linux VM with no GPU passthrough, so it is CPU-only.Use the native Ollama app on macOS. Keep the Docker service for Linux servers.

Part 1

Foundations

The vocabulary, the Python patterns you will use in every file for the rest of the course, and just enough mathematics that Part 2 reads as mechanism rather than magic. Part 1 ends with milestone M1: your own code talking to a model on your own machine.

1.1 AI vs ML vs Deep Learning vs Generative AI vs LLM

These are nested, not competing. Each one is a subset of the one before it.

TermPlain definitionThe distinguishing question
AI (Artificial Intelligence)Any system that performs a task we would call intelligent if a human did it.Does it do something clever? A thermostat with enough if statements counts. The term is nearly content-free on its own.
ML (Machine Learning)The system's behaviour is derived from data rather than written by a programmer.Did anyone write the rule, or did the rule come out of examples?
DL (Deep Learning)ML using neural networks with many layers, trained by gradient descent.Are there layers of learned weights? "Deep" just means "many layers".
GenAI (Generative AI)Deep learning models whose output is new content — text, images, audio, code — rather than a label or a number.Does it output a thing, or a judgement about a thing? "Is this email spam?" is not generative. "Write me an email" is.
LLM (Large Language Model)A generative model trained on enormous amounts of text to predict the next token.Is the output text (or code, which is text)? "Large" is vague and always relative — a 1.7B model that was large in 2022 is small today.

The one sentence that explains most LLM behaviour

An LLM is a function that takes a sequence of tokens and returns a probability distribution over what the next token should be. Everything else — chat, tool calling, agents, RAG — is scaffolding we build around repeatedly calling that function.

That framing predicts the model's weaknesses better than any other:

  • It hallucinates because a plausible-sounding next token is exactly what it was trained to produce. Truth was never a term in the objective.
  • It cannot count letters in a word because it never sees letters — it sees tokens (Part 2).
  • It has no memory between calls, because the function is stateless. Chat history only exists because we resend the whole conversation every time.
  • It is good at format and unreliable at fact, because format is a strong statistical pattern and facts are sparse ones.

What an "AI engineer" job actually is. Almost none of it is training models. It is: choosing a model, getting the right context in front of it, constraining its output into something a program can use, wrapping the result in an API, measuring whether it is any good, and stopping it from doing something expensive or dangerous. That is precisely the shape of this course.

Deeper dive: where the other buzzwords fit
  • Foundation model — a large model pretrained on broad data, intended to be adapted to many tasks. An LLM is a foundation model for text.
  • SLM (Small Language Model) — same architecture, 0.5B–8B parameters. What you will run locally, and increasingly what production systems use for routing and cheap subtasks.
  • Multimodal — one model handling more than one kind of input (text + images + audio). Covered in Part 8.
  • Transformer — the specific neural network architecture nearly all modern LLMs use. Part 2.
  • AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) — a hypothetical system with broad human-level competence. Not a technical spec, not something you build against, and not relevant to your job. Ignore it in interviews unless asked directly.
Quiz answer: is a spam filter generative AI?

No. It is machine learning (rules learned from labelled data) and probably not even deep learning (a linear model or gradient-boosted tree usually beats a neural net there). Its output is a label, not new content. If you asked a model to write a spam email, that would be generative.

1.2 Python type hints — the habit that makes the rest of this survivable

LLM applications pass dictionaries of loosely-shaped data between functions constantly: messages, tool arguments, retrieved chunks, agent state. Untyped, this becomes unmaintainable by about file four. Type hints are how you keep it readable. They do not slow anything down — Python ignores them at runtime; your editor and your validators use them.

Write a typed helper that formats chat messages, and see your editor catch a bug before you run it.

"""Typed helpers for building chat message lists."""

from typing import Literal, TypedDict


class Message(TypedDict):
    """One chat message, exactly as the model API expects it."""
    role: Literal["system", "user", "assistant"]
    content: str


def make_message(role: Literal["system", "user", "assistant"], content: str) -> Message:
    """Build a single message dict."""
    return {"role": role, "content": content}


def build_conversation(
    system_prompt: str,
    turns: list[tuple[str, str]],
) -> list[Message]:
    """Turn a system prompt plus (user, assistant) pairs into a message list."""
    messages: list[Message] = [make_message("system", system_prompt)]
    for user_text, assistant_text in turns:
        messages.append(make_message("user", user_text))
        messages.append(make_message("assistant", assistant_text))
    return messages


def total_chars(messages: list[Message]) -> int:
    """Rough size of a conversation. A stand-in for token counting until Part 2."""
    return sum(len(m["content"]) for m in messages)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    convo = build_conversation(
        system_prompt="You are a terse assistant.",
        turns=[("What is 2+2?", "4"), ("And times 10?", "40")],
    )
    for m in convo:
        print(f'{m["role"]:>9}: {m["content"]}')
    print(f"total characters: {total_chars(convo)}")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
from typing import Literal, TypedDictImports two type constructors from the standard library.Literal restricts a value to an exact set of strings. TypedDict describes the shape of a dictionary. No install needed — typing ships with Python.
class Message(TypedDict)Declares that a Message is a dict with exactly the keys role and content.Model APIs take lists of these dicts. Naming the shape once means your editor autocompletes m["content"] and flags m["contnet"] everywhere.
role: Literal["system","user","assistant"]Restricts role to those three strings.Passing "System" or "bot" is a real and annoying bug — the API rejects it at runtime, but your editor rejects it now.
-> MessageDeclares the return type.Callers get autocomplete on the result. Without it, everything downstream is Any and type checking silently stops working.
turns: list[tuple[str, str]]A list of two-string tuples.Built-in generics like list[...] need Python 3.9+; the X | Y union syntax needs 3.10+. This is why 0.5 said 3.11 minimum.
messages: list[Message] = [...]Annotates a local variable.Without the annotation the checker infers list[dict[str, str]] from the first element and later complains about correct code.
sum(len(m["content"]) for m in messages)A generator expression summing content lengths.Characters are a crude proxy for tokens. We replace it with real token counting in Part 4; measuring something now builds the habit.
if __name__ == "__main__":Runs the block only when the file is executed directly, not when imported.Every module in this course keeps a runnable demo without polluting importers.
f'{m["role"]:>9}'An f-string with right-alignment in a 9-character field.Aligned output is much easier to eyeball when you are staring at message traces all day.

Run it

cd second-brain
python backend/app/typing_demo.py

Expected output

   system: You are a terse assistant.
     user: What is 2+2?
assistant: 4

1.3 Pydantic — enforcing shape at runtime

Pydantic is a validation library (MIT, free). You declare a class describing the data you expect; Pydantic parses untrusted input into it and raises a precise error if it does not fit. It is the single most important non-AI library in this course, for one reason: an LLM returns a string, and you need that string to become a trustworthy Python object. Pydantic is the wall between "the model said something" and "my program believes it".

uv pip install "pydantic>=2.7"

Why Pydantic over the alternatives: dataclasses (stdlib) give you structure but do no validation — a str field will happily hold an int. attrs validates but has a smaller ecosystem here. Pydantic v2 has a Rust core (fast), is what FastAPI is built on, and every structured-output feature in the LLM ecosystem — function calling schemas, LangChain output parsers, Instructor — speaks Pydantic. Note that Pydantic v1 and v2 differ substantially; anything you find using .dict() or parse_obj() is v1 and needs translating to .model_dump() and .model_validate().

Define the structured answer we will eventually force a model to produce, and watch validation reject bad data.

"""Pydantic models shared by the whole application."""

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError


class Citation(BaseModel):
    """A pointer back to the source chunk that supported an answer."""
    source: str = Field(description="File name or URL the text came from")
    chunk_id: int = Field(ge=0, description="Index of the chunk within that source")
    quote: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=300)


class Answer(BaseModel):
    """The structured answer we will require from the model in Part 3."""
    answer: str = Field(min_length=1)
    confidence: float = Field(ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    citations: list[Citation] = Field(default_factory=list)

    def is_trustworthy(self) -> bool:
        """Our own rule: confident answers must be backed by at least one source."""
        return self.confidence < 0.7 or len(self.citations) > 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    good_json = """
    {
      "answer": "Ollama serves models on port 11434.",
      "confidence": 0.92,
      "citations": [
        {"source": "setup.md", "chunk_id": 3, "quote": "listens on 127.0.0.1:11434"}
      ]
    }
    """
    parsed = Answer.model_validate_json(good_json)
    print("parsed ok:", parsed.answer)
    print("first source:", parsed.citations[0].source)
    print("trustworthy:", parsed.is_trustworthy())
    print("back to a dict:", parsed.model_dump())

    bad_json = '{"answer": "", "confidence": 1.8, "citations": []}'
    try:
        Answer.model_validate_json(bad_json)
    except ValidationError as exc:
        print("\nrejected, and here is exactly why:")
        for err in exc.errors():
            print(f"  field={err['loc']} problem={err['msg']}")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationErrorImports the base class, the per-field constraint helper, and the exception raised on failure.These three cover 90% of Pydantic usage.
class Citation(BaseModel)Declares a validated data shape.Citations are what make a RAG answer checkable. Modelling them now means the frontend can render them in Part 9 with a matching TypeScript interface.
chunk_id: int = Field(ge=0, ...)Requires an integer ≥ 0.ge = greater-or-equal. A negative chunk index means an upstream bug; better to fail here than to index a list with -3 and silently get the wrong text.
quote: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=300)Bounds the quoted text.Models love to "cite" by pasting an entire chunk. A hard cap keeps the UI usable and the citation honest.
confidence: float = Field(ge=0.0, le=1.0)Constrains to the 0–1 range.Models routinely emit 95 when asked for a 0–1 confidence. This turns that into a caught error rather than a broken progress bar.
citations: list[Citation] = Field(default_factory=list)A list of nested models, defaulting to empty.Nested validation is automatic. default_factory (not = []) avoids the classic shared-mutable-default bug.
def is_trustworthy(self)A plain method on the model.Pydantic models are normal classes. Put small domain rules on them rather than scattering if statements through your routes.
Answer.model_validate_json(...)Parses a JSON string straight into a validated object.This is exactly what you do with an LLM response. (For a dict, use model_validate.) In Pydantic v1 these were parse_raw/parse_obj.
parsed.model_dump()Converts back to a plain dict.What you hand to json.dumps, a database, or FastAPI. v1 called this .dict().
except ValidationError as exc: exc.errors()Gets a structured list of every problem found.In Part 3 we feed these messages back to the model as a repair prompt: "your JSON was invalid because X, try again". That retry loop is why structured output works at all.

Expected output

parsed ok: Ollama serves models on port 11434.
first source: setup.md
trustworthy: True
back to a dict: {'answer': 'Ollama serves models on port 11434.', 'confidence': 0.92, 'citations': [{'source': 'setup.md', 'chunk_id': 3, 'quote': 'listens on 127.0.0.1:11434'}]}

rejected, and here is exactly why:
  field=('answer',) problem=String should have at least 1 character
  field=('confidence',) problem=Input should be less than or equal to 1

Two errors from one call — Pydantic reports every failure, not just the first. That detail matters when the "user" submitting bad data is a 1.7B model that needs telling exactly what to fix.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
AttributeError: 'Answer' object has no attribute 'dict'Following a Pydantic v1 tutorial on a v2 install..dict() → .model_dump(), .json() → .model_dump_json(), parse_obj → model_validate.
ValidationError: Input should be a valid dictionary or instance of CitationYou passed a list of strings where nested models were expected.Each citation must be an object with all three keys. This is the single most common failure when a model generates the JSON.
Model returns JSON wrapped in ```json fences and parsing explodesThe LLM added markdown around the JSON.Strip fences before validating. Part 3 gives the exact helper; do not try to fix it with a clever regex over the whole response.
Try this yourself. Add model_config = {"extra": "forbid"} as the first line inside Answer, then feed it JSON with an extra "mood": "cheerful" key. Without the config Pydantic ignores unknown keys; with it, it rejects them. Decide which behaviour you want when the model invents a field — for tool arguments, forbidding is usually right.

1.4 async / await — because model calls are mostly waiting

A call to an LLM takes 1–30 seconds, almost all of it spent waiting for bytes. If your code blocks during that wait, one slow request freezes your whole server. async lets a single Python process start many waits at once. It does not make anything run in parallel on multiple CPU cores — it makes waiting concurrent, which for our workload is what matters.

Prove that three "model calls" take as long as the slowest one, not the sum, without touching threads.

"""Show the difference between sequential and concurrent waiting."""

import asyncio
import time


async def fake_llm_call(name: str, seconds: float) -> str:
    """Pretend to call a model. asyncio.sleep stands in for network + inference time."""
    print(f"  start  {name}")
    await asyncio.sleep(seconds)
    print(f"  finish {name}")
    return f"{name} answered after {seconds}s"


async def run_sequentially() -> list[str]:
    """Await each call one at a time. Total time = sum of all."""
    results = []
    for name, secs in [("A", 1.0), ("B", 1.5), ("C", 0.5)]:
        results.append(await fake_llm_call(name, secs))
    return results


async def run_concurrently() -> list[str]:
    """Start all calls, then wait for all. Total time = the slowest one."""
    tasks = [
        fake_llm_call("A", 1.0),
        fake_llm_call("B", 1.5),
        fake_llm_call("C", 0.5),
    ]
    return await asyncio.gather(*tasks)


async def main() -> None:
    for label, runner in [("sequential", run_sequentially), ("concurrent", run_concurrently)]:
        print(f"\n--- {label} ---")
        started = time.perf_counter()
        results = await runner()
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started
        for r in results:
            print(f"  {r}")
        print(f"  elapsed: {elapsed:.2f}s")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
import asyncioPython's standard-library event loop.No install. FastAPI, httpx and most modern LLM SDKs are built on it.
import time + time.perf_counter()A high-resolution monotonic clock.Use this, not time.time(), for measuring durations — it cannot jump backwards when the system clock adjusts.
async def fake_llm_call(...)Defines a coroutine function. Calling it returns a coroutine object; it does not run yet.The "does not run yet" part is what confuses everyone. Nothing happens until you await it or hand it to the loop.
await asyncio.sleep(seconds)Yields control back to the event loop for that long.This is the stand-in for a network wait. Crucially, time.sleep() here would block the entire loop and destroy the effect.
results.append(await fake_llm_call(...))Awaits inside a loop — one finishes before the next starts.The trap. This is async code with zero concurrency, and it is the most common performance bug in LLM backends.
asyncio.gather(*tasks)Schedules every coroutine on the loop and waits for all of them.Results come back in the order you passed them in, regardless of finish order — which matters when you fan out to several retrievers or agents.
asyncio.run(main())Creates an event loop, runs main, closes the loop.The one place a synchronous program crosses into async. In a FastAPI app the framework does this for you and you never call it.

Expected output

--- sequential ---
  start  A
  finish A
  start  B
  finish B
  start  C
  finish C
  A answered after 1.0s
  B answered after 1.5s
  C answered after 0.5s
  elapsed: 3.00s

--- concurrent ---
  start  A
  start  B
  start  C
  finish C
  finish A
  finish B
  A answered after 1.0s
  B answered after 1.5s
  C answered after 0.5s
  elapsed: 1.50s

Read the interleaving: all three start before any finishes, C finishes first because it is shortest, and the results still come back in A-B-C order. 3.00s → 1.50s for free. In Part 5 those three calls become "embed the query, run BM25 keyword search, run vector search" — and this is why the retriever feels instant.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
SyntaxError: 'await' outside async functionUsing await in a normal def.await is only legal inside async def. From sync code, use asyncio.run(...).
RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'fake_llm_call' was never awaitedYou called the function and threw the coroutine away.Add await, or pass it to gather. Nothing ran — this warning means your code silently did nothing.
Concurrent version is as slow as sequentialA blocking call inside the coroutine — time.sleep, requests.get, or heavy CPU work.Use async-native libraries (httpx.AsyncClient instead of requests), or push blocking work to asyncio.to_thread(...).
RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loopCalling asyncio.run inside Jupyter or inside FastAPI.In a notebook, just await main(). In FastAPI, make the route async def and await directly.
Try this yourself. Swap await asyncio.sleep(seconds) for time.sleep(seconds) and rerun. The concurrent version will take 3.00s too. That single character difference is the entire lesson: async only helps if everything in the chain is non-blocking.
Deeper dive: when NOT to use async

Async has a real cost: every library in the call chain has to cooperate, error handling gets subtler, and debugging stack traces are worse. Use sync code for scripts, notebooks, ingestion pipelines, and anything CPU-bound (embedding a thousand chunks is CPU work — threads or processes help there, async does not). Use async for the API layer, where many users wait on many model calls at once. Our capstone is sync for M1–M14 and async from M15, when FastAPI arrives. That is deliberate: adding async before you need it makes every earlier milestone harder to debug for no gain.

1.5 .env, secrets, and config that does not leak

Even in a local-first course you will eventually hold a Groq or Google AI Studio key. The rule is absolute: keys never appear in source code. Not in a variable, not in a comment, not "just for now". Public repos are scraped for keys within minutes of a push.

We use pydantic-settings — the Pydantic companion library that reads environment variables and validates them into a typed object. It beats bare os.getenv because a missing or malformed setting fails loudly at startup instead of producing None that explodes three layers deeper.

uv pip install pydantic-settings

Create a settings object every other module imports, backed by a .env file that git will never see.

OLLAMA_HOST=http://localhost:11434
CHAT_MODEL=qwen3:1.7b
EMBED_MODEL=nomic-embed-text
GROQ_API_KEY=
LOG_LEVEL=INFO
OLLAMA_HOST=http://localhost:11434
CHAT_MODEL=qwen3:1.7b
EMBED_MODEL=nomic-embed-text
GROQ_API_KEY=gsk_replace_me_or_leave_blank
LOG_LEVEL=INFO
"""Application settings, loaded once from the environment and validated."""

from functools import lru_cache

from pydantic import Field
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    """Every knob the app has. Values come from .env or real env vars."""

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        env_file=".env",
        env_file_encoding="utf-8",
        extra="ignore",
    )

    ollama_host: str = "http://localhost:11434"
    chat_model: str = "qwen3:1.7b"
    embed_model: str = "nomic-embed-text"
    groq_api_key: str | None = None
    log_level: str = Field(default="INFO", pattern="^(DEBUG|INFO|WARNING|ERROR)$")

    @property
    def has_hosted_fallback(self) -> bool:
        """True when a hosted free-tier key is available as a faster alternative."""
        return bool(self.groq_api_key)


@lru_cache
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    """Return the one shared Settings instance."""
    return Settings()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    s = get_settings()
    print("ollama host      :", s.ollama_host)
    print("chat model       :", s.chat_model)
    print("hosted fallback  :", s.has_hosted_fallback)
    print("key in memory?   :", "yes" if s.groq_api_key else "no")
    print("same object twice:", get_settings() is get_settings())
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
from functools import lru_cacheStandard-library memoisation decorator.Caches the result of a zero-argument function, giving us a singleton without a global variable.
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettingsPydantic's environment-aware base class.It reads env vars by field name, case-insensitively: the field chat_model is filled from CHAT_MODEL.
env_file=".env"Also loads that file if present.Real environment variables still win, so the same code works locally (.env) and in Docker (real env vars) with no changes.
extra="ignore"Ignores env vars that do not match a field.Your shell has hundreds of unrelated variables. Without this, startup fails on PATH.
groq_api_key: str | None = NoneAn optional string, defaulting to nothing.The whole app must run with no key at all. The X | None syntax needs Python 3.10+.
Field(default="INFO", pattern="^(DEBUG|INFO|WARNING|ERROR)$")Validates the value against a regular expression.A typo like LOG_LEVEL=INFOO fails at startup with a clear message instead of silently disabling your logs.
@property def has_hosted_fallbackA computed, read-only attribute.Lets the rest of the code ask "can I use the fast path?" instead of testing for a key everywhere.
@lru_cache def get_settings()Builds Settings once and returns the same object thereafter.Re-reading and re-validating the file on every request is wasteful. It also gives FastAPI a clean dependency to override in tests (Part 10).
"yes" if s.groq_api_key else "no"Prints presence, never the value.Log lines end up in terminals, screenshots, and CI output. Never print a secret, even yours.
