4.2 Backend A — Ollama (local, free, no account)

The default for this course. Free (MIT), unlimited, offline, and it applies the correct chat template for whichever model you pulled.

Implement the ChatBackend interface against Ollama's HTTP API, reporting real token counts from the response.

"""ChatBackend implementation for a local Ollama server."""

import json
import time
from typing import Iterator

import requests

from app.config import get_settings
from app.llm import ChatResult

# Our common option names, mapped to Ollama's names.
OPTION_MAP = {
    "max_tokens": "num_predict",
    "temperature": "temperature",
    "top_p": "top_p",
    "top_k": "top_k",
    "stop": "stop",
    "seed": "seed",
    "context_length": "num_ctx",
}


def translate_options(options: dict) -> dict:
    """Convert our vocabulary into Ollama's."""
    out = {}
    for key, value in options.items():
        if key in OPTION_MAP and value is not None:
            out[OPTION_MAP[key]] = value
    return out


class OllamaBackend:
    """Talks to Ollama's /api/chat endpoint."""

    name = "ollama"

    def __init__(self, model: str | None = None, timeout: float = 180.0) -> None:
        settings = get_settings()
        self.host = settings.ollama_host.rstrip("/")
        self.model = model or settings.chat_model
        self.timeout = timeout

    def _body(self, messages: list[dict], stream: bool, options: dict) -> dict:
        return {
            "model": self.model,
            "messages": messages,
            "stream": stream,
            "options": translate_options(options),
        }

    def chat(self, messages: list[dict], **options) -> ChatResult:
        started = time.perf_counter()
        response = requests.post(
            f"{self.host}/api/chat",
            json=self._body(messages, False, options),
            timeout=self.timeout,
        )
        response.raise_for_status()
        data = response.json()
        return ChatResult(
            text=data["message"]["content"],
            model=self.model,
            prompt_tokens=data.get("prompt_eval_count", 0),
            completion_tokens=data.get("eval_count", 0),
            seconds=time.perf_counter() - started,
        )

    def stream(self, messages: list[dict], **options) -> Iterator[str]:
        with requests.post(
            f"{self.host}/api/chat",
            json=self._body(messages, True, options),
            stream=True,
            timeout=self.timeout,
        ) as response:
            response.raise_for_status()
            for line in response.iter_lines():
                if not line:
                    continue
                event = json.loads(line)
                if "error" in event:
                    raise RuntimeError(event["error"])
                fragment = event.get("message", {}).get("content", "")
                if fragment:
                    yield fragment
                if event.get("done"):
                    break


if __name__ == "__main__":
    backend = OllamaBackend()
    result = backend.chat(
        [{"role": "user", "content": "Name the capital of Japan in one word."}],
        temperature=0.0,
        max_tokens=20,
    )
    print(f"model  : {result.model}")
    print(f"text   : {result.text.strip()}")
    print(f"tokens : {result.prompt_tokens} in / {result.completion_tokens} out")
    print(f"time   : {result.seconds:.2f}s  ({result.tokens_per_second:.1f} tok/s)")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
OPTION_MAPMaps our common names to Ollama's.The whole point of the abstraction. Callers say max_tokens everywhere; only this dict knows Ollama calls it num_predict.
if key in OPTION_MAP and value is not NoneDrops unknown and unset options.Silently ignoring a typo'd option is bad, but so is forwarding None and getting a 400. In production you would log unknown keys rather than dropping them silently.
settings.ollama_host.rstrip("/")Strips a trailing slash.A .env value of http://localhost:11434/ would otherwise produce //api/chat. Small, real, and annoying to debug.
model or settings.chat_modelConstructor override, config default.Lets the router in Part 6 instantiate a cheap small model and an expensive large one from the same class.
_body() shared by both methodsOne place builds the payload.Streaming and non-streaming differing by one boolean is the kind of duplication that drifts. The leading underscore marks it private by convention.
data.get("prompt_eval_count", 0)Reads the real input token count.This is ground truth for your model's tokenizer, far better than any estimate. It is absent on some code paths, so default it.
time.perf_counter() around the callMeasures wall-clock duration.Ollama also reports total_duration, but measuring client-side captures network and serialisation too — which is what your user experiences.
with requests.post(..., stream=True)Streaming inside a context manager.As in M2: abandoning the generator closes the socket, which is how cancellation works.

Expected output

model  : qwen3:1.7b
text   : Tokyo
tokens : 21 in / 2 out
time   : 0.63s  (3.2 tok/s)

The tok/s figure is misleading on short answers — two tokens in 0.63 seconds mostly measures model load and prompt processing, not generation speed. Judge throughput on responses of 100+ tokens.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'app.backends'Missing backends/__init__.py.Create the empty file. Section 4.4 fills it with the factory.
prompt_tokens is always 0Older Ollama, or a field name change.Print the whole data dict and look. Field names have shifted before; the .get(..., 0) default keeps you running while you check the API docs.
Options appear to have no effectThey landed at the top level instead of inside "options".Print self._body(...) and check the nesting. This is the single most common Ollama mistake.
Try this yourself. Pass frequency_penalty=0.5. It is silently dropped, because it is not in OPTION_MAP. Now add a logging.warning in the else branch for unknown keys. Decide which behaviour you want — silently permissive is fine for a course, and a liability in production.

4.3 Backend B — Hugging Face transformers (local, in-process)

Same machine, completely different mechanism. Instead of an HTTP server holding the model, the model loads into your Python process. You get direct access to logits, tokenizers, and every knob — which is what you need for fine-tuning (Part 8) and for anything research-shaped. You also get a much heavier install and manual chat templating.

Ollamatransformers
Install size~1 GB app2–3 GB of PyTorch and friends
Model formatGGUF, quantised, curatedAny model on the Hub, usually fp16/bf16
Chat templateApplied for youYou must apply it
QuantisationBuilt inExtra libraries (bitsandbytes) and configuration
Access to internalsNoneTotal — logits, attention weights, embeddings
Use it forEverything in this course by defaultFine-tuning, embeddings, rerankers, research

Run the same task in-process, applying the model's own chat template correctly.

# CPU-only machines: install the CPU build of torch first, it is far smaller.
# Follow the selector at https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/ for your platform.
uv pip install "transformers>=4.44" torch
"""ChatBackend implementation using Hugging Face transformers in-process."""

import time
from typing import Iterator

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TextIteratorStreamer

from app.llm import ChatResult

DEFAULT_MODEL = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"   # ~1 GB download, Apache-2.0


class TransformersBackend:
    """Loads a model into this process. First call is slow; later ones are not."""

    name = "transformers"

    def __init__(self, model_id: str = DEFAULT_MODEL) -> None:
        self.model_id = model_id
        self.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
        self.model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
            model_id,
            dtype="auto",
            device_map="auto",
        )
        self.model.eval()

    def _prepare(self, messages: list[dict]):
        """Apply the model's chat template and move tensors to its device."""
        text = self.tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
            messages,
            tokenize=False,
            add_generation_prompt=True,
        )
        return self.tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt").to(self.model.device)

    def _generation_kwargs(self, options: dict) -> dict:
        temperature = options.get("temperature", 0.7)
        kwargs = {
            "max_new_tokens": options.get("max_tokens", 200),
            "pad_token_id": self.tokenizer.eos_token_id,
        }
        if temperature and temperature > 0:
            kwargs.update({"do_sample": True, "temperature": temperature,
                           "top_p": options.get("top_p", 0.95)})
        else:
            kwargs["do_sample"] = False
        return kwargs

    def chat(self, messages: list[dict], **options) -> ChatResult:
        inputs = self._prepare(messages)
        prompt_length = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

        started = time.perf_counter()
        with torch.no_grad():
            output = self.model.generate(**inputs, **self._generation_kwargs(options))
        seconds = time.perf_counter() - started

        new_token_ids = output[0][prompt_length:]
        text = self.tokenizer.decode(new_token_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
        return ChatResult(
            text=text,
            model=self.model_id,
            prompt_tokens=int(prompt_length),
            completion_tokens=int(new_token_ids.shape[-1]),
            seconds=seconds,
        )

    def stream(self, messages: list[dict], **options) -> Iterator[str]:
        from threading import Thread

        inputs = self._prepare(messages)
        streamer = TextIteratorStreamer(
            self.tokenizer, skip_prompt=True, skip_special_tokens=True
        )
        kwargs = {**inputs, **self._generation_kwargs(options), "streamer": streamer}
        thread = Thread(target=self.model.generate, kwargs=kwargs)
        thread.start()
        for fragment in streamer:
            yield fragment
        thread.join()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("loading model (first run downloads it)...")
    backend = TransformersBackend()
    print(f"device: {backend.model.device}")

    print("\n--- chat ---")
    result = backend.chat(
        [{"role": "user", "content": "Name the capital of Japan in one word."}],
        temperature=0.0,
        max_tokens=20,
    )
    print(f"text   : {result.text.strip()}")
    print(f"tokens : {result.prompt_tokens} in / {result.completion_tokens} out")
    print(f"time   : {result.seconds:.2f}s")

    print("\n--- stream ---")
    for fragment in backend.stream(
        [{"role": "user", "content": "Count from one to five."}], max_tokens=40
    ):
        print(fragment, end="", flush=True)
    print()
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
import torchPyTorch, the tensor and autograd library (BSD, free).transformers is a model zoo built on it. Needed here for no_grad and device handling.
AutoTokenizer / AutoModelForCausalLMFactory classes that pick the right implementation from the model's config."CausalLM" means decoder-only next-token prediction — section 2.4's architecture. Using AutoModel instead would give you hidden states with no output head, a classic confusing mistake.
DEFAULT_MODEL = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"A genuinely small instruct model.Fits an 8 GB machine in fp16 with room to spare, and downloads in a minute. Newer small models exist (Qwen 3 0.6B among them); check the Hub for what is current.
dtype="auto"Picks the precision recorded in the model's config.Loads in bf16/fp16 rather than upcasting to fp32, halving memory. Verify this keyword against your version — this argument was named torch_dtype for years and was renamed; if you get a warning or a TypeError, check the current docs for which your install expects.
device_map="auto"Places layers on GPU, then CPU as needed.Does the CPU/GPU split from section 0.8 automatically. Requires accelerate, which transformers usually pulls in.
self.model.eval()Switches off training-time behaviour like dropout.Inference-only. Forgetting it adds noise to your outputs for no reason.
apply_chat_template(..., add_generation_prompt=True)Renders the message list into the model's exact expected string.The most important line in this file. Section 3.2's flat string, generated correctly for whatever model you loaded. add_generation_prompt=True appends the trailing assistant header so the model knows to speak. Skip this and quality collapses in a way that looks like a bad model.
.to(self.model.device)Moves input tensors to the model's device.Otherwise: RuntimeError: Expected all tensors to be on the same device. The single most common PyTorch error.
if temperature and temperature > 0Chooses sampling or greedy.transformers warns if you pass temperature with do_sample=False, and silently ignores it. Section 1.7's distinction, enforced.
pad_token_id=self.tokenizer.eos_token_idSupplies a padding token.Many decoder-only models define no pad token, producing a warning on every call. Setting it to EOS is the conventional fix.
with torch.no_grad()Disables gradient tracking.Gradients are only needed for training. Skipping them cuts memory use substantially and speeds generation up.
output[0][prompt_length:]Slices off the prompt.generate returns prompt + completion. Without this slice you print the user's own question back at them — a very common bug.
TextIteratorStreamer + ThreadStreams by running generate on a background thread and iterating a queue.model.generate is blocking, so this is the standard pattern for streaming from transformers. skip_prompt=True avoids re-emitting the input.
thread.join()Waits for the generation thread after the stream ends.Without it, exceptions raised inside generate vanish and you leak threads.

Expected output

loading model (first run downloads it)...
device: cpu

--- chat ---
text   : Tokyo
tokens : 34 in / 2 out
time   : 0.71s

--- stream ---
One, two, three, four, five.

Note the input token count is higher than Ollama reported for the same message (34 vs 21) — different tokenizer, different chat template, more special tokens. Token counts are not portable between models, which is why section 4.7 measures rather than estimates.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
ValueError: Cannot use chat template functions because tokenizer.chat_template is not setYou loaded a base model, which has no chat template.Use an -Instruct model. Section 2.5's base-vs-instruct distinction, showing up as an exception.
RuntimeError: Expected all tensors to be on the same deviceMissing .to(model.device).Move the inputs. With device_map="auto" the model may not be on the device you assume.
TypeError: got an unexpected keyword argument 'dtype'Version mismatch on that renamed argument.Use torch_dtype="auto" instead, or upgrade. Check the docs rather than guessing.
Killed / out of memory on loadfp16 weights need roughly 2 bytes per parameter, with no quantisation.Use a smaller model, or install bitsandbytes and load in 4-bit. Or use Ollama, which quantises by default — this is exactly why we default to it.
Output repeats the questionForgot to slice off the prompt.output[0][prompt_length:].
Streaming prints nothing until the endMissing flush=True, or the streamer was not passed into generate.Both are required.
Try this yourself. Print the template output directly: print(backend.tokenizer.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)). That is the ground-truth version of the string I approximated in section 3.2 — for your model, with its real special tokens. Compare the two.

4.4 Backend C — free-tier hosted APIs

When your local model is too slow or too small, a hosted free tier gives you a 70B-class model at 200+ tokens/sec for no money. The trade: rate limits, an internet dependency, and — on most free tiers — your prompts may be used to improve the provider's products.

These numbers move constantly and sources disagree. I checked several independent trackers while writing this and found genuine contradictions, particularly on daily request caps. Treat the table as "the right order of magnitude, September 2026" and read the provider's own limits page before you depend on any figure. Each row links to it.

ProviderCard needed?Free limits (approximate)Data policyCheck here
GroqNo~30 requests/min, ~6,000 tokens/min, daily request cap varies by model (sources report anywhere from ~1,000 to ~14,400). Limits are per organisation, so extra API keys do not multiply them. Cached prompt tokens reportedly do not count toward limits.Check current terms.console.groq.com/settings/limits shows your actual limits — the only number that matters.
Google AI StudioNoVaries sharply by model and has been cut more than once. Flash-class models get the workable allowance; Pro-class models are effectively trial-only on free. Limits are per Google Cloud project, not per key; daily quotas reset at midnight Pacific.Free-tier prompts may be used to improve their products. Do not send private documents.ai.google.dev rate limits
OpenRouterNo20 requests/min on any model ID ending :free, and ~50 requests/day on an account that has never bought credits. (The widely-quoted 1,000/day requires a one-off $10 purchase, so it is not free.) Which models are free rotates without notice.Per-model; check the provider behind each free model.openrouter.ai docs · free model list
Hugging Face InferenceNoA small monthly credit allowance rather than a rate limit. This has been restructured repeatedly — the shape of the offer, not just the numbers, has changed.Check current terms.HF Inference Providers docs

One backend covers most of them

Groq, OpenRouter, Hugging Face's router, vLLM, LM Studio and (via a compatibility endpoint) Google all speak the OpenAI chat-completions shape: POST /chat/completions with a messages array, returning choices[0].message.content and a usage object. So one class with a configurable base_url talks to all of them.

Implement a backend for any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with SSE streaming and real usage accounting.

LLM_BACKEND=ollama                 # ollama | transformers | groq | openrouter | echo
GROQ_API_KEY=
GROQ_MODEL=llama-3.1-8b-instant
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=
OPENROUTER_MODEL=
"""ChatBackend for any OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint."""

import json
import time
from typing import Iterator

import requests

from app.llm import ChatResult

# base_url values, verified against each provider's docs before use.
PROVIDERS = {
    "groq": "https://api.groq.com/openai/v1",
    "openrouter": "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1",
}


class OpenAICompatBackend:
    """Works with Groq, OpenRouter, vLLM, LM Studio and similar."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        base_url: str,
        api_key: str,
        model: str,
        name: str = "openai-compat",
        timeout: float = 120.0,
    ) -> None:
        if not api_key:
            raise ValueError(f"{name}: no API key. Set it in .env, never in code.")
        self.base_url = base_url.rstrip("/")
        self.api_key = api_key
        self.model = model
        self.name = name
        self.timeout = timeout

    def _headers(self) -> dict:
        return {
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {self.api_key}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        }

    def _body(self, messages: list[dict], stream: bool, options: dict) -> dict:
        body = {
            "model": self.model,
            "messages": messages,
            "stream": stream,
            "max_tokens": options.get("max_tokens", 512),
        }
        for key in ("temperature", "top_p", "stop", "seed"):
            if options.get(key) is not None:
                body[key] = options[key]
        return body

    def chat(self, messages: list[dict], **options) -> ChatResult:
        started = time.perf_counter()
        response = requests.post(
            f"{self.base_url}/chat/completions",
            headers=self._headers(),
            json=self._body(messages, False, options),
            timeout=self.timeout,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"{self.name} rate limit hit. "
                f"retry-after={response.headers.get('retry-after')}"
            )
        response.raise_for_status()
        data = response.json()
        usage = data.get("usage") or {}
        return ChatResult(
            text=data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"],
            model=data.get("model", self.model),
            prompt_tokens=usage.get("prompt_tokens", 0),
            completion_tokens=usage.get("completion_tokens", 0),
            seconds=time.perf_counter() - started,
        )

    def stream(self, messages: list[dict], **options) -> Iterator[str]:
        with requests.post(
            f"{self.base_url}/chat/completions",
            headers=self._headers(),
            json=self._body(messages, True, options),
            stream=True,
            timeout=self.timeout,
        ) as response:
            response.raise_for_status()
            for raw in response.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True):
                if not raw or not raw.startswith("data:"):
                    continue
                payload = raw[len("data:"):].strip()
                if payload == "[DONE]":
                    break
                event = json.loads(payload)
                choices = event.get("choices") or []
                if not choices:
                    continue
                fragment = choices[0].get("delta", {}).get("content")
                if fragment:
                    yield fragment


if __name__ == "__main__":
    from app.config import get_settings

    settings = get_settings()
    if not settings.groq_api_key:
        print("no GROQ_API_KEY in .env — skipping. Get a free key at console.groq.com")
        raise SystemExit(0)

    backend = OpenAICompatBackend(
        base_url=PROVIDERS["groq"],
        api_key=settings.groq_api_key,
        model="llama-3.1-8b-instant",
        name="groq",
    )
    result = backend.chat(
        [{"role": "user", "content": "Name the capital of Japan in one word."}],
        temperature=0.0,
        max_tokens=20,
    )
    print(f"provider: {backend.name}  model: {result.model}")
    print(f"text    : {result.text.strip()}")
    print(f"tokens  : {result.prompt_tokens} in / {result.completion_tokens} out")
    print(f"time    : {result.seconds:.2f}s  ({result.tokens_per_second:.0f} tok/s)")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
PROVIDERS dict of base URLsNames the endpoints we support.Base URLs do change. Keeping them in one dict means one edit, and it documents which providers you have actually tested.
if not api_key: raise ValueErrorFails at construction, not at first call.An empty key produces a 401 from deep inside a request. Failing in the constructor points at the real problem: your .env.
f"Bearer {self.api_key}"Standard bearer-token auth.Nearly universal. Note the key is never logged or printed anywhere in this file — deliberate.
"max_tokens" rather than num_predictOpenAI's parameter name.Our common vocabulary happens to match here. The OPTION_MAP pattern from 4.2 would be needed if it did not.
the for key in (...) loopForwards only options that were set.Some providers reject null values, and some reject unknown keys outright. Sending only what you mean avoids both.
if response.status_code == 429Special-cases the rate limit and surfaces retry-after.429 is the error you will actually hit on a free tier. Section 4.6 turns this into an automatic retry; for now, an informative failure.
usage = data.get("usage") or {}Defensive: some providers omit usage when streaming or on error.or {} also handles an explicit null, which .get("usage", {}) would not.
data.get("model", self.model)Records what the provider says it used.Routers and aliases mean you do not always get the model you asked for. Log the returned value, not the requested one.
raw.startswith("data:")Parses SSE (Server-Sent Events).Different from Ollama's NDJSON: each event is a line prefixed data:, with blank lines and comment lines between. Skipping non-data: lines is required, not optional.
if payload == "[DONE]": breakThe sentinel that ends an OpenAI-style stream.It is the literal string [DONE], not JSON. json.loads on it raises — this is the first bug everyone writes.
choices[0].get("delta", {}).get("content")Extracts the incremental fragment.Streaming events carry delta, not message. The final event has an empty delta and a finish_reason.
iter_lines(decode_unicode=True)Yields str rather than bytes.Lets us compare against "data:" without decoding by hand.
raise SystemExit(0) when no keyExits cleanly rather than crashing.The whole course must run with no keys at all. A missing optional key is not an error.

Expected output

provider: groq  model: llama-3.1-8b-instant
text    : Tokyo
tokens  : 45 in / 3 out
time    : 0.21s  (14 tok/s)

# ...or, with no key:
no GROQ_API_KEY in .env — skipping. Get a free key at console.groq.com

The factory that ties all three together

Choose a backend from configuration, so the rest of the app never names a provider.

"""Backend selection. Everything else imports get_backend() and nothing more."""

from functools import lru_cache

from app.config import get_settings
from app.llm import ChatBackend, EchoBackend


@lru_cache
def get_backend(kind: str | None = None) -> ChatBackend:
    """Build the configured backend once and reuse it."""
    settings = get_settings()
    kind = (kind or settings.llm_backend).lower()

    if kind == "echo":
        return EchoBackend()

    if kind == "ollama":
        from app.backends.ollama_backend import OllamaBackend
        return OllamaBackend()

    if kind == "transformers":
        from app.backends.hf_backend import TransformersBackend
        return TransformersBackend()

    if kind in {"groq", "openrouter"}:
        from app.backends.openai_compat import PROVIDERS, OpenAICompatBackend
        key = settings.groq_api_key if kind == "groq" else settings.openrouter_api_key
        model = settings.groq_model if kind == "groq" else settings.openrouter_model
        return OpenAICompatBackend(
            base_url=PROVIDERS[kind], api_key=key or "", model=model, name=kind
        )

    raise ValueError(
        f"unknown LLM_BACKEND {kind!r}. "
        "Valid: echo, ollama, transformers, groq, openrouter"
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    backend = get_backend()
    print(f"configured backend: {backend.name}")
    result = backend.chat(
        [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with one word: pong"}],
        temperature=0.0,
        max_tokens=10,
    )
    print(f"reply: {result.text.strip()!r}")
    print(f"same instance on second call: {get_backend() is backend}")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
@lru_cacheBuilds each backend once per process.Critical for TransformersBackend, which loads gigabytes on construction. Rebuilding it per request would be catastrophic.
imports inside the branchesLazy importing.So a machine with no PyTorch installed can still run the Ollama backend. A top-level import torch would make the heaviest dependency mandatory for everyone.
kind or settings.llm_backendArgument overrides config.Lets tests request get_backend("echo") explicitly while production reads .env.
-> ChatBackendReturns the Protocol type.Callers get autocomplete for chat and stream and cannot accidentally depend on a provider-specific method.
raise ValueError listing valid valuesHelpful failure on a typo.LLM_BACKEND=olama is a five-second fix if the error says so, and a twenty-minute one if it says KeyError.

Expected output

configured backend: ollama
reply: 'pong'
same instance on second call: True

You will need to add three fields to Settings in config.py for this: llm_backend: str = "ollama", groq_model: str = "llama-3.1-8b-instant", openrouter_api_key: str | None = None and openrouter_model: str = "". Same pattern as section 1.5.

Try this yourself. Run LLM_BACKEND=echo PYTHONPATH=backend python -m app.backends. It answers instantly with no model at all. Now imagine writing the Angular frontend in Part 9 against that — no GPU spinning, no waiting, perfectly reproducible responses. That is why the echo backend exists.
Deeper dive: Google AI Studio, which is the odd one out

Google's native API is a different shape: POST /v1beta/models/{model}:generateContent with contents and parts instead of messages, and system instructions in a separate field. Two ways to use it:

  • Their OpenAI-compatibility endpoint, which lets you point the class above at a Google base URL. It exists but has had gaps in feature coverage; verify streaming and tool calling work for your case before building on it.
  • The official google-genai Python package, which is the supported path.

Either way, treat the model name as volatile: Google's naming has moved quickly and hardcoded model IDs are the most common source of sudden 404s. List available models via the API at startup, or read the models page and pin something current.

4.5 Async streaming with httpx

Everything so far is synchronous, which is right for scripts. FastAPI in Part 10 is async, and mixing a blocking requests call into an async route blocks the entire event loop — section 1.4's failure mode, at production scale.

httpx (BSD, free) is the async-capable HTTP client with a requests-shaped API. It is what you want for streaming inside a web server, and it is FastAPI's usual companion.

uv pip install httpx

Stream from Ollama without blocking the event loop, and prove concurrency by streaming two prompts at once.

"""Async streaming from Ollama, suitable for use inside FastAPI."""

import asyncio
import json
import time
from typing import AsyncIterator

import httpx

from app.config import get_settings


async def astream_chat(
    messages: list[dict],
    model: str | None = None,
    timeout: float = 180.0,
    **options,
) -> AsyncIterator[str]:
    """Yield text fragments as they arrive, without blocking the event loop."""
    settings = get_settings()
    body = {
        "model": model or settings.chat_model,
        "messages": messages,
        "stream": True,
        "options": {"num_predict": options.get("max_tokens", 300),
                    "temperature": options.get("temperature", 0.3)},
    }

    limits = httpx.Timeout(timeout, connect=10.0)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=limits) as client:
        async with client.stream(
            "POST", f"{settings.ollama_host}/api/chat", json=body
        ) as response:
            response.raise_for_status()
            async for line in response.aiter_lines():
                if not line:
                    continue
                event = json.loads(line)
                if "error" in event:
                    raise RuntimeError(event["error"])
                fragment = event.get("message", {}).get("content", "")
                if fragment:
                    yield fragment
                if event.get("done"):
                    break


async def collect(label: str, question: str) -> tuple[str, float, int]:
    """Consume one stream, returning the label, its TTFT, and a fragment count."""
    started = time.perf_counter()
    ttft = None
    fragments = 0
    async for _ in astream_chat([{"role": "user", "content": question}], max_tokens=120):
        if ttft is None:
            ttft = time.perf_counter() - started
        fragments += 1
    return label, ttft or 0.0, fragments


async def main() -> None:
    print("--- one stream, printed live ---")
    async for fragment in astream_chat(
        [{"role": "user", "content": "In one sentence: what is a KV cache?"}]
    ):
        print(fragment, end="", flush=True)
    print("\n")

    print("--- two streams concurrently ---")
    started = time.perf_counter()
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        collect("A", "In one sentence: what is tokenization?"),
        collect("B", "In one sentence: what is an embedding?"),
    )
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started
    for label, ttft, fragments in results:
        print(f"  stream {label}: ttft {ttft:.2f}s, {fragments} fragments")
    print(f"  wall clock for both: {elapsed:.2f}s")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
AsyncIterator[str]Types an async generator.A function with both async def and yield is an async generator, consumed with async for. This is the exact shape FastAPI's streaming response wants in Part 10.
httpx.Timeout(timeout, connect=10.0)Separate connect and read timeouts.Connecting should take milliseconds; generating can take minutes. One combined number forces you to choose between failing slowly on a dead host and killing legitimate long generations.
async with httpx.AsyncClient(...)Creates and closes a client.In real FastAPI code you create one client for the app's lifetime and reuse it — per-request clients throw away connection pooling. Shown per-call here for a self-contained script; Part 10 fixes it.
client.stream("POST", ...)httpx's streaming request form.Note the method is a positional argument, unlike requests.post. Small API difference that catches everyone once.
async for line in response.aiter_lines()Asynchronously iterates lines.Each await point releases the event loop, so other requests progress while this one waits for the next token. That is the whole reason for this file.
async for _ in astream_chat(...)Consumes the stream, discarding fragments.We only want the timing here. The underscore signals the value is deliberately unused.
asyncio.gather(collect(...), collect(...))Runs two streams concurrently.Section 1.4's demonstration, now with real model calls. Note both streams share one Ollama server, so throughput is split — concurrency here buys request handling, not raw speed.
ttft or 0.0Handles a stream that produced nothing.Prevents a None from reaching the format string and crashing the report.

Expected output

--- one stream, printed live ---
A KV cache stores the key and value vectors for tokens already processed, so the
model does not recompute them for every new token.

--- two streams concurrently ---
  stream A: ttft 0.58s, 41 fragments
  stream B: ttft 0.61s, 38 fragments
  wall clock for both: 9.12s

Read that result honestly. Two concurrent streams did not halve the total time, because a single Ollama instance processes them roughly serially — one model, one set of weights, limited batching. Async gives you non-blocking request handling, so 50 users can each have their own stream without one blocking the others. It does not multiply your GPU. Real throughput scaling needs a batching server like vLLM (Part 7).

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loopRunning this inside Jupyter or FastAPI.In a notebook just await main(). In FastAPI make the route async def and await directly.
httpx.ReadTimeout on a long generationThe read timeout is shorter than the gap between tokens.Raise the read timeout, or pass httpx.Timeout(None, connect=10.0) to disable it for streams — but then you must enforce a cap another way.
TypeError: 'async_generator' object is not iterableUsed for instead of async for.Async generators need async for, inside an async def.
Streams do not overlap at allA blocking call sneaked in, or the server is fully serialising them.Check nothing uses requests or time.sleep. Then accept the note above: one Ollama instance is one worker.
Try this yourself. Wrap the async for in asyncio.wait_for(..., timeout=2.0) and catch asyncio.TimeoutError. The stream is cancelled, httpx closes the connection, and Ollama stops generating. You have just built the server-side half of Part 9's cancel button.

4.6 Retries, timeouts, and rate limits

Model APIs fail. Free tiers fail more. The failures you must handle: a 429 rate limit, a 503 while the provider reloads a model, a connection reset, and a request that simply never returns.

The rules, before the code

RuleWhy
Always set a timeout.The default in most clients is "wait forever". A hung request holds a worker and a socket indefinitely.
Only retry idempotent, retryable failures.Retrying a 400 (your payload is malformed) just wastes quota. Retrying a 401 (bad key) does too. Retry 429, 5xx, and connection errors.
Use exponential backoff with jitter.Doubling the wait gives the server room to recover. Jitter — randomising the delay — stops many clients retrying in lockstep and hammering the server in synchronised waves.
Honour Retry-After.When the server tells you how long to wait, your clever backoff maths is not better than that instruction.
Cap the attempts and the total time.Infinite retries turn a provider outage into your outage, with a user watching a spinner for ten minutes.

Build the retry decorator the whole application will use, and inspect the delays it produces without waiting for them.

"""Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, for flaky model APIs."""

import random
import time

RETRYABLE_STATUS = {408, 409, 425, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504}


def backoff_delay(attempt: int, base: float = 0.5, cap: float = 30.0,
                  rng: random.Random | None = None) -> float:
    """Full-jitter exponential backoff: a random point between 0 and the capped ceiling."""
    rng = rng or random
    ceiling = min(cap, base * (2 ** (attempt - 1)))
    return rng.uniform(0, ceiling)


def retry_after_seconds(headers: dict) -> float | None:
    """Honour the server's Retry-After header when it sends one."""
    value = headers.get("retry-after") or headers.get("Retry-After")
    if value is None:
        return None
    try:
        return float(value)
    except ValueError:
        return None


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = random.Random(42)
    print("full-jitter delays for 6 attempts (base 0.5s, cap 30s):")
    for attempt in range(1, 7):
        ceiling = min(30.0, 0.5 * (2 ** (attempt - 1)))
        delay = backoff_delay(attempt, rng=rng)
        print(f"  attempt {attempt}: ceiling {ceiling:5.1f}s  ->  slept {delay:5.2f}s")

    print("\nheader handling:")
    print("  {'retry-after': '12'}  ->", retry_after_seconds({"retry-after": "12"}))
    print("  {}                     ->", retry_after_seconds({}))
    print("  {'retry-after': 'Wed'} ->", retry_after_seconds({"retry-after": "Wed"}))

    print(f"\n429 retryable? {429 in RETRYABLE_STATUS}")
    print(f"400 retryable? {400 in RETRYABLE_STATUS}")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
RETRYABLE_STATUS as a setThe status codes worth retrying.Set membership is the clearest way to express this, and the explicit list documents the decision. 408 timeout, 425 too-early, 429 rate limit, 5xx server-side.
base * (2 ** (attempt - 1))Doubles the ceiling each attempt: 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.Exponential growth gives an overloaded server progressively more room. Linear backoff barely helps.
min(cap, ...)Caps the ceiling at 30 seconds.Without a cap, attempt 12 waits over an hour. Nobody wants that, including your user.
rng.uniform(0, ceiling)Full jitter: uniform between zero and the ceiling.Not ceiling exactly. If a thousand clients all get 429 at once and all sleep exactly 4 seconds, they all return simultaneously and the server falls over again. Randomising spreads the herd. Full jitter is the variant AWS's own guidance recommends.
rng: random.Random | None = NoneInjectable random generator.Lets the demo pass a seeded generator and produce reproducible delays. Without this, the function is untestable — a real design consideration, not a nicety.
the or in headers.get("retry-after") or headers.get("Retry-After")Handles both casings.HTTP headers are case-insensitive, but a plain dict is not. requests and httpx give you case-insensitive mappings; other sources may not.
try: float(value) except ValueErrorHandles the HTTP-date form of Retry-After.The spec allows either a number of seconds or an absolute date. We support the common form and fall back to our own backoff for the other, rather than crashing on it.

Expected output

full-jitter delays for 6 attempts (base 0.5s, cap 30s):
  attempt 1: ceiling   0.5s  ->  slept  0.32s
  attempt 2: ceiling   1.0s  ->  slept  0.03s
  attempt 3: ceiling   2.0s  ->  slept  0.55s
  attempt 4: ceiling   4.0s  ->  slept  0.89s
  attempt 5: ceiling   8.0s  ->  slept  5.89s
  attempt 6: ceiling  16.0s  ->  slept 10.83s

header handling:
  {'retry-after': '12'}  -> 12.0
  {}                     -> None
  {'retry-after': 'Wed'} -> None

429 retryable? True
400 retryable? False

Attempt 2 sleeping 0.03s looks wrong and is not: full jitter means the delay is anywhere in the range, including near zero. Across many clients the average wait grows exponentially while individual clients stay unpredictable, which is exactly the property you want.

Wrapping a real call

Apply the backoff to an actual backend call, retrying only what should be retried.

def with_retry(call, max_attempts: int = 4, base: float = 0.5, cap: float = 30.0):
    """Call a zero-argument function, retrying retryable HTTP and network failures."""
    import requests

    last_exception: Exception | None = None

    for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
        try:
            return call()
        except requests.exceptions.HTTPError as exc:
            status = exc.response.status_code if exc.response is not None else None
            if status not in RETRYABLE_STATUS:
                raise
            wait = retry_after_seconds(dict(exc.response.headers)) or backoff_delay(
                attempt, base, cap
            )
            last_exception = exc
            print(f"  attempt {attempt} failed with {status}, waiting {wait:.2f}s")
        except (requests.exceptions.ConnectionError, requests.exceptions.Timeout) as exc:
            wait = backoff_delay(attempt, base, cap)
            last_exception = exc
            print(f"  attempt {attempt} failed with {type(exc).__name__}, waiting {wait:.2f}s")

        if attempt == max_attempts:
            break
        time.sleep(wait)

    raise RuntimeError(f"all {max_attempts} attempts failed") from last_exception
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
with_retry(call, ...) taking a callableWraps any zero-argument function.Same dependency-injection pattern as validate_with_retry in section 3.4. Use with a lambda: with_retry(lambda: backend.chat(messages)).
if status not in RETRYABLE_STATUS: raiseRe-raises non-retryable errors immediately.A 401 or 400 will fail identically four times. Failing fast surfaces the real bug.
retry_after_seconds(...) or backoff_delay(...)Server instruction first, our maths second.The provider knows when its window resets. Ignoring that header on a free tier is how you get temporarily blocked.
if attempt == max_attempts: breakSkips the final sleep.Sleeping 16 seconds and then giving up anyway is pure waste, and it is a real bug in a lot of published retry code.
raise RuntimeError(...) from last_exceptionChains the original exception.from preserves the underlying traceback, so the log shows why it failed, not just that it did.
print on each failureVisibility.In Part 10 this becomes a structured log line with the attempt count as a metric. Silent retries hide a degrading provider until it fails completely.

You do not have to write this yourself in production. tenacity (Apache-2.0, free) does all of the above as decorators, with better ergonomics. Writing it once by hand is worth it because it means you can read tenacity's options and know exactly which behaviour each one buys.

Try this yourself. Point the Groq backend at a nonsense model name and wrap the call in with_retry. You get a 404, which is not in RETRYABLE_STATUS, so it raises immediately instead of burning four attempts. Then set GROQ_API_KEY=wrong and confirm the 401 also fails fast. Fast failure on unfixable errors is as valuable as retrying on fixable ones.

4.7 Counting tokens and measuring what calls cost

Everything in this course is free, so this section teaches a habit rather than saving you money. Build it now and it is already there when the numbers become dollars — and even at $0, tokens and latency are your real constraints.

Three ways to count tokens, in order of accuracy

MethodAccuracyWhen to use
Read usage from the responseExactAlways, after the fact. Ollama's prompt_eval_count/eval_count; OpenAI-shaped APIs' usage object.
Tokenize locally with the model's own tokenizerExact for that modelBefore sending, when you need to know whether a prompt fits the context window. len(tokenizer.encode(text)).
Estimate at ~4 characters per token±25%, worse for code and non-EnglishRough budgeting when no tokenizer is available. Never for a hard limit check.

Build the meter that records every call and reports tokens, latency percentiles, and notional cost.

"""Measure what every model call costs you in tokens, time and (notional) money."""

import statistics
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

# USD per million tokens, (prompt, completion). Illustrative — check current pricing.
PRICES_PER_MTOK = {
    "local": (0.0, 0.0),
    "llama-3.1-8b-instant": (0.05, 0.08),
    "llama-3.3-70b-versatile": (0.59, 0.79),
}


@dataclass
class CallRecord:
    """One model call, measured."""
    model: str
    prompt_tokens: int
    completion_tokens: int
    seconds: float
    ttft: float | None = None

    @property
    def total_tokens(self) -> int:
        return self.prompt_tokens + self.completion_tokens

    @property
    def tokens_per_second(self) -> float:
        return self.completion_tokens / self.seconds if self.seconds > 0 else 0.0

    def cost_usd(self) -> float:
        prompt_price, completion_price = PRICES_PER_MTOK.get(self.model, (0.0, 0.0))
        return (self.prompt_tokens * prompt_price
                + self.completion_tokens * completion_price) / 1_000_000


@dataclass
class Meter:
    """Collects call records and summarises them."""
    records: list[CallRecord] = field(default_factory=list)

    def add(self, record: CallRecord) -> None:
        self.records.append(record)

    def report(self) -> str:
        if not self.records:
            return "no calls recorded"
        latencies = sorted(r.seconds for r in self.records)
        prompt = sum(r.prompt_tokens for r in self.records)
        completion = sum(r.completion_tokens for r in self.records)
        cost = sum(r.cost_usd() for r in self.records)
        p50 = statistics.median(latencies)
        p95 = latencies[min(len(latencies) - 1, int(round(0.95 * (len(latencies) - 1))))]
        return (
            f"calls        : {len(self.records)}\n"
            f"tokens in/out: {prompt} / {completion}\n"
            f"latency p50  : {p50:.2f}s\n"
            f"latency p95  : {p95:.2f}s\n"
            f"mean tok/s   : {statistics.mean(r.tokens_per_second for r in self.records):.1f}\n"
            f"cost         : ${cost:.6f}"
        )


def estimate_tokens(text: str) -> int:
    """Crude fallback when no tokenizer is available: ~4 characters per token."""
    return max(1, round(len(text) / 4))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    meter = Meter()
    samples = [
        ("local", 320, 96, 6.40, 0.42),
        ("local", 512, 210, 13.10, 0.51),
        ("local", 180, 40, 2.90, 0.38),
        ("llama-3.1-8b-instant", 1200, 400, 0.85, 0.11),
        ("llama-3.3-70b-versatile", 1200, 400, 1.90, 0.19),
    ]
    for model, pin, pout, secs, ttft in samples:
        meter.add(CallRecord(model, pin, pout, secs, ttft))

    print(meter.report())

    text = "Retrieval augmented generation puts real documents in the prompt."
    print(f"\nestimate_tokens({len(text)} chars) -> {estimate_tokens(text)}")
    hypothetical = CallRecord("llama-3.3-70b-versatile", 500_000, 100_000, 60.0)
    print(f"same traffic at 70B scale would cost ${hypothetical.cost_usd():.2f}")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
PRICES_PER_MTOK with separate prompt/completion ratesPrices differ by direction.Output tokens usually cost several times input tokens. A single blended rate makes long-answer workloads look cheaper than they are.
@dataclass for CallRecordA plain measured record.Deliberately mirrors ChatResult from 4.1, so converting one to the other is trivial.
cost_usd() divided by 1_000_000Prices are quoted per million tokens.The underscores are Python numeric separators — purely for readability, and they prevent the classic factor-of-ten error.
.get(self.model, (0.0, 0.0))Unknown models cost zero.Local models should not raise a KeyError in your metrics path. Failing metrics must never break a working request.
field(default_factory=list)Fresh list per instance.records: list = [] in a dataclass raises at class-definition time precisely because it would be shared. Same trap as Pydantic in 1.3.
statistics.median for p50, index arithmetic for p95Reports percentiles, not just an average.The important idea here. A mean latency of 2s hides the fact that one user in twenty waits 13s. Users experience your p95, not your mean.
min(len(latencies) - 1, ...)Clamps the index.With fewer than 20 samples the p95 index can round past the end. Note that percentiles from 5 samples are not statistics — they are a habit you are forming.
estimate_tokens with max(1, ...)Never returns zero.A zero token count divides badly downstream.
the "hypothetical" lineScales the same traffic to 500k input tokens.Makes the free-vs-paid comparison concrete. This is the calculation that gets your project approved or rejected.

Expected output

calls        : 5
tokens in/out: 3412 / 1146
latency p50  : 2.90s
latency p95  : 13.10s
mean tok/s   : 145.2
cost         : $0.001116

estimate_tokens(65 chars) -> 16
same traffic at 70B scale would cost $0.37

Two things worth staring at. The p50 is 2.90s and the p95 is 13.10s — a 4.5× spread, entirely because the hosted calls are fast and the local ones are not. And "mean tok/s 145.2" is a nearly meaningless number, because averaging a 470 tok/s hosted call with a 15 tok/s local one describes nothing real. Segment your metrics by model, or you will draw confident conclusions from a blended average.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
ValueError: mutable default ... is not allowedrecords: list = [] in the dataclass.Use field(default_factory=list).
Token counts are zero for hosted streaming callsMany providers omit usage from streamed responses.Some accept a stream_options: {"include_usage": true} flag — verify per provider. Otherwise count locally with the tokenizer, or accept an estimate for streams.
Cost reads as $0 on a paid modelThe returned model name did not match a key in PRICES_PER_MTOK (aliases, suffixes, dates).Log unknown model names loudly. Silent zero-cost is worse than a crash here.
p95 equals the maximumToo few samples.Expected below ~20 calls. Do not tune anything on a five-sample percentile.
Try this yourself. Add a ttft percentile alongside the latency ones, then compare p95 TTFT against p95 total. TTFT is what your user feels (section 3.5); total is what your capacity planning cares about. Watching those two diverge is how you learn which one to optimise.

4.8 Caching responses

During development you will send the same prompt dozens of times. During evaluation, hundreds. Caching turns a 6-second call into a 0.2-millisecond one, and it costs about forty lines.

The rule that makes caching safe

Only cache deterministic calls. If temperature is above zero, the whole point is variation — caching it means your "creative" endpoint returns the same sentence forever. And the cache key must include everything that affects the output: model, every message, and every sampling option. Miss one and you serve a stale answer from a different configuration, which is a genuinely nasty bug to track down.

Cache deterministic responses on disk, keyed by a hash of the full request.

"""Cache model responses on disk, keyed by everything that affects the output."""

import hashlib
import json
import time
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Callable

CACHE_DIR = Path("data/llm_cache")


def cache_key(model: str, messages: list[dict], options: dict) -> str:
    """A stable hash of every input that changes the answer."""
    payload = {
        "model": model,
        "messages": messages,
        "options": {k: options[k] for k in sorted(options)},
    }
    blob = json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
    return hashlib.sha256(blob.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()


def cached_call(
    model: str,
    messages: list[dict],
    options: dict,
    call: Callable[[], str],
    cache_dir: Path = CACHE_DIR,
) -> tuple[str, bool]:
    """Return (text, was_cached). Only caches deterministic calls."""
    if options.get("temperature", 1.0) > 0.0:
        return call(), False

    cache_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    key = cache_key(model, messages, options)
    path = cache_dir / f"{key}.json"

    if path.exists():
        record = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        return record["response"], True

    response = call()
    path.write_text(
        json.dumps({"key": key, "model": model, "messages": messages,
                    "options": options, "response": response,
                    "created": time.time()}, indent=2),
        encoding="utf-8",
    )
    return response, False


if __name__ == "__main__":
    calls = {"n": 0}

    def slow_model() -> str:
        calls["n"] += 1
        time.sleep(0.4)
        return "The Ollama API listens on port 11434."

    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What port does Ollama use?"}]
    deterministic = {"temperature": 0.0, "num_predict": 100}

    for label in ("first", "second", "third"):
        started = time.perf_counter()
        text, hit = cached_call("qwen3:1.7b", messages, deterministic, slow_model)
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started
        print(f"{label:<7} cached={hit!s:<5} {elapsed*1000:6.1f} ms  {text}")

    print(f"\nmodel actually called {calls['n']} time(s)")
    print(f"key: {cache_key('qwen3:1.7b', messages, deterministic)[:16]}...")

    creative = {"temperature": 0.8, "num_predict": 100}
    _, hit = cached_call("qwen3:1.7b", messages, creative, slow_model)
    print(f"temperature 0.8 -> cached={hit} (sampling is never cached)")
    print(f"model called {calls['n']} time(s) in total")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
import hashlibStandard-library cryptographic hashes.SHA-256 gives a fixed-length, filesystem-safe key from arbitrary input. Not for security here — just a stable fingerprint.
json.dumps(..., sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))Canonical serialisation.The critical detail. Without sort_keys, two dicts with the same contents in different insertion orders hash differently and you get a cache miss on every call. separators removes whitespace so formatting cannot affect the key.
{k: options[k] for k in sorted(options)}Sorts the options explicitly too.Belt and braces alongside sort_keys, and it makes the intent obvious to the next reader.
if options.get("temperature", 1.0) > 0.0Refuses to cache sampled calls.Note the default is 1.0, not 0.0: if temperature is unspecified, assume sampling and do not cache. Defaulting the other way would silently cache non-deterministic calls.
Path rather than string pathspathlib from the standard library.cache_dir / f"{key}.json" works identically on Windows and Unix. String concatenation with / does not.
mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)Creates the folder if needed, silently if present.No "does it exist" check, no race condition, no crash on the second run.
storing messages and options in the fileSaves the inputs, not just the answer.A cache directory full of opaque hashes is undebuggable. With the inputs stored you can grep the cache and see what produced what.
returns (text, was_cached)Tells the caller whether it was a hit.Cache hit rate is a metric you want. It also feeds the cached flag on ChatResult from 4.1, so a cached call is not counted in your latency percentiles.
encoding="utf-8" on both read and writeExplicit encoding.Windows still defaults to a legacy codepage in some configurations. Model output contains em-dashes and emoji; this line prevents a UnicodeDecodeError that only ever happens on someone else's machine.

Expected output

first   cached=False  401.0 ms  The Ollama API listens on port 11434.
second  cached=True     0.2 ms  The Ollama API listens on port 11434.
third   cached=True     0.1 ms  The Ollama API listens on port 11434.

model actually called 1 time(s)
key: 707664a65274297a...
temperature 0.8 -> cached=False (sampling is never cached)
model called 2 time(s) in total

401 ms to 0.2 ms — a 2,000× speedup, from forty lines and no cleverness. When you run the eval suite in Part 10 over a hundred fixed questions, this is the difference between a ten-minute feedback loop and a three-second one.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
Cache never hitsSomething varying in the key: a timestamp in the prompt, a session id, a randomly ordered dict.Print the key on each call and compare. If it changes, something in the payload changed.
Stale answers after you edit a prompt templateCorrect behaviour — the prompt text is part of the key, but only if it actually reached the messages.Include a prompt-library version in the key (section 3.7's VERSION), or delete the cache directory. Add it to .gitignore.
Thousands of files in one directoryOne file per key with no eviction.Fine for development. For real use, shard by the first two hex characters, or use diskcache (Apache-2.0) which handles eviction and locking.
Cache directory committed to gitMissing gitignore entry.data/ is already ignored per section 0.6. Confirm with git status.
Try this yourself. Add a ttl_seconds parameter and treat a record older than that as a miss, using the stored created timestamp. Then ask yourself whether a cached LLM answer should ever expire. For a fixed eval suite: no. For a RAG answer over documents that change: absolutely, and the cache key should include the retrieved chunk ids too — which is exactly the bug you would otherwise ship in Part 5.
Deeper dive: three other kinds of caching you will meet
  • Prompt caching (provider-side). Several providers cache the prefix of your prompt — a long system prompt or a fixed document — so repeated calls skip re-processing it. This cuts latency and cost substantially, and on some free tiers cached tokens do not count toward rate limits. It requires keeping the prefix byte-identical and at the start, which is a real design constraint on how you assemble prompts.
  • KV cache (runtime-side). Section 2.7's mechanism, inside the model. Ollama and vLLM reuse it across turns of the same conversation when the prefix matches, which is why the second message in a chat often produces its first token faster than the first did.
  • Semantic caching. Cache on embedding similarity rather than exact match, so "what port does Ollama use" hits the entry for "which port is Ollama on". Tempting and genuinely risky: near-miss questions get confidently wrong cached answers. If you use it, set a high similarity threshold and log every hit so you can audit what it decided was "the same question".

4.9 Part 4 checkpoint

Quiz answer 1: why a Protocol rather than an abstract base class?

Structural typing. A backend does not import or inherit from the Protocol, so provider-specific modules never become dependencies of your core, and heavy imports like torch can stay lazy inside a branch of the factory. You also get a six-line fake backend for tests with no inheritance ceremony. ABCs are fine too — they just couple implementations to the interface, which is exactly what we are avoiding here.

Quiz answer 2: your transformers output is much worse than Ollama's on the same model. Why?

You almost certainly skipped tokenizer.apply_chat_template(...) and passed a raw string. Ollama applies the chat template for you; transformers does not. Without it the model never sees the special tokens that mark the assistant's turn, so it continues your text instead of answering it — section 2.5's base-versus-instruct failure, self-inflicted. Second possibility: you forgot add_generation_prompt=True.

Quiz answer 3: what is full jitter and why not just double the delay?

Full jitter picks a random delay between zero and the exponentially growing ceiling, rather than waiting the ceiling exactly. If many clients are rate-limited simultaneously and all wait exactly 4 seconds, they all return at the same instant and re-overload the server — a thundering herd. Randomising spreads them out. The average wait still grows exponentially, which is the property you wanted.

Quiz answer 4: which requests must never be cached, and what must the key contain?

Never cache anything with temperature above zero — variation is the point. The key must include the model, every message verbatim, and every sampling option, serialised canonically with sorted keys so that dict ordering cannot cause spurious misses. For RAG, add the retrieved chunk ids: otherwise re-indexing your documents leaves the old answer cached against the new corpus.

Quiz answer 5: mean latency is 2s and p95 is 13s. What do you report and what do you fix?

Report the p95 — that is what one user in twenty experiences, and it is what makes people call your app slow. Then segment by model before concluding anything, because a blended average across a fast hosted model and a slow local one describes no real request. Fix the slow segment: smaller model, shorter prompt, caching, or route that class of request elsewhere.

You are done with Part 4 when you can

  • Swap your whole application between Ollama, a hosted free tier, and a fake backend by editing one line of .env.
  • Explain what apply_chat_template does and what breaks without it.
  • Say which HTTP statuses to retry and which to fail fast on, and why jitter matters.
  • Get exact token counts from a response rather than estimating them.
  • Quote your own p50 and p95 latency for your local model.
  • Explain why a cache key must be canonically serialised.

Part 5

RAG — Retrieval Augmented Generation

The longest part of the course, because this is what most GenAI engineering jobs actually are. By the end you will have replaced the fake context in M2 with real retrieval over your own documents, with citations that are verified rather than trusted, hybrid search, reranking, and a way to measure whether any of it helped.

5.1 Why RAG exists — and when not to use it

RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) means: before answering, find relevant text and put it in the prompt. That is all. There is no special model, no training, no magic. It works because of two facts you already know from Part 2 — the model has no access to your documents (section 2.8, cause 1), and its context window is small and position-sensitive (section 2.7).

Everything RAG does can be summarised as: get a small amount of relevant text into the privileged positions of a short context.

What RAG buys you

BenefitWhy it matters
Answers about data the model never sawYour notes, your company's wiki, last week's news, a PDF you were handed this morning.
CitationsThe user can check the claim. This is the difference between a toy and a tool.
Freshness without retrainingAdd a document, and the next answer uses it. No fine-tuning cycle.
Access controlFilter retrieval by who is asking. You cannot do this with knowledge baked into weights.
Cheap correctionA wrong answer is usually a retrieval bug you can fix in minutes, not a model flaw.

When NOT to use RAG

This section exists because RAG is the default reflex now, and it is often the wrong tool.

SituationDo this insteadWhy
You have fewer than ~20 pages of source material, total.Put all of it in the prompt every time.20 pages is roughly 12k tokens. That fits. A retrieval pipeline that can pick the wrong chunk is strictly worse than one that cannot.
The question is about the whole corpus: "summarise all 400 tickets", "what themes recur?"Map-reduce over documents, or a proper data pipeline.Retrieval fetches the top-k most similar chunks. It structurally cannot answer aggregate questions — it will confidently summarise 5 tickets out of 400.
You need format, tone or behaviour changed.Prompting, then fine-tuning (Part 8).RAG adds knowledge, not skills. No amount of retrieved text teaches a model your house style.
The answer needs computation: totals, joins, filters, "how many customers in Q3".SQL, or a tool the agent calls (Part 6).Text similarity cannot count. Retrieving three invoices and asking for a sum is a hallucination generator.
The data is highly structured (a database, a spreadsheet).Text-to-SQL, or a query tool.Embedding table rows destroys exactly the structure that makes them useful.
The model already knows it: "what is a for loop in Python".Just ask.Retrieval adds latency, tokens, and a chance of retrieving something worse than the model's own knowledge.

The honest summary. RAG is a search problem wearing an AI costume. Roughly 90% of "the LLM gave a bad answer" in a RAG system is actually "the retriever fetched the wrong text", and almost all the engineering effort in this part goes into retrieval quality rather than generation. If you take one thing from Part 5, take that.

Deeper dive: "long context killed RAG" — why that keeps being wrong

Every time a model ships with a bigger context window, someone declares RAG obsolete. Paste the whole corpus in, let attention sort it out. Four reasons this has not happened:

  • Cost and latency scale with context. Section 2.7: prompt processing is quadratic and the KV cache grows linearly. A 100k-token prompt on every question is enormously more expensive than a 2k-token one — even at $0, it is the difference between a 1-second and a 40-second answer locally.
  • Lost in the middle. Long contexts are not used uniformly. Retrieval exists partly to put the right thing in the right position.
  • Corpora are bigger than any context. 128k tokens is about 300 pages. Your company wiki is not 300 pages.
  • No citations, no access control. If everything is in the prompt, you cannot say which document supported the claim, and you cannot withhold documents from a user who should not see them.

What long context has genuinely changed: you can retrieve more generously (10 chunks instead of 3), keep chunks larger, and stop obsessing over squeezing context. It made RAG easier, not unnecessary.

5.2 The pipeline, end to end

Two phases. Ingestion happens once per document, offline. Query happens on every question, and every millisecond counts.

The capstone milestones for this part

MilestoneSectionWhat you end up with
M3 — ingest and chunk5.3, 5.4Documents loaded from PDF, markdown and web, cleaned, chunked with metadata.
M4 — embed and store5.5, 5.6A persistent vector index you can query.
M5 — retrieval with citations5.7Real answers with verified sources, replacing M2's fake context.
M6 — hybrid + rerank5.8, 5.9Keyword and dense search fused, then reranked.

5.3 M3, part one — loading and cleaning documents

Boring, unglamorous, and the source of most RAG failures. A PDF that extracts as two interleaved columns produces chunks of scrambled nonsense, and no amount of clever retrieval recovers from that.

The libraries, and why these ones

uv pip install pypdf beautifulsoup4 httpx
LibraryLicenceWhat it doesWhy this one
pypdfBSDExtracts text from PDFs.Pure Python, no system dependencies, installs in seconds. Weak on complex layouts. pymupdf is much better at layout but is AGPL, which matters if you ever ship commercially; pdfplumber is better at tables and slower. Start here, upgrade when your PDFs demand it.
beautifulsoup4MITParses HTML.The standard. trafilatura (Apache-2.0) is better at stripping navigation and boilerplate from real web pages — worth adding when you start ingesting messy sites.
httpxBSDFetches URLs.Already installed in 4.5.

Load documents from three sources into one uniform shape, cleaning as we go.

"""Load documents from disk or the web into a uniform, cleaned shape."""

import re
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

import httpx
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
from pypdf import PdfReader


@dataclass
class Document:
    """One source document, before chunking."""
    source: str
    text: str
    metadata: dict = field(default_factory=dict)


# Collapse 3+ newlines to 2; collapse runs of spaces; drop soft hyphens.
MULTI_NEWLINE = re.compile(r"\n{3,}")
MULTI_SPACE = re.compile(r"[ \t]{2,}")
HYPHEN_BREAK = re.compile(r"(\w)-\n(\w)")
CONTROL = re.compile(r"[\x00-\x08\x0b\x0c\x0e-\x1f]")


def clean_text(text: str) -> str:
    """Normalise whitespace and repair common extraction artefacts."""
    text = text.replace("\r\n", "\n").replace("\r", "\n")
    text = CONTROL.sub("", text)
    text = HYPHEN_BREAK.sub(r"\1\2", text)
    text = MULTI_SPACE.sub(" ", text)
    text = MULTI_NEWLINE.sub("\n\n", text)
    return text.strip()


def load_markdown(path: Path) -> Document:
    """Read a .md or .txt file."""
    raw = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
    return Document(
        source=path.name,
        text=clean_text(raw),
        metadata={"kind": "markdown", "path": str(path)},
    )


def load_pdf(path: Path) -> Document:
    """Extract text from a PDF, keeping page numbers as markers."""
    reader = PdfReader(str(path))
    pages = []
    for number, page in enumerate(reader.pages, start=1):
        extracted = page.extract_text() or ""
        if extracted.strip():
            pages.append(f"[page {number}]\n{clean_text(extracted)}")
    return Document(
        source=path.name,
        text="\n\n".join(pages),
        metadata={"kind": "pdf", "path": str(path), "pages": len(reader.pages)},
    )


def load_url(url: str, timeout: float = 20.0) -> Document:
    """Fetch a web page and keep only the readable text."""
    response = httpx.get(
        url,
        timeout=timeout,
        follow_redirects=True,
        headers={"User-Agent": "SecondBrain/0.1 (personal research tool)"},
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    soup = BeautifulSoup(response.text, "html.parser")

    for tag in soup(["script", "style", "nav", "header", "footer", "aside", "form"]):
        tag.decompose()

    title = soup.title.string.strip() if soup.title and soup.title.string else url
    body = soup.get_text(separator="\n")
    return Document(
        source=url,
        text=clean_text(body),
        metadata={"kind": "web", "title": title, "url": url},
    )


def load_path(path: Path) -> list[Document]:
    """Load one file or every supported file in a directory."""
    if path.is_file():
        candidates = [path]
    else:
        candidates = sorted(
            p for p in path.rglob("*") if p.suffix.lower() in {".md", ".txt", ".pdf"}
        )

    documents = []
    for candidate in candidates:
        try:
            if candidate.suffix.lower() == ".pdf":
                documents.append(load_pdf(candidate))
            else:
                documents.append(load_markdown(candidate))
        except Exception as exc:                      # noqa: BLE001
            print(f"  skipped {candidate.name}: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")
    return documents


if __name__ == "__main__":
    folder = Path("data/docs")
    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    sample = folder / "setup.md"
    if not sample.exists():
        sample.write_text(
            "# Installing Ollama\n\nDownload from ollama.com.\n\n\n\n"
            "## Verifying\n\nThe   API listens on 127.0.0.1:11434 by de-\nfault.\n",
            encoding="utf-8",
        )

    for doc in load_path(folder):
        print(f"source   : {doc.source}")
        print(f"metadata : {doc.metadata}")
        print(f"chars    : {len(doc.text)}")
        print(f"text     :\n{doc.text}\n")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
@dataclass class DocumentOne shape for every source.Everything downstream — chunking, embedding, storing — works on Document and does not care whether it came from a PDF or a URL. Adding a new loader later touches nothing else.
metadata: dict = field(default_factory=dict)Free-form provenance.Metadata is what makes filtering (5.11) and citations possible. Capture it at load time; you cannot recover it later.
HYPHEN_BREAK and \1\2Rejoins words split across lines by hyphenation.PDFs are full of de-\nfault. Left alone, "default" becomes two tokens that match nothing, and your keyword search silently fails on exactly the technical terms people search for.
CONTROL regexStrips non-printable control characters.PDF extraction emits form feeds and null bytes. Some vector stores reject them; worse, some accept them and corrupt your index.
MULTI_NEWLINE.sub("\n\n", ...)Collapses blank-line runs to exactly two.Paragraph breaks are the primary signal the recursive chunker uses in 5.4. Normalising them makes chunking predictable.
order of operations in clean_textLine endings, then control chars, then hyphens, then spaces, then newlines.Order matters: fixing hyphens after collapsing newlines would miss them. This is the kind of thing you only get right once and then never touch.
errors="replace"Substitutes undecodable bytes instead of raising.One badly-encoded file should not abort ingestion of two hundred good ones.
f"[page {number}]\n..."Inlines page markers into the text.A crude but effective way to preserve page numbers through chunking, so a citation can say "page 6". The alternative — per-page documents — loses cross-page context.
page.extract_text() or ""Handles pages that extract as None.Scanned or image-only pages return nothing. Without the or "" you get a TypeError halfway through a long document.
soup(["script", "style", "nav", ...]) + decompose()Deletes non-content elements from the tree.Otherwise every chunk from every page contains your site navigation, which then matches every query. Boilerplate is the "vector pointing everywhere" problem from section 1.6, at scale.
follow_redirects=Truehttpx does not follow redirects by default.Unlike requests. Without it you silently ingest a 301 response body.
a custom User-AgentIdentifies your tool honestly.Many sites block default client user-agents. Also basic courtesy — and check robots.txt and the site's terms before crawling anything you do not own.
except Exception ... print(f"skipped ...")Per-file error isolation.Broad except is usually bad practice; in a batch loader it is correct. The noqa comment tells the linter this is deliberate. What matters is that it reports rather than swallowing.
path.rglob("*") with a suffix filterRecursive directory walk.Handles nested folders of notes without extra code.

Expected output

source   : setup.md
metadata : {'kind': 'markdown', 'path': 'data/docs/setup.md'}
chars    : 105
text     :
# Installing Ollama

Download from ollama.com.

## Verifying

The API listens on 127.0.0.1:11434 by default.

Check the two repairs: the four blank lines became one paragraph break, and by de-\nfault became by default. Those are the two most common extraction artefacts, and both would have degraded retrieval invisibly.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
PDF extracts as empty or near-emptyIt is a scan — images of text, no text layer.You need OCR. ocrmypdf (MPL, free) plus Tesseract, or a vision model (Part 8). Detect it: if extracted characters per page is under ~100, flag the document rather than indexing noise.
Two-column PDF extracts as interleaved gibberishpypdf reads in stream order, not visual order.Try pymupdf (check the AGPL licence for your use) or pdfplumber. Always eyeball the extracted text of a few documents before indexing hundreds.
Tables become word soupLayout is lost in plain text extraction.Extract tables separately with pdfplumber and store them as markdown tables in their own chunks. Do not let a mangled table pollute a prose chunk.
httpx.HTTPStatusError: 403The site blocks you.Respect that. Do not build a scraper-evasion layer into a learning project.
Web page text is 90% menu itemsBeautifulSoup's tag list did not catch this site's markup.Add trafilatura, which is purpose-built for main-content extraction.
Try this yourself. Add a quality gate to load_path: if len(doc.text) / max(1, doc.metadata.get("pages", 1)) is below 100 characters per page, print a warning instead of returning the document. You have just built scanned-PDF detection, and you will be glad of it the first time someone drops 40 scanned invoices into your ingestion folder.

5.4 M3, part two — chunking, the biggest lever you have

Chunking decides what a retrieval hit can possibly contain. Get it wrong and no downstream trick saves you, because the right answer is split across two chunks and neither one is retrievable on its own.

Why chunk at all

  • Embeddings compress. One vector for a 40-page document averages away everything specific. One vector per paragraph keeps detail.
  • Context is finite. You can fit 5 paragraphs in a prompt, not 5 documents.
  • Precision. Retrieving a whole chapter to answer one question wastes context on irrelevant text — and section 2.7 says the model will use the middle of it poorly anyway.

The four strategies

StrategyHowGoodBad
Fixed sizeCut every N characters, with overlap.Trivial, predictable sizes, never fails.Cuts mid-word and mid-sentence. Destroys meaning at boundaries.
RecursiveTry to split on paragraphs; if a piece is still too big, try newlines, then sentences, then words.The sensible default. Respects natural boundaries when it can, always terminates.Headings get orphaned from their content; still splits mid-sentence at the last resort.
By document structureSplit on markdown headings, HTML sections, PDF pages.Chunks are semantically coherent units. Headings become metadata.Wildly variable sizes — one heading may cover two lines or twelve pages. Needs a recursive pass on top.
SemanticEmbed each sentence, cut where consecutive-sentence similarity drops.Cuts at genuine topic changes.Requires an embedding call per sentence at ingestion time, has thresholds to tune, and in practice is frequently no better than recursive-plus-structural. Try it last, and only after measuring.

Recommended default. Structural first, recursive within each section, chunk size roughly 500–1,000 characters with 10–20% overlap, and the heading prepended to every chunk. That combination is what the code below implements, and it beats sophisticated approaches often enough that you should make it prove otherwise before replacing it.

Implement all four boundary strategies, run them on the same text, and see exactly where each one breaks.

"""Split documents into chunks. Strategies compared on the same text."""

import re
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

SAMPLE = """# Installing Ollama

Ollama runs open-weight models locally. Download the installer from ollama.com
and run it. On Linux, use the shell script instead.

## Verifying the install

Run `ollama --version` to confirm the CLI can reach the background server.
The server listens on 127.0.0.1:11434 by default. If the command fails, the
service is not running.

## Hardware requirements

An 8B model at Q4_K_M needs roughly 5.5 GB of memory including the KV cache.
On an 8 GB machine, prefer a 1.7B or 3B model. Check `ollama ps` to see whether
the model loaded onto the GPU or stayed on the CPU.
"""


def fixed_chunks(text: str, size: int = 200, overlap: int = 40) -> list[str]:
    """Cut every `size` characters, stepping back `overlap` each time."""
    chunks = []
    start = 0
    while start < len(text):
        end = start + size
        chunks.append(text[start:end])
        if end >= len(text):
            break
        start = end - overlap
    return chunks


SEPARATORS = ["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""]
