hyde       : 'Inference slows as context grows because attention cost scales with
              the square of sequence length, and the KV cache consumes memory
              proportional to the number of tokens...'...

The condensed question is the one that matters. "and on Windows?" retrieves nothing useful from any index; "How do I install Ollama on Windows?" retrieves the right chunk. Every multi-turn RAG chat needs this, and systems that skip it feel mysteriously broken from turn two onward.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
Condensed question is a paragraph of explanationThe model ignored "reply with the question only".Add "stop": ["\n"], or one-shot it with an example. Small models need the example.
Condensing breaks a question that was already standaloneThe model "improves" a fine question into a worse one.Retrieve with both the original and the condensed version and fuse with RRF. Costs one retrieval, removes the risk.
Multi-query makes results worseParaphrases drifted off topic and outvoted the original in RRF.Generate fewer (2, not 5), and weight the original query's ranking higher in fusion.
HyDE returns "I don't have information about that"Alignment training resisting the invention request.Reword to emphasise it is a search aid, or drop HyDE. It is the most skippable technique here.
Latency doubledYou added one or two model calls before retrieval.Real cost, honestly. Condense only when history exists; run multi-query retrievals concurrently with asyncio.gather (section 1.4).
Try this yourself. Take five real follow-up questions from a conversation with your own system, and measure recall@5 with and without condensing using the eval script in 5.13. This is the cheapest experiment in Part 5 and it will show the largest single improvement.

5.11 Metadata filtering

Your store already supports it — store.search(vector, where={"source": "setup.md"}) from section 5.6. What matters is designing the metadata before you ingest, because you cannot filter on what you did not capture.

Metadata fieldEnablesCapture it at
source, path, urlCitations, "search only this document", deduplication.Load time (5.3).
heading, page, sectionPrecise citations the user can actually navigate to.Chunk time (5.4).
kind (pdf / web / markdown)"Only search my notes, not the web pages I saved."Load time.
created_at, ingested_atRecency filters and boosts. Critical for anything time-sensitive.Load time. Filesystem mtime is a reasonable fallback.
owner, tenant_id, aclAccess control. The one reason filtering is not optional.Load time, from your application's model.
flagged (from the injection scan in 3.6)Quarantining hostile documents.Load time.

Access control must be a pre-filter, not a post-filter. Our NumPy store scores every chunk and then masks non-matches with -inf — fine for correctness, since a masked chunk can never be returned. But the moment you have real tenants, do not rely on filtering results after the model has seen them, and never let unfiltered chunks reach the prompt. The safe pattern: resolve the user's permitted document set first, pass it as the filter, and treat any code path that can retrieve without a filter as a bug. Qdrant and pgvector do this efficiently at scale; that is the main reason to graduate to them.

Self-querying: letting the model write the filter

"What did I write about Ollama last March?" contains both a semantic part ("Ollama") and a structured part ("March"). Self-query retrieval asks the model to split the question into a search string plus a filter dict, using the structured-output machinery from section 3.4:

Split the question into a semantic search query and metadata filters.
Available filter fields: source (string), kind (pdf|web|markdown),
created_after (YYYY-MM-DD), created_before (YYYY-MM-DD).

Reply with JSON: {"query": "...", "filters": {...}}
Use only the listed fields. Omit filters you cannot determine.

Question: What did I write about Ollama last March?

Validate the result with a Pydantic model whose fields are exactly your allowed filter keys, and reject anything else. That validation is not a nicety: an unvalidated model-generated filter is a model-generated database query, which in a multi-tenant system is an access-control hole. Never merge model-supplied filters over your own security filters — apply yours last, always.

Try this yourself. Add "ingested_at": time.time() to doc_metadata in build_index.py, then extend LocalVectorStore.search to accept a min_ingested_at argument. You now have recency filtering, and you have discovered why metadata design is an ingestion-time decision rather than a query-time one.

5.12 Advanced patterns, with honest tradeoffs

These are the techniques you will see in conference talks. Some are genuinely useful; some are solutions to problems you do not have. Each entry says which.

Parent-document retrieval (also called small-to-big)

Problem it solves: small chunks retrieve precisely but lack context; large chunks have context but retrieve imprecisely.

How: index small chunks, but when one is retrieved, return its parent — the larger surrounding section — to the model.

Verdict: use this. It is cheap (store a parent_id on each chunk and keep the parent text), needs no extra model calls, and resolves a real tension. With the chunker from 5.4 you already have the structure: the structural section is the parent, the recursive pieces are the children.

Contextual retrieval

Problem it solves: a chunk saying "it dropped by 8% that quarter" is unretrievable and uninterpretable alone.

How: at ingestion, ask a model to write one sentence situating each chunk within its document, and prepend that before embedding.

Verdict: effective and expensive. Published results show solid retrieval improvements, and the cost is one model call per chunk at ingestion — for 10,000 chunks on a local 1.7B model, that is hours. Prompt caching makes it cheaper on hosted APIs. The heading prefix in section 5.4 is the free 80% version of this idea; do that first and only reach for the full technique if measurement says you need it.

GraphRAG

Problem it solves: questions requiring connections across many documents. "Which of our suppliers are affected by the policy change described in the compliance memo?"

How: extract entities and relationships into a knowledge graph at ingestion, then traverse the graph at query time, optionally with community summaries.

Verdict: powerful, and almost certainly overkill for you. Ingestion becomes many model calls per document, the graph needs schema decisions and maintenance, and query latency rises substantially. It genuinely beats vector RAG on multi-hop and corpus-wide questions — and those are a small minority of real queries. Do not build this until you have measured that plain RAG fails on your actual users' questions.

Agentic RAG

Problem it solves: one retrieval is not always enough. The right answer may need a follow-up search, a different query, or a decision that retrieval is not the right tool at all.

How: make retrieval a tool the model can call, in a loop, deciding for itself whether to search again, search differently, or answer.

Verdict: this is where the capstone goes next. It is Part 6's entire subject. Agentic RAG subsumes decomposition, self-correction on bad retrievals, and multi-source lookups. The cost is unpredictable latency and the failure modes in section 6 — loops, tool thrashing, and cost overruns.

The honest ranking

Do this firstThen thisOnly if measuredProbably never
Heading prefixes on chunks (5.4)
Reranking (5.9)
Query condensing (5.10)
Hybrid search (5.8)		Parent-document retrieval
Multi-query
Metadata filtering (5.11)		Contextual retrieval
Semantic chunking
HyDE		GraphRAG, unless your questions are genuinely multi-hop
Fine-tuning an embedding model, unless you have thousands of labelled pairs

5.13 Evaluating RAG

Everything above is a hypothesis until you measure it. Without evaluation you are tuning by vibes, and the specific failure mode is real: you make three changes, the system feels better, and it is measurably worse on questions you did not happen to try.

The two layers to measure

LayerMetricQuestion it answersNeeds an LLM?
RetrievalRecall@kOf the chunks that should have been found, how many were in the top k?No
MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank)How high up was the first correct chunk?No
GenerationFaithfulnessIs every claim in the answer supported by the retrieved context? (Measures hallucination directly.)Yes
Answer relevanceDoes the answer address the question asked?Yes
Context precisionOf the chunks retrieved, how many were actually useful? (Measures noise.)Yes
Context recallDid retrieval find everything needed to answer fully?Yes, plus a reference answer

Start with the retrieval metrics. They need no LLM, no reference answers, and no judge model — just a list of questions and which chunks should answer them. They are cheap, fast, deterministic, and they catch the majority of RAG regressions, because most generation failures are retrieval failures in disguise.

Build the retrieval eval harness, including a golden set file you grow over time.

"""Measure retrieval quality against a golden set. No LLM needed."""

import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Callable

GOLDEN_PATH = Path("backend/evals/retrieval_golden.json")


@dataclass
class Case:
    """One evaluation question and the chunks that should answer it."""
    question: str
    expected_sources: list[str]


def recall_at_k(retrieved_sources: list[str], expected: list[str], k: int) -> float:
    """Fraction of expected chunks that appear in the top k."""
    top = set(retrieved_sources[:k])
    found = sum(1 for e in expected if e in top)
    return found / len(expected) if expected else 0.0


def reciprocal_rank(retrieved_sources: list[str], expected: list[str]) -> float:
    """1/position of the first correct hit, or 0 if none."""
    for position, source in enumerate(retrieved_sources, start=1):
        if source in expected:
            return 1.0 / position
    return 0.0


def evaluate(cases: list[Case],
             retriever: Callable[[str, int], list[str]],
             k: int = 5) -> dict:
    """Run every case and aggregate, keeping the misses for inspection."""
    recalls, rrs, misses = [], [], []
    for case in cases:
        sources = retriever(case.question, k)
        r = recall_at_k(sources, case.expected_sources, k)
        rr = reciprocal_rank(sources, case.expected_sources)
        recalls.append(r)
        rrs.append(rr)
        if r < 1.0:
            misses.append((case.question, case.expected_sources, sources[:k]))
    n = len(cases)
    return {
        "cases": n,
        f"recall@{k}": sum(recalls) / n,
        "mrr": sum(rrs) / n,
        "perfect": sum(1 for r in recalls if r == 1.0),
        "misses": misses,
    }


def load_golden(path: Path = GOLDEN_PATH) -> list[Case]:
    """Read the golden set from disk."""
    raw = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    return [Case(c["question"], c["expected_sources"]) for c in raw]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # A tiny fake retriever so this file runs with no index and no model.
    FAKE = {
        "what port does ollama use": ["setup.md#4", "setup.md#3", "hardware.md#9"],
        "how much memory for an 8B model": ["hardware.md#9", "setup.md#3"],
        "what is a KV cache": ["setup.md#3", "setup.md#4"],
    }

    def fake_retriever(question: str, k: int) -> list[str]:
        return FAKE.get(question, [])[:k]

    cases = [
        Case("what port does ollama use", ["setup.md#4"]),
        Case("how much memory for an 8B model", ["hardware.md#9"]),
        Case("what is a KV cache", ["theory.md#2"]),
    ]

    GOLDEN_PATH.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    GOLDEN_PATH.write_text(json.dumps(
        [{"question": c.question, "expected_sources": c.expected_sources} for c in cases],
        indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

    report = evaluate(cases, fake_retriever, k=3)
    print(f"cases     : {report['cases']}")
    print(f"recall@3  : {report['recall@3']:.2f}")
    print(f"MRR       : {report['mrr']:.2f}")
    print(f"perfect   : {report['perfect']}/{report['cases']}")
    for question, expected, got in report["misses"]:
        print(f"\nMISS: {question!r}")
        print(f"  expected: {expected}")
        print(f"  got     : {got}")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
expected_sources as "file#id" stringsIdentifies chunks by source and id.Matches the citation identity from 5.7. Note the fragility: if you re-chunk, these ids shift. For a durable golden set, key on a distinctive phrase the chunk must contain instead.
retriever: Callable[[str, int], list[str]]The retriever is injected.Same pattern as sections 3.4 and 4.6. Lets you evaluate dense-only, hybrid, and hybrid+rerank by passing three different functions — which is exactly the A/B you need.
recall_at_kFraction of expected chunks found.The primary retrieval metric. If recall is low, nothing downstream can fix it: the answer simply is not in the prompt.
reciprocal_rank returning 1/positionRewards ranking the right chunk higher.Recall@5 cannot distinguish "correct chunk was first" from "correct chunk was fifth". Section 2.7 says position matters, so measure it.
if r < 1.0: misses.append(...)Records what went wrong, with what was returned instead.The most useful output. An aggregate score tells you whether you regressed; the miss list tells you why. Never build an eval harness that only prints numbers.
writing GOLDEN_PATHPersists the cases as JSON.The golden set is an asset, not a script. Commit it. Every user-reported bad answer becomes a new case, and it never regresses again.
the FAKE retriever in __main__Lets the file run with no index.So you can develop and test the harness itself offline — the echo-backend principle from 4.1.

Expected output

cases     : 3
recall@3  : 0.67
MRR       : 0.67
perfect   : 2/3

MISS: 'what is a KV cache'
  expected: ['theory.md#2']
  got     : ['setup.md#3', 'setup.md#4']

Two of three cases found the right chunk at rank 1. The third failed completely, and the miss report shows the retriever returned setup documentation instead of the theory chunk — which is the kind of specific, actionable failure that a single aggregate number would have hidden.

RAGAS and DeepEval, for the generation metrics

Faithfulness and answer relevance need a model to judge — an LLM-as-judge. Two free libraries do this:

LibraryLicenceWhat it gives youNotes
RAGASApache-2.0The RAG-specific metric set: faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision, context recall.The standard for RAG evaluation. Configurable to use a local Ollama model as the judge, which keeps it free — but a 1.7B judge is a weak judge, so expect noise.
DeepEvalApache-2.0A broader test framework with a pytest-style interface, including RAG metrics plus general LLM assertions.Fits naturally into CI (Part 10). Also supports local models as judges.
promptfooMITPrompt and model comparison matrices, config-driven.Best for "which prompt or model is better", less RAG-specific.

Both libraries' APIs move. RAGAS in particular has changed its metric classes and its model-configuration interface across versions, and any code I wrote here would likely be stale by the time you run it. Read docs.ragas.io and deepeval's docs for the current shape, and pin the version you develop against. I am not going to invent function signatures for you to debug.

What is stable and worth internalising is the concepts: faithfulness decomposes the answer into individual claims and checks each against the context; answer relevance checks the answer addresses the question; context precision measures how much retrieved text was noise. You could implement rough versions of all three yourself with the structured-output machinery from Part 3, and doing so is a genuinely good exercise.

Be sceptical of LLM-as-judge numbers, especially local ones. A judge model has the same blind spots as the model it judges, it favours verbose answers, and small judges are noisy enough that a 5-point "improvement" can be nothing. Use judged metrics for direction across many cases, never as precise scores. Hand-label 30 answers yourself once, compare against your judge, and you will know how much to trust it.

Try this yourself. Run evaluate three times against your real system: once with dense-only retrieval, once with hybrid, once with hybrid plus reranking. Write down the three recall@5 and MRR numbers. That table is the empirical justification for everything in sections 5.8 and 5.9 — measured on your documents rather than taken on my word.

5.14 Part 5 checkpoint

Quiz answer 1: your RAG system answers "summarise all 300 support tickets" badly. Why, and what fixes it?

Retrieval fetches the top-k most similar chunks — five tickets, not three hundred. It structurally cannot answer aggregate questions, and it will confidently summarise the five it found as though they were the whole corpus. RAG is the wrong tool. Fix it with a map-reduce pass over all documents, or a data pipeline that computes the aggregate, or an agent that recognises the question type and routes it elsewhere (Part 6). No amount of chunking or reranking helps.

Quiz answer 2: you switch embedding models and quality collapses. What are the three likely causes?

(1) You did not re-index — the old vectors are incomparable with the new query vectors. The load guard in 5.6 exists to make this impossible. (2) The new model requires a prefix (BGE, Nomic) and you are not applying it, which costs real quality with no error. (3) The new model has a shorter sequence limit and your chunks are being silently truncated. Check max_seq_length against your chunk size.

Quiz answer 3: why can't you just compare BM25 scores to cosine scores directly?

They are different scales with different meanings. BM25 is unbounded and depends on corpus statistics — 1.9 might be excellent or mediocre depending on the query's term rarity. Cosine on normalised vectors is bounded in [-1, 1] and compressed in practice to roughly 0.3–0.9. Normalising them to a common scale requires assumptions that break as your corpus changes. RRF sidesteps the problem entirely by using ranks and discarding scores.

Quiz answer 4: a citation names a real file but the quote does not appear in it. Which check catches this, and why isn't Pydantic enough?

verify_citations catches it, by normalising whitespace and testing that the quote is a substring of the chunk that was actually retrieved. Pydantic validates shape — that source is a string and chunk_id is a non-negative integer. It has no way to know whether the quoted sentence exists in the world. Shape validation and reality validation are different jobs, and the second one is what stops a credible-looking fabricated citation from shipping.

Quiz answer 5: when is a vector database the wrong choice?

Below roughly 50,000 chunks, where a NumPy matrix multiply answers in single-digit milliseconds and gives you a fully inspectable index with zero dependencies. Also wrong when your data is genuinely structured (use SQL), when your questions are aggregate (use a pipeline), or when your corpus fits in a context window (just paste it). Adopt one when you have measured a specific need: scale, concurrent writes, or efficient pre-filtered search for multi-tenancy.

You are done with Part 5 when you can

  • Name three situations where RAG is the wrong tool, and say what to use instead.
  • Explain why chunking matters more than which vector database you chose.
  • Say what a cross-encoder sees that a bi-encoder cannot, and why you use both.
  • Explain RRF without mentioning score normalisation.
  • Show a citation your system rejected, and say which check caught it.
  • Quote your own recall@5 and MRR for dense-only versus hybrid-plus-rerank.

Part 6

AI agents

The deepest part of the course. You will build the agent loop by hand before touching a framework, see the raw message-by-message trace of a full run, give the model tools that validate their own arguments, add memory that summarises itself, put a human in front of the dangerous operations, and expose your knowledge base over MCP. Capstone milestones M7 through M13.

6.1 What actually separates an agent from a chatbot or a chain

"Agent" is the most abused word in this field. Here is a definition you can test against code:

An agent is a loop where the model decides what happens next. If the sequence of steps is fixed by your code, it is a chain. If the model chooses — including choosing to stop — it is an agent.

ChatbotChainAgent
Control flowOne call in, one answer out.Fixed pipeline you wrote: retrieve → generate → format.A loop. The model picks the next action each iteration.
Number of model calls1Known in advance (1–3)Unknown. Could be 2, could be 40.
Can it act on the world?NoOnly where you wired itYes, through tools it selects
Can it recover from a failure?NoOnly if you coded the branchYes — it reads the error and tries something else
Cost predictabilityExactGoodPoor. This is the central engineering problem.
Your M5 RAG system is…a chainnot yet

When you actually need one

Agents cost more, take longer, and fail in more interesting ways. Use one when at least one of these is true:

  • The number of steps depends on the question. "Compare the memory needs of the models in my notes" needs one retrieval per model, and you do not know how many models there are.
  • Different questions need different tools. Some need retrieval, some need arithmetic, some need the web.
  • Failure should be recoverable. If retrieval returns nothing useful, an agent can rephrase and search again. A chain returns nothing useful.
  • The task requires acting, not just answering: writing a file, sending a request, updating a record.

And when you do not. If your task is "answer questions from my documents", the M5 chain is better than an agent: faster, cheaper, and it cannot decide to do something surprising. A huge amount of production "agentic AI" is a two-step chain wearing a costume, and the teams that shipped it that way were right. Reach for the loop when the fixed pipeline demonstrably cannot do the job.

Deeper dive: the levels of autonomy, and where to stop
LevelWho decidesExampleRisk
0 — Fixed chainYouM5 RAGNone beyond a wrong answer.
1 — RouterModel picks one branch, you wrote the branches"Is this a maths question or a document question?"Wrong branch. Bounded.
2 — Tool-using loopModel picks tools and when to stop, from a fixed setThe capstone. M8.Loops, cost, wrong tool arguments.
3 — Planning agentModel writes a multi-step plan and executes itPlan-and-Execute (6.8)A bad plan wastes the whole budget before you notice.
4 — Multi-agentAgents delegate to agentsM11 supervisorCompounding errors, opaque traces, cost multiplication.
5 — Open-endedModel writes and runs its own code against real systemsComputer-use agents (6.14)Real damage. Needs sandboxing and approval gates.

Level 2 with good guardrails covers the overwhelming majority of useful work. Every level above it multiplies your debugging cost. Climb only when forced.

6.2 The loop, and the raw trace of one full run

Five phases, repeated until the model says stop or you cut it off:

The raw trace — every message, in order

This is the whole point of building the loop by hand. Below is the complete message list from a real run of the code you write in 6.4, printed at the end. Nothing is hidden and nothing is paraphrased.

[0] role=system
     You are Second Brain, a research agent. You work in a loop.

     On every turn reply with EXACTLY ONE JSON object and nothing else, in one of two shapes:

       {"thought": "why this step", "tool": "<tool name>", "args": {...}}
       {"thought": "why I am done", "final": "the answer for the user"}
       [... tool docs ...]

[1] role=user
     A server handles 240 requests per minute. Using my notes, can it keep up?

[2] role=assistant
     {"thought": "I need the request time and worker count from the notes.", "tool": "search_notes", "args": {"query": "request takes ms server runs workers"}}

[3] role=user
     OBSERVATION: [{"source": "hardware.md", "chunk_id": 10, "text": "A single request takes about 150 ms and the server runs 4 workers."}]

[4] role=assistant
     {"thought": "Now compute capacity per minute.", "tool": "calculator", "args": {"expression": "4 * (1/0.150) * 60"}}

[5] role=user
     OBSERVATION: {"expression": "4 * (1/0.150) * 60", "result": 1600.0}

[6] role=assistant
     {"thought": "I have the number.", "final": "Yes, capacity is about 1600 req/min."}

total messages: 7
total chars   : 1650

Six things to notice, because they explain most agent behaviour

  1. There are three separate model calls here, at messages 2, 4 and 6. Each one receives everything above it. Message 6's call re-sent all 1,650 characters. Section 3.2's resend cost, now multiplied by the number of loop iterations.
  2. The tool result comes back as a plain user message prefixed OBSERVATION:. There is no magic channel. Some APIs offer a dedicated tool role (see 6.5); with the JSON protocol we control it ourselves, and the model cannot tell the difference.
  3. The model never sees the tool run. It emits an intention, your code executes it, and the result appears as text. The model has no idea whether you actually called anything — which is exactly why it can hallucinate an observation if your prompt lets it.
  4. The thought field is doing real work. It is chain-of-thought (section 3.3) inside a structured action, so the reasoning conditions the tool choice in the same generation. It also gives you a readable trace for the UI in M18.
  5. The loop terminates because the model chose final. Nothing in the architecture guarantees that will ever happen. Your limits are the only thing that does.
  6. Context grows monotonically. Seven messages here; a 20-step run with verbose tool output can be 30,000 tokens by the end, and section 2.7 says the middle of that will be used poorly. This is why 6.7 exists.

6.3 M7 — tools, with schemas that validate themselves

A tool is a Python function plus three things the model needs: a name, a description, and an argument schema. Getting these right is most of what makes an agent work or not.

Tool design rules, learned the hard way

RuleWhy
One job per tool.A manage_files(action, ...) tool with a mode switch confuses models badly. Three small tools beat one polymorphic one.
Describe when to use it, not just what it does."Search the user's indexed documents" is better than "search". "Use for arithmetic; never compute numbers yourself" is better still.
Few parameters, flat, all typed.Nested objects and optional-everything schemas produce malformed calls. Small models manage 1–3 flat arguments reliably.
Validate every argument. Always.A tool argument is untrusted input generated by a text predictor. Treat it exactly as you would treat a query string from the internet.
Return structured text the model can read.JSON strings work well: compact, unambiguous, and the model can quote fields from them.
Errors are messages, not exceptions.An error that reaches the model as an observation gets fixed by the model. An exception that propagates kills the run.
Keep the set small.Beyond roughly 10–15 tools, selection accuracy drops noticeably on small models. Route to subsets instead (6.9).

Build the tool registry with Pydantic-validated arguments, a safe calculator, the retriever from Part 5, and an approval-gated file writer.

"""Tools the agent may call. Each one declares a validated argument schema."""

import ast
import json
import operator
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Callable, Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError

OUTPUT_DIR = Path("data/agent_out")


@dataclass
class ToolSpec:
    """Everything the agent needs to know about one tool."""
    name: str
    description: str
    args_model: type[BaseModel]
    fn: Callable[[BaseModel], str]
    requires_approval: bool = False

    def json_schema(self) -> dict:
        return {
            "name": self.name,
            "description": self.description,
            "parameters": self.args_model.model_json_schema(),
            "requires_approval": self.requires_approval,
        }


REGISTRY: dict[str, ToolSpec] = {}


def register(spec: ToolSpec) -> ToolSpec:
    if spec.name in REGISTRY:
        raise ValueError(f"duplicate tool name {spec.name!r}")
    REGISTRY[spec.name] = spec
    return spec


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- calculator
class CalculatorArgs(BaseModel):
    expression: str = Field(description="A pure arithmetic expression, e.g. '4 * (1/0.15)'",
                            min_length=1, max_length=200)


SAFE_OPS = {
    ast.Add: operator.add, ast.Sub: operator.sub, ast.Mult: operator.mul,
    ast.Div: operator.truediv, ast.Pow: operator.pow, ast.Mod: operator.mod,
    ast.USub: operator.neg, ast.UAdd: operator.pos, ast.FloorDiv: operator.floordiv,
}


def _eval_node(node):
    """Walk the syntax tree, allowing only numbers and arithmetic operators."""
    if isinstance(node, ast.Expression):
        return _eval_node(node.body)
    if isinstance(node, ast.Constant):
        if isinstance(node.value, (int, float)):
            return node.value
        raise ValueError("only numbers are allowed")
    if isinstance(node, ast.BinOp) and type(node.op) in SAFE_OPS:
        return SAFE_OPS[type(node.op)](_eval_node(node.left), _eval_node(node.right))
    if isinstance(node, ast.UnaryOp) and type(node.op) in SAFE_OPS:
        return SAFE_OPS[type(node.op)](_eval_node(node.operand))
    raise ValueError(f"unsupported expression element: {type(node).__name__}")


def calculator(args: CalculatorArgs) -> str:
    tree = ast.parse(args.expression, mode="eval")
    value = _eval_node(tree)
    return json.dumps({"expression": args.expression, "result": value})


register(ToolSpec("calculator", "Evaluate an arithmetic expression exactly.",
                  CalculatorArgs, calculator))


# ------------------------------------------------------------- search_notes
class SearchArgs(BaseModel):
    query: str = Field(description="What to look for in the indexed documents", min_length=2)
    top_k: int = Field(3, description="How many chunks to return", ge=1, le=10)


DEMO_CORPUS = [
    {"source": "setup.md", "chunk_id": 4,
     "text": "The Ollama HTTP API listens on 127.0.0.1:11434 by default."},
    {"source": "hardware.md", "chunk_id": 9,
     "text": "An 8B model at Q4_K_M needs roughly 5.5 GB of memory including the KV cache."},
    {"source": "hardware.md", "chunk_id": 10,
     "text": "A single request takes about 150 ms and the server runs 4 workers."},
]


def search_notes(args: SearchArgs) -> str:
    """Use the real retriever from Part 5; fall back to a demo corpus if no index exists."""
    try:
        from app.rag import retrieve
        hits = retrieve(args.query, top_k=args.top_k)
    except Exception:                                  # noqa: BLE001
        words = set(args.query.lower().split())
        scored = [(len(words & set(c["text"].lower().split())), c) for c in DEMO_CORPUS]
        scored.sort(key=lambda p: p[0], reverse=True)
        hits = [c for score, c in scored[:args.top_k] if score > 0] or DEMO_CORPUS[:1]
    return json.dumps([
        {"source": h["source"], "chunk_id": h["chunk_id"], "text": h["text"][:400]}
        for h in hits
    ])


register(ToolSpec(
    "search_notes",
    "Search the user's indexed documents. Returns chunks with source and chunk_id.",
    SearchArgs, search_notes))


# --------------------------------------------------------------- write_file
class WriteArgs(BaseModel):
    filename: str = Field(description="File name only, no directories",
                          min_length=1, max_length=64)
    content: str = Field(description="Text to write", min_length=1)
    mode: Literal["create", "append"] = Field("create", description="create or append")


def write_file(args: WriteArgs) -> str:
    if "/" in args.filename or "\\" in args.filename or args.filename.startswith("."):
        raise ValueError("filename must be a plain name with no path separators")
    OUTPUT_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    target = (OUTPUT_DIR / args.filename).resolve()
    if OUTPUT_DIR.resolve() not in target.parents:
        raise ValueError("refusing to write outside the output directory")
    with open(target, "a" if args.mode == "append" else "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        fh.write(args.content)
    return json.dumps({"written": str(target), "bytes": len(args.content)})


register(ToolSpec("write_file", "Write text to a file in the agent output directory.",
                  WriteArgs, write_file, requires_approval=True))


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ dispatch
def format_errors(exc: ValidationError) -> str:
    return "; ".join(
        f"{'.'.join(str(p) for p in e['loc']) or '(root)'}: {e['msg']}"
        for e in exc.errors()
    )


def call_tool(name: str, raw_args: dict) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    """Validate and run a tool. Returns (ok, observation). Never raises."""
    spec = REGISTRY.get(name)
    if spec is None:
        return False, (f"ERROR unknown tool {name!r}. "
                       f"Available tools: {', '.join(sorted(REGISTRY))}")
    try:
        args = spec.args_model.model_validate(raw_args)
    except ValidationError as exc:
        return False, f"ERROR invalid arguments for {name}: {format_errors(exc)}"
    try:
        return True, spec.fn(args)
    except Exception as exc:                           # noqa: BLE001
        return False, f"ERROR {name} failed: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"


def tool_docs() -> str:
    """Render the tool list for the system prompt."""
    lines = []
    for spec in REGISTRY.values():
        schema = spec.args_model.model_json_schema()
        params = ", ".join(
            f"{k}: {v.get('type')}" + ("" if k in schema["required"] else " (optional)")
            for k, v in schema["properties"].items()
        )
        approval = "  [REQUIRES APPROVAL]" if spec.requires_approval else ""
        lines.append(f"- {spec.name}({params}) -- {spec.description}{approval}")
    return "\n".join(lines)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("tool documentation given to the model:\n")
    print(tool_docs())
    print("\nfull JSON schema for one tool:")
    print(json.dumps(REGISTRY["calculator"].json_schema(), indent=2))

    print("\n--- dispatch tests ---")
    cases = [
        ("calculator", {"expression": "4 * (1/0.150) * 60"}),
        ("calculator", {"expresion": "2+2"}),
        ("calculator", {"expression": "__import__('os').system('rm -rf /')"}),
        ("calculator", {"expression": "1/0"}),
        ("search_notes", {"query": "how much memory does an 8B model need"}),
        ("search_notes", {"query": "hi", "top_k": 99}),
        ("web_search", {"query": "anything"}),
        ("write_file", {"filename": "../../etc/passwd", "content": "x"}),
        ("write_file", {"filename": "notes.md", "content": "hello from the agent\n"}),
    ]
    for name, args in cases:
        ok, observation = call_tool(name, args)
        flag = "ok " if ok else "ERR"
        print(f"[{flag}] {name}({json.dumps(args)[:52]}) -> {observation[:110]}")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
ToolSpec as a dataclassBundles name, description, schema, function and approval flag.One object holds everything: what the model is told, how arguments are checked, what runs, and whether a human must confirm. Splitting these across files is how tool documentation drifts from tool behaviour.
args_model: type[BaseModel]The class, not an instance.We need it both to generate the schema (model_json_schema()) and to validate incoming arguments. The same declaration serves both, so the documentation cannot disagree with the validation.
model_json_schema()Pydantic generates JSON Schema from the model.This is why the ecosystem standardised on Pydantic for tools: JSON Schema is exactly the format native function-calling APIs want (6.5). Write the model once, get docs and API schema free.
if spec.name in REGISTRY: raiseRejects duplicate names.Two tools with one name means one silently shadows the other, and the model's calls go somewhere you did not expect.
ast.parse(..., mode="eval") + SAFE_OPSParses the expression and walks the tree, permitting only numeric literals and arithmetic operators.Never use eval() on model output. eval("__import__('os').system('rm -rf /')") does exactly what it looks like. This allow-list approach makes the dangerous cases structurally impossible rather than filtered.
raise ValueError("only numbers are allowed")Rejects string constants.Closes a gap: ast.Constant covers strings too, and allowing them re-opens paths you just closed.
try: from app.rag import retrieve ... exceptUses the real Part 5 retriever, falling back to a demo corpus.So this file runs before you have built an index, and so tests do not need one. The echo-backend principle from 4.1.
top_k: int = Field(3, ge=1, le=10)Bounds the result count.A model that asks for top_k: 500 would blow up your context window. The bound is enforced by validation, not by hoping.
h["text"][:400]Truncates each chunk in the observation.Tool output goes straight into context and is re-sent on every subsequent loop iteration. Verbose tools are the number-one cause of context overflow in agents.
the three checks in write_fileRejects path separators, resolves the path, and confirms it is inside OUTPUT_DIR.Defence in depth against path traversal. The string check catches the obvious case; .resolve() plus the parents check catches symlinks and clever encodings. Never trust one check on a filesystem path.
requires_approval=True on the writerMarks it as needing a human.Read-only tools run freely; anything that changes the world asks first. This flag is what M12's approval gate reads.
call_tool returning (ok, str)Converts every failure into an observation.The most important design decision in this file. Unknown tool, invalid arguments, and runtime exceptions all become text the model reads and can respond to. The agent self-corrects instead of crashing — you will see it happen in 6.4.
except Exception in call_toolCatches everything from the tool function.Normally poor practice; correct here. One misbehaving tool must not end a 20-step run. The message includes the exception type so the model gets a real hint.
tool_docs()Renders the registry into prose for the system prompt.Generated from the same source of truth as validation, so adding a tool updates the prompt automatically. Hand-written tool docs go stale within a week.

Expected output

tool documentation given to the model:

- calculator(expression: string) -- Evaluate an arithmetic expression exactly.
- search_notes(query: string, top_k: integer (optional)) -- Search the user's indexed documents. Returns chunks with source and chunk_id.
- write_file(filename: string, content: string, mode: string (optional)) -- Write text to a file in the agent output directory.  [REQUIRES APPROVAL]

full JSON schema for one tool:
{
  "name": "calculator",
  "description": "Evaluate an arithmetic expression exactly.",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "expression": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "A pure arithmetic expression, e.g. '4 * (1/0.15)'"
      }
    },
    "required": [
      "expression"
    ]
  },
  "requires_approval": false
}

--- dispatch tests ---
[ok ] calculator({"expression": "4 * (1/0.150) * 60"}) -> {"expression": "4 * (1/0.150) * 60", "result": 1600.0}
[ERR] calculator({"expresion": "2+2"}) -> ERROR invalid arguments for calculator: expression: Field required
[ERR] calculator({"expression": "__import__('os').system('rm -rf /')" -> ERROR calculator failed: ValueError: unsupported expression element: Call
[ERR] calculator({"expression": "1/0"}) -> ERROR calculator failed: ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
[ok ] search_notes({"query": "how much memory does an 8B model need"}) -> [{"source": "hardware.md", "chunk_id": 9, "text": "An 8B model at Q4_K_M needs roughly 5.5 GB of memory includ
[ERR] search_notes({"query": "hi", "top_k": 99}) -> ERROR invalid arguments for search_notes: top_k: Input should be less than or equal to 10
[ERR] web_search({"query": "anything"}) -> ERROR unknown tool 'web_search'. Available tools: calculator, search_notes, write_file
[ERR] write_file({"filename": "../../etc/passwd", "content": "x"}) -> ERROR write_file failed: ValueError: filename must be a plain name with no path separators
[ok ] write_file({"filename": "notes.md", "content": "hello from the ) -> {"written": "/…/data/agent_out/notes.md", "bytes": 21}

Nine cases, six of them failures, every one turned into a readable message instead of a crash. The third is worth pausing on: a model that emitted a code-injection payload got unsupported expression element: Call, because the AST allow-list refuses function calls by construction. That is what "secure by design rather than by filter" looks like in twenty lines.

Pydantic wording caveat. The exact validation messages (Field required, Input should be less than or equal to 10) come from Pydantic v2 and may be phrased slightly differently in your version. The structure — field name, then problem — is what matters, and it is what the model reads.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
Model keeps calling a tool that does not existIt invented a plausible name, often one from its training data like web_search.The "Available tools:" list in the error message fixes this in one turn — which is why the error includes it. Do not just say "unknown tool".
Model passes a JSON string where an object is expectedDouble-encoded arguments: "args": "{\"expression\": \"2+2\"}".Common with small models. Detect a str in the args position and json.loads it once before validating.
write_file succeeds with a weird pathOnly the string check ran.Keep both checks. Test with "..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd" and a symlink.
Tool output floods the contextNo truncation.Cap every tool's output. 400–800 characters per chunk, and consider returning ids the model can expand on request.
Try this yourself. Add a web_search tool using the ddgs package (uv pip install ddgs, MIT, no API key) with a max_results field bounded to 5. Then rerun the dispatch tests: the "unknown tool" case becomes a real search. Note what you had to decide — result truncation, timeout, and what to return when the network is down. Every tool needs those three answers.

6.4 M8 — the agent loop, by hand

No framework. Roughly 100 lines. When you rebuild this in LangGraph in 6.6 you will know exactly what the framework is doing, because you will have done it.

Build the loop: decide, validate, act, observe, with hard limits and an approval hook.

"""M8: the agent loop, written by hand so nothing is hidden."""

import json
import re
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Callable

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError

from app.agent.tools import REGISTRY, call_tool, tool_docs

SYSTEM = """You are Second Brain, a research agent. You work in a loop.

On every turn reply with EXACTLY ONE JSON object and nothing else, in one of two shapes:

  {{"thought": "why this step", "tool": "<tool name>", "args": {{...}}}}
  {{"thought": "why I am done", "final": "the answer for the user"}}

Available tools:
{tools}

Rules:
- One tool per turn. Wait for the OBSERVATION before deciding the next step.
- Never invent tool output. If a tool errors, read the error and fix your arguments.
- Use calculator for arithmetic. Never compute numbers yourself.
- Cite source and chunk_id for facts that came from search_notes.
- If you have enough information, reply with "final"."""

FENCE = re.compile(r"```(?:json)?\s*(.*?)\s*```", re.DOTALL)


def extract_json(text: str) -> str:
    """Recover the JSON object from whatever the model wrapped it in."""
    fenced = FENCE.search(text)
    if fenced:
        return fenced.group(1).strip()
    start, end = text.find("{"), text.rfind("}")
    return text[start:end + 1].strip() if start != -1 and end > start else text.strip()


class Action(BaseModel):
    """One decision from the model."""
    thought: str = Field(min_length=1)
    tool: str = Field("")
    args: dict = Field(default_factory=dict)
    final: str = Field("")


@dataclass
class Step:
    """One iteration, recorded for the trace viewer in M18."""
    n: int
    thought: str
    tool: str | None
    args: dict | None
    observation: str | None
    ok: bool


@dataclass
class AgentResult:
    answer: str
    steps: list[Step] = field(default_factory=list)
    messages: list[dict] = field(default_factory=list)
    stop_reason: str = "final"
    tool_calls: int = 0


def run_agent(
    question: str,
    call_model: Callable[[list[dict]], str],
    approve: Callable[[str, dict], bool] | None = None,
    max_steps: int = 6,
    max_tool_calls: int = 8,
    verbose: bool = True,
) -> AgentResult:
    """Perceive, decide, act, observe, repeat -- with hard limits."""
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM.format(tools=tool_docs())},
        {"role": "user", "content": question},
    ]
    result = AgentResult(answer="", messages=messages)

    for n in range(1, max_steps + 1):
        raw = call_model(messages)
        if verbose:
            print(f"\n--- step {n}: model -> ---\n{raw.strip()}")
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": raw})

        try:
            action = Action.model_validate_json(extract_json(raw))
        except (ValidationError, json.JSONDecodeError) as exc:
            observation = f"ERROR your reply was not a valid action object: {exc}"
            messages.append({"role": "user", "content": f"OBSERVATION: {observation}"})
            result.steps.append(Step(n, "(unparseable)", None, None, observation, False))
            if verbose:
                print(f"--- step {n}: observation -> ---\n{observation}")
            continue

        if action.final:
            result.answer = action.final
            result.steps.append(Step(n, action.thought, None, None, None, True))
            if verbose:
                print(f"--- step {n}: FINAL ---\n{action.final}")
            return result

        if not action.tool:
            observation = "ERROR you must supply either 'tool' or 'final'."
            messages.append({"role": "user", "content": f"OBSERVATION: {observation}"})
            result.steps.append(Step(n, action.thought, None, None, observation, False))
            continue

        if result.tool_calls >= max_tool_calls:
            result.stop_reason = "tool budget exhausted"
            result.answer = "Stopped: too many tool calls without reaching an answer."
            return result

        spec = REGISTRY.get(action.tool)
        if spec is not None and spec.requires_approval:
            granted = approve(action.tool, action.args) if approve else False
            if not granted:
                observation = (f"DENIED the user refused the {action.tool} call. "
                               f"Do not retry it; continue without it.")
                messages.append({"role": "user", "content": f"OBSERVATION: {observation}"})
                result.steps.append(Step(n, action.thought, action.tool, action.args,
                                         observation, False))
                if verbose:
                    print(f"--- step {n}: observation -> ---\n{observation}")
                continue

        ok, observation = call_tool(action.tool, action.args)
        result.tool_calls += 1
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": f"OBSERVATION: {observation}"})
        result.steps.append(Step(n, action.thought, action.tool, action.args, observation, ok))
        if verbose:
            print(f"--- step {n}: {action.tool}({json.dumps(action.args)[:60]}) ---")
            print(f"--- step {n}: observation -> ---\n{observation[:200]}")

    result.stop_reason = "step limit"
    result.answer = result.answer or "Stopped: reached the step limit without an answer."
    return result


def scripted_model(replies: list[str]) -> Callable[[list[dict]], str]:
    """A fake model that returns a fixed sequence. Lets us test the loop offline."""
    state = {"i": 0}

    def call(messages: list[dict]) -> str:
        reply = replies[min(state["i"], len(replies) - 1)]
        state["i"] += 1
        return reply

    return call


if __name__ == "__main__":
    question = ("A server handles 240 requests per minute. Using my notes for the "
                "request time and worker count, can it keep up? Save the answer to capacity.md.")

    replies = [
        json.dumps({"thought": "I need the request time and worker count from the notes.",
                    "tool": "search_notes",
                    "args": {"query": "request takes ms server runs workers"}}),
        json.dumps({"thought": "Now compute capacity per minute.",
                    "tool": "calculator",
                    "args": {"expresion": "4 * (1/0.150) * 60"}}),
        json.dumps({"thought": "Fix the argument name and retry.",
                    "tool": "calculator",
                    "args": {"expression": "4 * (1/0.150) * 60"}}),
        json.dumps({"thought": "Save the conclusion for the user.",
                    "tool": "write_file",
                    "args": {"filename": "capacity.md",
                             "content": "Capacity is ~1600 req/min vs 240 required.\n"}}),
        json.dumps({"thought": "I have the number and the file is written.",
                    "final": ("Yes. Your notes say each request takes 150 ms with 4 workers, "
                              "so capacity is about 1600 requests/minute against the 240 "
                              "required (hardware.md#10). Saved to capacity.md.")}),
    ]

    print("=" * 72)
    print("RUN 1 -- approval granted")
    print("=" * 72)
    result = run_agent(question, scripted_model(replies), approve=lambda t, a: True)

    print("\n" + "=" * 72)
    print(f"stop reason : {result.stop_reason}")
    print(f"steps       : {len(result.steps)}   tool calls: {result.tool_calls}")
    print(f"messages    : {len(result.messages)} in the final context")
    print("\nstep summary:")
    for s in result.steps:
        status = "ok " if s.ok else "ERR"
        print(f"  {s.n} [{status}] {s.tool or 'FINAL':<13} {s.thought[:46]}")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
{{"thought": ...}} in SYSTEMDoubled braces.Because we call .format(tools=...) on this string, literal braces must be escaped. Section 3.1's error, avoided.
"One tool per turn. Wait for the OBSERVATION"Constrains the model to one action.Without it, models emit a whole imagined transcript — tool call, made-up observation, second tool call, answer. That is the single most common agent failure, and it is a prompt problem.
"Never invent tool output"Explicit prohibition.Same failure from the other side. Weak defence, free to include, measurably helps small models.
"Use calculator for arithmetic"Tells it not to compute in its head.Section 2.1: numbers tokenize badly and models are unreliable at arithmetic. The tool exists precisely so the model does not have to be.
Action with both tool and final optionalOne model covers both shapes.Simpler than two models plus discrimination logic. Empty-string defaults mean "absent", which is easy to test.
Action.model_validate_json(extract_json(raw))Parse and validate in one step.Reuses the fence-stripping from section 3.4. A model that returns prose around its JSON still works.
except (ValidationError, JSONDecodeError) → observationAn unparseable reply becomes feedback, not a crash.The model gets told its output was malformed and tries again. This is the repair loop from 3.4, operating inside the agent loop.
if action.final: checked before action.toolOrder matters.Models sometimes emit both. Preferring final means a model that has decided it is done gets to stop, rather than making one more pointless tool call.
for n in range(1, max_steps + 1)A bounded loop, not while True.Non-negotiable. The architecture provides no termination guarantee. A while True agent loop is how people wake up to a 40,000-call bill.
max_tool_calls as a separate limitTwo independent budgets.Steps count model calls; tool calls count actions. A model that emits five malformed replies burns steps without touching tools — you want to catch both patterns.
spec.requires_approval check before call_toolThe approval gate.Placed before execution, so nothing happens until a human agrees. And note the default: approve=None means deny, not allow. Fail closed.
"Do not retry it; continue without it."Instruction inside the denial observation.Without it, models retry the denied call two or three times. The observation is your only channel to steer behaviour mid-loop — use it.
continue after a failed stepThe loop proceeds, error in context.This is what makes the agent self-correcting. You will see it fix its own argument typo in the output below.
result.messages retainedKeeps the full transcript.Feeds the trace viewer in M18 and your tracing in Part 10. Also the only way to debug an agent that went sideways.
scripted_modelA fake model returning a fixed sequence.The most useful test tool in the file. You can exercise every branch — malformed JSON, unknown tool, denial, step limit — deterministically, offline, in milliseconds. Every output in this section came from it.

Step 2 is the payoff. The model typed expresion. Pydantic rejected it, the error became an observation, and step 3 fixed it — no exception, no crash, no human. That self-correction loop is what an agent is, and it exists because call_tool returns a message instead of raising.
