Note tool calls: 0 in run 2 — the denied call never executed, so nothing was written and nothing was counted. And run 3 shows the limit doing its job: three identical searches, then a clean stop with an honest answer rather than an infinite loop. Section 6.11 adds detection so you catch that pattern at step 2 instead of the limit.

M7 and M8 are done. git commit -m "M7+M8: tools and a hand-built agent loop". You have an agent. It is about 250 lines including tools, it self-corrects, it asks permission before writing, and it cannot run away.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
Model writes the whole conversation itself, inventing observationsIt is completing a document, and your transcript looks like one.Add "stop": ["OBSERVATION:"] to your sampling options (section 2.6). This mechanically prevents it, which is far more reliable than asking.
Every step fails to parse on a small model1.7B models struggle to emit clean JSON unprompted.Turn on JSON mode or schema-constrained decoding (section 3.4), and put one complete example action in the system prompt.
Agent loops on the same tool foreverThe observation does not answer the question and the model has no better idea.The step limit catches it. Add the thrashing detector from 6.10, and consider injecting "that approach is not working, try something different" after two identical calls.
KeyError: 'tools' from .format()Unescaped braces in the system prompt.Double every literal brace, or switch to string.Template as in section 3.7.
Approval prompt never appearsapprove=None, which denies by default.Pass a callable. The fail-closed default is deliberate.
Try this yourself. Replace scripted_model with a real call to your Ollama backend from section 4.2 — the signature is Callable[[list[dict]], str], so it is a three-line adapter. Then run the same question. Expect your 1.7B model to fail at JSON, hallucinate observations, or loop. Fix it with JSON mode plus a stop sequence, and you will have earned every line of section 3.4.

6.5 Native tool calling versus the JSON protocol

We used a hand-rolled JSON protocol. Most APIs also offer native tool calling: you send a tools array of JSON Schemas, and the model returns a structured tool_calls field instead of text.

JSON protocol (what we built)Native tool calling
Works onEvery model, including 1B localsOnly models fine-tuned for it, and only on APIs that expose it
ReliabilityDepends on your prompt and JSON modeHigher — the format is trained in, and often grammar-constrained
Parallel tool callsNo (one per turn by design)Yes, many APIs return several at once
VisibilityTotal. You can read every byte.Provider-shaped. Fine, but more magic.
PortabilityYours, works everywhereBroadly OpenAI-shaped, with per-provider differences

In production, prefer native tool calling where available. For learning — and for staying model agnostic on tiny local models — the JSON protocol is better, which is why the capstone uses it.

I am not going to write the native version for you. Ollama, Groq and the OpenAI-compatible providers all accept a tools parameter, and your ToolSpec.json_schema() already produces most of what they want — but the exact envelope (tool_choice, how tool_calls come back, whether the reply uses a tool role and requires a tool_call_id) differs between providers and has changed across versions. Read Ollama's API docs and your provider's tool-calling page, print one real response, and build against what you actually see. Inventing a signature here would cost you an hour of debugging.

What transfers unchanged: the registry, the Pydantic argument models, call_tool's validate-and-report behaviour, the limits, and the approval gate. Only the parsing step changes.

6.6 M9 — the same loop in LangGraph, and an honest comparison

LangGraph (MIT, free) models an agent as a state graph: nodes are functions, edges are transitions, and a conditional edge decides whether to loop back to the model or finish. It is the most widely used agent framework, and it maps almost one-to-one onto what you just built.

Your hand-built loopLangGraph equivalent
messages listThe graph State, typically with an add_messages reducer
call_model(messages)An agent node
call_tool(name, args)A ToolNode
if action.final: returnA conditional edge to END
for n in range(max_steps)recursion_limit in the config
approve=... gateinterrupt_before plus a checkpointer
result.messages for the traceCheckpointed state, inspectable per step

Version caution, stated plainly. LangGraph's API has moved quickly — create_react_agent's location and signature, the checkpointer packages, and the interrupt API have all changed across releases. Any concrete code I write here has a real chance of being stale by the time you run it, and debugging a framework example that was wrong to begin with is a miserable way to spend an evening. So: the shape below is stable and worth knowing; get the exact imports and signatures from the LangGraph docs and pin the version you develop against.

"""M9: the same agent as a LangGraph state machine. SKETCH -- check the docs."""

# The concepts, in the order they appear in every LangGraph agent:
#
# 1. A State: a TypedDict whose "messages" key uses the add_messages reducer,
#    so returning a message from a node appends rather than replaces.
#
# 2. Nodes: plain functions State -> partial State.
#      def agent(state): return {"messages": [llm_with_tools.invoke(state["messages"])]}
#    plus a prebuilt ToolNode that executes whatever tool calls the model emitted.
#
# 3. Edges: START -> "agent", then a conditional edge from "agent" that routes to
#    "tools" if the last message contains tool calls, or to END if it does not.
#    Then "tools" -> "agent", which closes the loop.
#
# 4. Compile with a checkpointer (in-memory or SQLite) to get persistence,
#    time travel, and interrupt/resume for human approval.
#
# 5. Invoke with a config carrying a thread_id (the conversation) and a
#    recursion_limit (your max_steps).

When the framework wins, and when it does not

Use LangGraph whenKeep your own loop when
You need persistence and resume across process restarts — checkpointers give you this properly, and rolling your own is real work.The agent is simple: one loop, a handful of tools, one process.
You need human-in-the-loop with interrupt and resume days later, not just a synchronous prompt.Approval is a synchronous question, as in 6.4.
The control flow is genuinely a graph: branches, parallel nodes, subgraphs, cycles with different exits.The control flow is a loop with one exit.
You want the streaming and tracing integrations (LangSmith, and Langfuse via callbacks) for free.You want to read every byte and own every dependency.
A team needs a shared vocabulary — "add a node" is a clearer instruction than "edit the loop".You are learning, or debugging something subtle.

My honest recommendation. Build M8 by hand — you have — and keep it as the capstone's agent. Then rebuild it once in LangGraph as an exercise, and compare the traces. You will find the framework version is shorter, harder to debug, and better at persistence. Adopt it when you need checkpointing or interrupt/resume; those are the two features genuinely painful to write yourself. Do not adopt it because a tutorial did. A lot of "we need an agent framework" is a 100-line loop and a dependency you now have to keep upgrading.

6.7 M10 — memory

Section 6.2 showed context growing monotonically. Memory is how you stop that from becoming your whole context window. Four kinds, and they solve different problems:

KindWhat it holdsWhere it livesRetrieved how
Short-term / workingThe current conversation's messages.A Python list, sent every turn.All of it, until it gets too big.
Summarised short-termA compressed account of older turns.One string in the same context.Always included.
Long-term semanticDurable facts about the user: preferences, project names, constraints.A vector store, or a plain key-value file.Retrieved by similarity, or always loaded if small.
Long-term episodicWhat happened in past sessions: "last Tuesday you asked me to compare X and Y and we concluded Z".A vector store of session summaries.Retrieved by similarity to the current question.

Start with the first two. Buffer plus summarisation covers most real needs and is forty lines. Long-term memory sounds impressive and introduces a genuinely hard problem: deciding what is worth remembering, and what to do when a remembered "fact" is stale or was wrong. A system that confidently recalls a preference you changed three months ago is worse than one with no memory at all.

Build a message buffer that summarises its own oldest turns when it exceeds a token budget, and persists between runs.

"""M10: short-term memory with summarisation, plus session persistence."""

import json
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Callable

STATE_DIR = Path("data/sessions")


def estimate_tokens(text: str) -> int:
    """The ~4-chars-per-token rule from section 2.1. Replace with a real count if precision matters."""
    return max(1, round(len(text) / 4))


@dataclass
class ConversationMemory:
    """A message buffer that summarises its own oldest turns when it grows too big."""
    token_budget: int = 200
    keep_recent: int = 4
    summary: str = ""
    messages: list[dict] = field(default_factory=list)

    def add(self, role: str, content: str) -> None:
        self.messages.append({"role": role, "content": content})

    def used_tokens(self) -> int:
        return sum(estimate_tokens(m["content"]) for m in self.messages) + \
               estimate_tokens(self.summary)

    def compact(self, summarise: Callable[[str], str]) -> bool:
        """Summarise everything except the most recent turns. Returns True if it ran."""
        if self.used_tokens() <= self.token_budget:
            return False
        if len(self.messages) <= self.keep_recent:
            return False
        old = self.messages[:-self.keep_recent]
        recent = self.messages[-self.keep_recent:]
        transcript = "\n".join(f"{m['role']}: {m['content']}" for m in old)
        if self.summary:
            transcript = f"Earlier summary: {self.summary}\n{transcript}"
        self.summary = summarise(transcript)
        self.messages = recent
        return True

    def render(self, system_prompt: str) -> list[dict]:
        """Build the message list actually sent to the model."""
        out = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}]
        if self.summary:
            out.append({"role": "system",
                        "content": f"Notes from earlier in this conversation:\n{self.summary}"})
        out.extend(self.messages)
        return out

    def save(self, session_id: str, path: Path = STATE_DIR) -> None:
        path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        (path / f"{session_id}.json").write_text(json.dumps(
            {"summary": self.summary, "messages": self.messages}, indent=1), encoding="utf-8")

    @classmethod
    def load(cls, session_id: str, path: Path = STATE_DIR, **kwargs):
        """Resume a session, or start a fresh one if it does not exist."""
        file = path / f"{session_id}.json"
        memory = cls(**kwargs)
        if file.exists():
            data = json.loads(file.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
            memory.summary = data.get("summary", "")
            memory.messages = data.get("messages", [])
        return memory


if __name__ == "__main__":
    def fake_summariser(transcript: str) -> str:
        """Stand-in for a model call, so this file runs offline and deterministically."""
        carried = [l[len("Earlier summary: "):].replace("Topics so far: ", "")
                   for l in transcript.splitlines()
                   if l.startswith("Earlier summary: ")]
        asked = [l[len("user: "):].strip()[:34] for l in transcript.splitlines()
                 if l.startswith("user: ")]
        parts = carried + asked
        return "Topics so far: " + "; ".join(p for p in parts if p)

    memory = ConversationMemory(token_budget=40, keep_recent=4)
    turns = [
        ("user", "What port does Ollama use?"),
        ("assistant", "Port 11434 on localhost."),
        ("user", "How much memory for an 8B model?"),
        ("assistant", "About 5.5 GB at Q4_K_M including the KV cache."),
        ("user", "And for a 3B model?"),
        ("assistant", "Roughly 2.8 GB at the same quantisation."),
        ("user", "Which should I run on 8 GB?"),
        ("assistant", "The 3B, so the OS keeps headroom."),
    ]

    for i, (role, content) in enumerate(turns, start=1):
        memory.add(role, content)
        ran = memory.compact(fake_summariser)
        print(f"turn {i}: {memory.used_tokens():>3} tokens, "
              f"{len(memory.messages)} messages, compacted={ran}")

    print(f"\nsummary: {memory.summary}")
    print(f"\nrendered context ({len(memory.render('SYSTEM'))} messages):")
    for m in memory.render("SYSTEM"):
        print(f"  {m['role']:<9} {m['content'][:64]}")

    memory.save("demo-session")
    reloaded = ConversationMemory.load("demo-session", token_budget=40)
    print(f"\nreloaded: {len(reloaded.messages)} messages, "
          f"summary present: {bool(reloaded.summary)}")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
token_budget and keep_recentTwo independent controls.The budget decides when to compact; keep_recent decides how much stays verbatim. Recent turns must stay literal because pronouns and follow-ups depend on exact wording.
used_tokens including the summaryCounts the summary too.Otherwise a growing summary silently eats the budget you thought you were protecting.
if used_tokens() <= budget: return FalseCompacts only when necessary.Summarising costs a model call. Doing it every turn triples your latency for nothing.
old = messages[:-keep_recent]Everything except the tail.Negative slicing keeps this readable. Note it can be empty, hence the length guard above.
if self.summary: transcript = f"Earlier summary: ..."Feeds the previous summary into the new one.Essential and dangerous. Without it, the second compaction throws away everything the first one preserved. With it, you get summary drift: each pass re-summarises a summary, and detail decays. Mitigate by keeping the summary short and prefixed clearly, and by never compacting more often than you must.
summarise: Callable[[str], str]The summariser is injected.Same pattern as sections 3.4 and 4.6 — so this file is testable offline, as the output below demonstrates.
summary rendered as a system messageNot as a user or assistant turn.It is metadata about the conversation, not part of it. Putting it in a user message invites the model to respond to it as though the user just said it.
render() building the list freshAssembles system, summary, then messages.Keeps ordering in one place. Section 3.2: order is meaningful, and the system prompt must be first.
save / load by session_idJSON file per session.Gives you resume across process restarts — the "state persistence between runs" requirement. Enough for a local-first app; use SQLite or Postgres when you have concurrent users.
load returning a fresh instance when absentNo exception on first use."Resume or start" is one call. A FileNotFoundError here would force every caller to handle it.

Expected output

turn 1:   7 tokens, 1 messages, compacted=False
turn 2:  13 tokens, 2 messages, compacted=False
turn 3:  21 tokens, 3 messages, compacted=False
turn 4:  33 tokens, 4 messages, compacted=False
turn 5:  38 tokens, 5 messages, compacted=False
turn 6:  45 tokens, 4 messages, compacted=True
turn 7:  53 tokens, 4 messages, compacted=True
turn 8:  49 tokens, 4 messages, compacted=True

summary: Topics so far: What port does Ollama use?; How much memory for an 8B model?

rendered context (6 messages):
  system    SYSTEM
  system    Notes from earlier in this conversation:
Topics so far: What por
  user      And for a 3B model?
  assistant Roughly 2.8 GB at the same quantisation.
  user      Which should I run on 8 GB?
  assistant The 3B, so the OS keeps headroom.

reloaded: 4 messages, summary present: True

Watch turn 6: the buffer crossed 40 tokens, compacted, and dropped from 6 messages back to 4 — with the first two questions now living in the summary. From then on the message count stays flat while the conversation continues. That flat line is the whole objective: a conversation of unbounded length in a context of bounded size.

Turn 8 dipping to 49 tokens from 53 is the summariser producing a shorter summary than the text it replaced. That will not always happen, and it is why you must count the summary in the budget.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
The agent forgets something it was told two turns agokeep_recent is too small, or compaction dropped a detail.Raise keep_recent. Also improve the summariser prompt — section 3.7's SUMMARISE_HISTORY explicitly asks it to keep decisions, facts, names and open questions.
Summary becomes vague nonsense after a long chatSummary drift from repeated re-summarisation.Summarise from the original transcript when you can afford to keep it, rather than from the previous summary. Or cap compaction count per session and start a new session.
Context still overflows despite the budgetTool observations are large and land in messages.Truncate tool output (section 6.3) and consider dropping old observations entirely while keeping the model's own turns — observations are usually the bulkiest and least reusable content.
Two browser tabs corrupt each other's session fileLast write wins on a shared JSON file.Fine for local-first single-user. For real concurrency use SQLite with a transaction, or a checkpointer (6.6).
Try this yourself. Wire the real summariser: pass a lambda that calls render("summarise_history", words="120", history=transcript) from section 3.7's template library through your Ollama backend. Then have a 30-turn conversation and read the summary. If it has lost something important, the fix is in the prompt, not the code — which is a useful thing to discover on purpose.
Deeper dive: long-term memory, and the hard part nobody mentions

The mechanics are easy: embed each fact, store it, retrieve by similarity — you built all of that in Part 5. The hard parts are policy questions with no library answer:

  • What is worth storing? Store everything and retrieval fills with noise. Store selectively and you need a model call per turn deciding, which is expensive and unreliable. A common compromise: store only explicit statements of preference and constraint ("I only use Angular", "my machine has 8 GB"), which you can detect with a cheap classifier.
  • How do you update a fact? The user upgrades their machine. The old memory is now wrong, and vector search has no notion of supersession. You need keys and overwrites, which means structured memory, not just embeddings.
  • How do you forget? Legally (deletion requests) and practically (stale preferences). Design for deletion from day one; retrofitting it into a vector index is painful.
  • What if the memory is wrong? A confidently recalled false fact is a hallucination with extra credibility. Surface memories in the UI — "using your saved note: 8 GB RAM" — so the user can correct them. Invisible memory is unfixable memory.

My advice for the capstone: implement a small explicit user_facts.json the user can see and edit, loaded into every prompt. It is more useful than a semantic memory store, and it has none of these problems.

6.8 Planning patterns

Five named patterns you will see in papers and framework docs. What each actually is, and whether it is worth your time.

PatternMechanismExtra costVerdict
ReAct (Reason + Act)Interleave a thought with each action, one step at a time. You already built this — the thought field in Action is ReAct.None beyond the thought tokens.The default. Simple, robust, self-correcting. Start and usually finish here.
Plan-and-ExecuteModel writes a full multi-step plan first, then executes each step, optionally replanning.One extra model call up front; often fewer total calls afterwards.Useful for long tasks where ReAct wanders. Risk: a bad plan burns the entire budget before anyone notices, and models are worse at planning than at reacting. Add replanning after failures or do not bother.
ReflexionAfter a failed attempt, the model critiques its own trajectory and retries with that critique in context.Roughly doubles cost on failures.Genuinely helps where success is verifiable — code that runs, a test that passes, a citation that checks out. Near-useless where it cannot tell it failed. Note your citation verifier from 5.7 is exactly the verifiable signal Reflexion needs.
Tree of ThoughtsExplore several reasoning branches, score them, keep the best, backtrack.5–20× the calls.Overrated for applications. Impressive on puzzles with a clear scoring function; almost never worth it on document questions or tool use, where the cost multiple buys very little. Know the name for interviews; do not build it.
RouterOne cheap classification call picks a specialised path, tool subset, or model.One small call, often on a smaller model.Underrated. Cheapest meaningful quality win available: keeps tool counts low per path, lets you send easy questions to a 1.7B model and hard ones to a 8B, and makes traces legible. Section 6.9 builds one.

The pattern that matters most is not on this list: stopping. Most agent failures are not bad reasoning, they are failure to stop — looping, re-searching, re-asking. Spend your effort on termination conditions, thrashing detection and budgets (6.10, 6.11) before you spend it on fancier planning.

6.9 M11 — a supervisor routing between two agents

Multi-agent means one agent's output becomes another's input. The useful shapes:

TopologyShapeGood forHonest risk
SequentialA → B → C, fixedPipelines with distinct phases: research then write.It is a chain. Do not call it multi-agent in an interview without noticing that.
Supervisor / workerA router delegates to specialists and collects resultsThe one to use. Keeps each worker's tool set and prompt small.The supervisor becomes a single point of confusion. Keep its job to routing only.
HierarchicalSupervisors of supervisorsGenuinely large task trees.Traces become unreadable, costs multiply, errors compound silently. Rarely justified.
Debate / criticTwo agents argue, or one critiques the otherWhere you have no automatic verifier and want a second opinion.Both agents share the same blind spots. Frequently produces confident agreement rather than useful disagreement.

When multi-agent is overkill, which is most of the time. Two agents cost twice the calls, and information is lost at every handoff — worker B only sees what A chose to write down. Before splitting, ask whether a single agent with a larger tool set would do. The legitimate reasons to split are: tool-count pressure (one agent with 25 tools picks badly), different permissions (a read-only researcher and a write-capable author), and different models (a 1.7B router, an 8B writer). "It seems more organised" is not a reason.

Route a request, run a read-only research agent, then hand its findings to a writer agent that may write files.

"""M11: a supervisor that routes between a research agent and a writer agent."""

import json
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Callable

from app.agent.loop import AgentResult, run_agent, scripted_model

ROUTER_PROMPT = """Classify the request into exactly one route.

Routes:
- research: needs facts from the user's documents or a calculation
- write: needs a document produced from facts already established
- direct: can be answered immediately with no tools

Reply with only the route name.

Request: {request}
Route:"""


@dataclass
class SupervisorRun:
    route: str
    legs: list[tuple[str, AgentResult]] = field(default_factory=list)
    answer: str = ""

    def total_tool_calls(self) -> int:
        return sum(r.tool_calls for _, r in self.legs)


def route(request: str, ask: Callable[[str], str]) -> str:
    """One cheap classification call. Defaults to research if unclear."""
    raw = ask(ROUTER_PROMPT.format(request=request)).strip().lower()
    for candidate in ("research", "write", "direct"):
        if candidate in raw:
            return candidate
    return "research"


def run_supervised(
    request: str,
    ask: Callable[[str], str],
    research_model: Callable[[list[dict]], str],
    writer_model: Callable[[list[dict]], str],
    approve: Callable[[str, dict], bool] | None = None,
) -> SupervisorRun:
    """Route once, then run the chosen worker(s) in sequence."""
    chosen = route(request, ask)
    run = SupervisorRun(route=chosen)

    if chosen == "direct":
        run.answer = ask(request)
        return run

    findings = run_agent(request, research_model, approve=approve, verbose=False)
    run.legs.append(("research", findings))
    run.answer = findings.answer

    if chosen == "write":
        handoff = (f"Findings from the research agent:\n{findings.answer}\n\n"
                   f"Original request: {request}")
        written = run_agent(handoff, writer_model, approve=approve, verbose=False)
        run.legs.append(("writer", written))
        run.answer = written.answer

    return run


if __name__ == "__main__":
    request = ("Work out whether my server can handle 240 requests per minute using my "
               "notes, then save a short memo about it.")

    def ask(prompt: str) -> str:
        """Stand-in for a small routing model, so this runs offline."""
        return "write" if "Route:" in prompt else "(direct answer)"

    research_replies = [
        json.dumps({"thought": "Find the request time and worker count.",
                    "tool": "search_notes",
                    "args": {"query": "request takes ms server runs workers"}}),
        json.dumps({"thought": "Compute capacity.",
                    "tool": "calculator", "args": {"expression": "4 * (1/0.150) * 60"}}),
        json.dumps({"thought": "Done researching.",
                    "final": "Capacity is 1600 req/min vs 240 required (hardware.md#10)."}),
    ]
    writer_replies = [
        json.dumps({"thought": "Write the memo.", "tool": "write_file",
                    "args": {"filename": "memo.md",
                             "content": "# Capacity\n\n1600 req/min vs 240 required.\n"}}),
        json.dumps({"thought": "Memo saved.",
                    "final": "Memo written to memo.md: capacity 1600 req/min vs 240 required."}),
    ]

    run = run_supervised(request, ask,
                         scripted_model(research_replies),
                         scripted_model(writer_replies),
                         approve=lambda t, a: True)

    print(f"route            : {run.route}")
    print(f"legs             : {[name for name, _ in run.legs]}")
    print(f"total tool calls : {run.total_tool_calls()}")
    for name, result in run.legs:
        print(f"\n[{name}] {len(result.steps)} steps, stop={result.stop_reason}")
        for s in result.steps:
            print(f"   {s.n} {s.tool or 'FINAL':<13} {'ok' if s.ok else 'ERR'}")
    print(f"\nfinal answer     : {run.answer}")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
ROUTER_PROMPT ending in Route:Section 3.1's completion cue, reused.Makes a bare label the most likely continuation. Routing is classification, so use the classification prompt shape.
for candidate in (...): if candidate in rawSubstring matching rather than equality.Models say "research." or "Route: research". Tolerant parsing here is correct; the route set is closed and safe, so there is no injection risk in accepting a substring.
return "research" as the fallbackUnclear routing defaults to the safe path.Fail toward the read-only agent, never toward the one that can write files. Defaults are security decisions.
ask: Callable[[str], str] separate from the agent modelsThe router uses a plain completion, not the agent loop.Routing needs one token, not a loop. In production point ask at a 1.7B model and the workers at something larger — most of the router's value is being cheap.
SupervisorRun.legsRecords each worker's full result.Without this the trace is a black box. The M18 trace viewer renders these as collapsible sections per leg.
handoff = f"Findings from the research agent:..."Explicit handoff message.The critical design point. The writer sees only this text, not the researcher's tool calls or retrieved chunks. Information loss at handoffs is the main cost of multi-agent, so make the handoff carry everything the next agent needs — including citations.
including the original request in the handoffNot just the findings.Otherwise the writer does not know what it is writing for. Handoffs that pass only results produce documents that answer the wrong question.
both workers share the same approveOne approval policy.The researcher never triggers it (no approval-gated tools), the writer does. The gate belongs to the tool, not the agent — which is why requires_approval lives on ToolSpec.
run.answer reassigned after each legThe last leg's answer wins.Simple and predictable. If you need both, return the whole legs list — which it does.

Expected output

route            : write
legs             : ['research', 'writer']
total tool calls : 3

[research] 3 steps, stop=final
   1 search_notes  ok
   2 calculator    ok
   3 FINAL         ok

[writer] 2 steps, stop=final
   1 write_file    ok
   2 FINAL         ok

final answer     : Memo written to memo.md: capacity 1600 req/min vs 240 required.

Five steps across two agents, three tool calls, one approval prompt. Compare that with running a single agent that has all three tools: it would work too, and it would be simpler. What the split buys here is that the research agent structurally cannot write files — enforced by which tools it is given, not by asking it nicely. That is the honest justification for this topology.

M10 and M11 are done. git commit -m "M10+M11: memory and a supervisor".

Try this yourself. Give each worker its own tool subset by passing an allowed-tools set into run_agent and filtering tool_docs() accordingly — the allow-list from 6.10 gives you the data. Then confirm the research agent's prompt no longer mentions write_file at all. A tool the model cannot see is a tool it cannot misuse.

6.10 M12 — guardrails and human-in-the-loop

Your agent can now search, calculate and write files, in a loop, on behalf of text produced by a statistical model that may have read a hostile PDF (section 3.6). This section is where that stops being alarming.

The layers, in order of how much they actually protect you

LayerWhat it stops
1. Tool allow-lists per roleA research agent writing files at all. The strongest control, because it removes the capability rather than policing its use.
2. Argument validationPath traversal, oversized requests, code injection. Built in 6.3.
3. Human approval on risky toolsAnything irreversible: writing, sending, spending, deleting. Built in 6.4.
4. Budget capsRunaway loops burning tokens, time and money.
5. Loop / thrashing detectionThe specific pattern of an agent repeating itself pointlessly.
6. PII redactionPersonal data reaching a hosted model or a log file.
7. Output checksLeaked system prompts, unverified citations, unexpected URLs.

Build the guardrail primitives: redaction, allow-lists, budgets, and thrashing detection.

"""M12: guardrails -- input/output checks, PII redaction, and budget caps."""

import re
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

EMAIL = re.compile(r"\b[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]{2,}\b")
PHONE = re.compile(r"\b(?:\+?\d{1,3}[ -]?)?(?:\(?\d{2,4}\)?[ -]?){2,4}\d{2,4}\b")
CARD = re.compile(r"\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b")
IBAN = re.compile(r"\b[A-Z]{2}\d{2}[A-Z0-9]{10,30}\b")

# Order matters: cards and IBANs before phones, or the phone pattern eats them.
REDACTIONS = [("EMAIL", EMAIL), ("CARD", CARD), ("IBAN", IBAN), ("PHONE", PHONE)]


def redact(text: str) -> tuple[str, dict[str, int]]:
    """Replace obvious personal data. Returns the cleaned text and what was found."""
    counts: dict[str, int] = {}
    for label, pattern in REDACTIONS:
        text, n = pattern.subn(f"[{label}_REDACTED]", text)
        if n:
            counts[label] = n
    return text, counts


class BudgetExceeded(RuntimeError):
    pass


@dataclass
class Budget:
    """Hard caps so a runaway agent stops instead of running all night."""
    max_tool_calls: int = 8
    max_model_calls: int = 10
    max_tokens: int = 20_000
    max_seconds: float = 120.0
    tool_calls: int = 0
    model_calls: int = 0
    tokens: int = 0
    started: float = field(default_factory=time.perf_counter)

    def spend_tool(self) -> None:
        self.tool_calls += 1
        self.check()

    def spend_model(self, tokens: int) -> None:
        self.model_calls += 1
        self.tokens += tokens
        self.check()

    def elapsed(self) -> float:
        return time.perf_counter() - self.started

    def check(self) -> None:
        if self.tool_calls > self.max_tool_calls:
            raise BudgetExceeded(f"tool calls: {self.tool_calls} > {self.max_tool_calls}")
        if self.model_calls > self.max_model_calls:
            raise BudgetExceeded(f"model calls: {self.model_calls} > {self.max_model_calls}")
        if self.tokens > self.max_tokens:
            raise BudgetExceeded(f"tokens: {self.tokens} > {self.max_tokens}")
        if self.elapsed() > self.max_seconds:
            raise BudgetExceeded(f"time: {self.elapsed():.1f}s > {self.max_seconds}s")


ALLOWED_TOOLS_BY_ROLE = {
    "reader": {"search_notes", "calculator"},
    "writer": {"search_notes", "calculator", "write_file"},
}


def tool_allowed(role: str, tool: str) -> bool:
    """Unknown roles get nothing. Fail closed."""
    return tool in ALLOWED_TOOLS_BY_ROLE.get(role, set())


LOOP_WINDOW = 3


def is_thrashing(history: list[tuple[str, str]]) -> bool:
    """True if the last LOOP_WINDOW tool calls are identical."""
    if len(history) < LOOP_WINDOW:
        return False
    return len(set(history[-LOOP_WINDOW:])) == 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    text = ("Contact me at ada@example.com or +44 20 7946 0958. "
            "Card 4111 1111 1111 1111, IBAN GB29NWBK60161331926819.")
    clean, counts = redact(text)
    print("redaction:")
    print(f"  before: {text}")
    print(f"  after : {clean}")
    print(f"  counts: {counts}")

    print("\nallow-lists:")
    for role, tool in [("reader", "search_notes"), ("reader", "write_file"),
                       ("writer", "write_file"), ("ghost", "calculator")]:
        print(f"  {role:<7} -> {tool:<13} {tool_allowed(role, tool)}")

    print("\nbudget:")
    budget = Budget(max_tool_calls=3)
    try:
        for i in range(1, 6):
            budget.spend_tool()
            print(f"  tool call {i}: ok ({budget.tool_calls}/{budget.max_tool_calls})")
    except BudgetExceeded as exc:
        print(f"  STOPPED: {exc}")

    print("\nloop detection:")
    history = [("search_notes", '{"query": "ollama port"}')] * 2
    print(f"  after 2 identical calls: thrashing={is_thrashing(history)}")
    history.append(("search_notes", '{"query": "ollama port"}'))
    print(f"  after 3 identical calls: thrashing={is_thrashing(history)}")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
REDACTIONS as an ordered listCards and IBANs are matched before phone numbers.The phone pattern is greedy enough to swallow a card number. Ordering is the fix, and it is why this is a list rather than a dict.
pattern.subn(...)Substitutes and returns a count.You want the count: "3 emails redacted" is a log line and a UI badge. sub alone would silently hide how much was found.
Budget with four independent limitsTool calls, model calls, tokens, wall clock.Different runaways look different. A model emitting malformed JSON burns model calls and no tools. A verbose tool burns tokens. A slow local model burns time. One limit catches one pattern.
field(default_factory=time.perf_counter)Starts the clock when the object is created.started = time.perf_counter() as a plain default would freeze at import time and every budget would already be expired.
check() called from both spend methodsOne place enforces all limits.Adding a limit later means editing one function. Scattered checks drift.
raise BudgetExceeded rather than returning FalseAn exception, not a flag.Unlike tool errors, this is not something the model should see and work around — it is your code deciding to stop. Catch it at the top of the loop and return a partial answer.
ALLOWED_TOOLS_BY_ROLE.get(role, set())Unknown role → empty set.Fail closed. A typo in a role name must deny everything, not allow everything. Same principle as approve=None meaning deny.
is_thrashing on (tool, args_json) tuplesCompares name and arguments.Three searches with different queries is progress; three identical searches is a loop. The distinction is in the arguments, so the history must include them.
len(set(history[-3:])) == 1All three identical.Concise and clear. Tune the window: 2 is trigger-happy, 5 wastes budget before firing.

Expected output

redaction:
  before: Contact me at ada@example.com or +44 20 7946 0958. Card 4111 1111 1111 1111, IBAN GB29NWBK60161331926819.
  after : Contact me at [EMAIL_REDACTED] or +[PHONE_REDACTED]. Card [CARD_REDACTED], IBAN [IBAN_REDACTED].
  counts: {'EMAIL': 1, 'CARD': 1, 'IBAN': 1, 'PHONE': 1}

allow-lists:
  reader  -> search_notes  True
  reader  -> write_file    False
  writer  -> write_file    True
  ghost   -> calculator    False

budget:
  tool call 1: ok (1/3)
  tool call 2: ok (2/3)
  tool call 3: ok (3/3)
  STOPPED: tool calls: 4 > 3

loop detection:
  after 2 identical calls: thrashing=False
  after 3 identical calls: thrashing=True

Look closely at the redacted output: +[PHONE_REDACTED]. The leading + survived, because the pattern matched starting at 44. That is a small, real imperfection and I have left it in deliberately — regex-based PII detection is always approximate. It will leak edge cases and it will also redact things that were not personal data (a version string, a product code). Treat it as risk reduction, never as compliance. If you have a legal obligation, use a purpose-built tool such as Microsoft Presidio (MIT, free) which combines named-entity recognition with pattern matching, and get the policy reviewed by someone whose job that is.

Human-in-the-loop: three shapes, increasingly serious

ShapeHow it worksFits
Synchronous promptThe loop blocks on approve() — a terminal input, or an HTTP request that waits.What 6.4 built. Correct for a local CLI, and for a web app where the user is watching.
Interrupt and resumeThe loop saves its state, returns "awaiting approval", and a later call resumes from the checkpoint.Necessary when approval may take minutes or days, or when the process may restart. This is the LangGraph checkpointer's main selling point (6.6).
Post-hoc reviewThe agent acts freely, everything is logged, a human audits afterwards.Only acceptable for genuinely reversible actions. Never for sending, spending or deleting.

The M12 requirement is the first shape, and the Angular approval dialog in M18 is its UI: the agent pauses, the frontend renders the pending tool name and arguments, the user clicks Approve or Deny, and the loop continues with the answer as an observation. You have already seen both branches work in section 6.4's runs 1 and 2.

What the approval dialog must show. The tool name, every argument in full, and — for a file write — the actual content. An approval prompt that says "the agent wants to write a file. OK?" trains users to click yes, which is worse than no gate at all, because now everyone believes there is one. Show the payload, and make Deny the easier button.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
Redaction breaks legitimate contentVersion numbers and product codes match the phone or card patterns.Redact only on the boundary that needs it — outbound to a hosted model, and log lines — not inside your own retrieval corpus. And log what you redacted so you can see false positives.
Budget never firesYou built the Budget but never called spend_*.Wire it into the loop: spend_model after every model call, spend_tool before every tool call. A guardrail you forgot to invoke is decoration.
Users approve everything without readingThe dialog is vague, or fires too often.Gate fewer tools, and show full arguments. Approval fatigue is a real security failure mode.
Thrashing detector fires on legitimate repeatsSome tasks genuinely re-search with the same query after new information.Widen the window, or exempt read-only tools and only guard side-effecting ones.
Try this yourself. Wire Budget and is_thrashing into run_agent: call spend_tool() inside the tool branch, catch BudgetExceeded around the loop, and when thrashing is detected inject the observation "you have repeated the same call three times; that approach is not working — try a different tool or answer with what you have". Then rerun section 6.4's run 3. It now stops at step 3 with a useful message instead of silently exhausting the limit.

6.11 Failure modes, and what actually fixes them

Every one of these will happen to you. Knowing the name and the mitigation is most of what separates a demo from something you can leave running.

FailureWhat you seeRoot causeMitigation
Infinite loopThe same tool, forever.The observation does not advance the task and the model has no better idea.Step and tool-call limits (6.4). Thrashing detection (6.10). Inject a "change approach" observation.
Tool thrashingAlternating between two tools, making no progress.Ambiguous tool descriptions, or genuinely insufficient information.Sharpen descriptions to say when to use each. Add an explicit "if you cannot find it, say so" instruction — models loop partly because giving up feels unhelpful.
Hallucinated observationsThe model writes its own tool output and continues confidently.It is completing a document that looks like a transcript."stop": ["OBSERVATION:"] in sampling options. One tool per turn in the prompt. This is a mechanical fix; do not rely on instructions alone.
Context overflowErrors about context length, or the agent forgetting the original question mid-run.Every observation accumulates, forever.Truncate tool output (6.3). Compact memory (6.7). Drop old observations while keeping the model's own turns.
Cascading errorsOne wrong fact early, then five steps built on it.Nothing verifies intermediate results.Verify what you can: citations (5.7), arithmetic via the calculator, schema validation. Reflexion (6.8) needs a verifier to work at all — this is what it needs.
Premature stoppingA confident final answer after one failed search.The model does not know it lacks information.Require citations for factual claims and reject answers without them. Add "if search returns nothing relevant, search again with different words before answering".
Cost blowoutA ten-minute run and an empty free-tier quota.No budget, verbose tools, large context, many steps.All four Budget limits. Log tokens per run (4.7). Route easy questions to a smaller model (6.8).
Silent tool failureA plausible answer built on an error message.The model read ERROR ... and treated it as data.Make error observations unmistakable (they start with ERROR for a reason), and check Step.ok in your code — if the last tool call failed, do not present its answer as verified.
Prompt injection through a tool resultThe agent does something nobody asked for, after reading a document.Retrieved text arrives with the same authority as your instructions (3.6).Tool allow-lists and approval gates. Fence and neutralise retrieved text. Accept that the prompt-wording defences are weak and constrain capability instead.

The debugging method. When an agent misbehaves, do not reread your prompt first — print the full message list, exactly as in 6.2, and read it in order. The bug is almost always visible: a truncated observation, an error the model ignored, the original question buried 8,000 tokens back, or a tool description that genuinely does not say what you meant. This is why AgentResult.messages exists, and why Part 10's tracing matters more for agents than for anything else in this course.

6.12 M13 — Model Context Protocol, and a server you write yourself

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. Anthropic introduced it in late 2024 and it has since been adopted well beyond them. The problem it solves is combinatorial: without a standard, every AI client needs a bespoke integration for every tool, so N clients × M tools means N×M integrations. With MCP, a tool implements the protocol once and every compliant client can use it.

TermWhat it isIn our capstone
Host / clientThe AI application that wants tools — an IDE, a desktop assistant, your agent.Your agent loop, or any MCP-capable editor or desktop app.
ServerA process exposing capabilities over the protocol.What you write below: your knowledge base, exposed to any client.
ToolsFunctions the model may call.search_notes, list_sources.
ResourcesReadable data identified by URI, more like files than functions.A document by name.
PromptsReusable prompt templates the client can offer the user.Your Part 3 templates.
TransportHow client and server talk: stdio for local subprocesses, HTTP-based transports for remote.stdio locally.

Why it matters to you specifically

Once your knowledge base is an MCP server, it stops being locked inside your app. The same index you built in M4 becomes available to any MCP-capable client on your machine — which is a genuinely different value proposition from "my app can search my notes". It is also the clearest demonstration that your retrieval layer is properly separated from your agent layer: if you can expose it over a protocol, you have designed it well.

uv pip install mcp

Expose the Second Brain knowledge base as an MCP server over stdio.

"""M13: expose the Second Brain knowledge base as an MCP server."""

import json
from collections import Counter

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("second-brain")


@mcp.tool()
def search_notes(query: str, top_k: int = 3) -> str:
    """Search the user's indexed documents. Returns chunks with source and chunk_id.

    Args:
        query: What to look for.
        top_k: How many chunks to return (1-10).
    """
    top_k = max(1, min(10, top_k))
    try:
        from app.rag import retrieve
        hits = retrieve(query, top_k=top_k)
    except Exception as exc:                           # noqa: BLE001
        return json.dumps({"error": f"index unavailable: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"})
    return json.dumps([
        {"source": h["source"], "chunk_id": h["chunk_id"], "text": h["text"][:600]}
        for h in hits
    ])


@mcp.tool()
def list_sources() -> str:
    """List every document in the index, with how many chunks each contributed."""
    try:
        from app.embeddings import SentenceTransformerEmbedder
        from app.store import LocalVectorStore

        embedder = SentenceTransformerEmbedder()
        store = LocalVectorStore.load(embedder.name, embedder.dimensions)
    except Exception as exc:                           # noqa: BLE001
        return json.dumps({"error": f"index unavailable: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"})

    counts = Counter(chunk.source for chunk in store.chunks)
    return json.dumps({
        "documents": [{"source": s, "chunks": n} for s, n in counts.most_common()],
        "total_chunks": len(store.chunks),
    })


if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="stdio")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCPImports the high-level server helper from the official Python SDK.The low-level API means implementing JSON-RPC handlers by hand. FastMCP turns decorated functions into protocol-compliant tools. Verify this import path — see the warning below.
FastMCP("second-brain")Names the server.The name clients display when listing available servers.
@mcp.tool()Registers the function as a callable tool.The decorator derives the JSON Schema from your type hints and the tool description from your docstring. This is why the type hints from section 1.2 matter — here they become the API contract.
the docstring with an Args: blockDocuments each parameter.It is not a comment — it becomes the description the calling model reads. A vague docstring here is a vague tool description, which produces wrong calls.
max(1, min(10, top_k))Clamps rather than validates.Deliberate difference from 6.3: an MCP client is not our agent loop, and returning an error for an out-of-range value is less useful than quietly doing something sensible. Clamp inputs at protocol boundaries; validate strictly inside your own loop.
return json.dumps({"error": ...})Errors as data, not exceptions.Same principle as call_tool. An exception crossing the protocol boundary is far less useful to the calling model than a readable error string.
lazy imports inside the functionsapp.rag and the store load on first use.Keeps server startup fast — MCP clients spawn servers on demand — and means a missing index does not prevent the server from starting.
list_sources as a second toolLets a client see what is indexed.Enormously useful in practice: a model that can list documents asks better questions than one that can only search blindly.
Counter(chunk.source ...)Groups chunks by document.Turns 84 chunks into "7 documents", which is what a human or model actually wants to know.
mcp.run(transport="stdio")Serves over standard input/output.The client launches your script as a subprocess and talks over its stdin/stdout. Consequence: never print() in an MCP stdio server — stray output corrupts the protocol stream. Log to stderr or a file.

Verify the SDK surface before you rely on this. MCP is young and moving: the Python SDK's module layout, the transport names, and the shape of remote transports have all changed since the protocol launched, and a standalone fastmcp package exists alongside the version bundled in the official mcp SDK. The concepts in the table above are stable; the exact import path and run() arguments are what I would check first. Read modelcontextprotocol.io and the Python SDK repository, and pin the version you develop against.

How to run and test it

# The official inspector is the fastest way to see your tools listed and call them.
# Check the current command in the MCP docs; historically:
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python -m app.mcp_server

# Or configure it in an MCP-capable client's config file, roughly:
#   "second-brain": {
#     "command": "python",
#     "args": ["-m", "app.mcp_server"],
#     "env": {"PYTHONPATH": "backend"}
#   }

Security, because this is a real boundary. An MCP server is a process on your machine that an AI client can invoke. Expose read-only tools unless you have a strong reason otherwise — this server deliberately has no write_file. If you add a writing tool, the approval gate must live on your side, because you cannot assume the client has one. And treat the arguments as untrusted input, exactly as in 6.3: they arrive from a model, possibly one that has read a hostile document.

M13 is done. git commit -m "M13: MCP server over the knowledge base". Your index is now usable by any MCP client, not just your own app.

Try this yourself. Add a third tool, get_chunk(source: str, chunk_id: int), returning one chunk's full text. Then notice what you have built: a client can search for ids, then fetch full text on demand — which is the parent-document retrieval pattern from 5.12, expressed as two tools instead of one bigger response. Splitting retrieval into search-then-fetch is often better for agents than returning everything at once.

6.13 Agent-to-agent communication and interop

MCP standardises agent-to-tool. The harder, less settled problem is agent-to-agent: how independently built agents, possibly from different vendors, discover each other, negotiate a task, and report results.

LayerQuestion it answersState of play
Tool accessHow does an agent use a tool or data source?Largely settled on MCP. Broad adoption.
Agent discoveryHow do I find an agent that can do X, and learn its capabilities?Active standardisation effort. Google's A2A (Agent2Agent) proposes agent cards describing capabilities, and was donated to the Linux Foundation; other proposals exist. Not settled.
Task delegationHow do I send a task, stream progress, and get a result?Same protocols, same immaturity.
Identity, auth, paymentWho is this agent, what may it do, who pays?Genuinely unsolved. Several competing proposals, none dominant.

Deliberately not going deeper, and here is why. This layer is moving fast enough that specifics written today are likely to be wrong or superseded within months, and I would rather tell you that than hand you confident detail. What is worth knowing for interviews and architecture discussions: MCP for tools, A2A-style protocols for agent-to-agent, and the identity/permissions layer is the unsolved part. For anything current, check the protocol sites directly — I would verify the state of A2A before quoting it in a design review.

Practically: in your own system, multi-agent communication is just function calls and message passing (6.9), and you should keep it that way until you have a real need to talk to an agent you did not write. The interop standards matter when crossing organisational boundaries, which is a problem most teams do not yet have.

6.14 Computer-use and browser agents

The most-demoed and least-reliable category. An agent that controls a browser or a whole desktop: it receives a screenshot or an accessibility tree, decides on an action, and emits a click, keypress or scroll.

How they actually work

ApproachPerceptionActionTrade-off
Screenshot + coordinatesAn image of the screen, fed to a vision model."Click at (412, 380)."Works on anything, including canvas apps and native software. Brittle: a 10-pixel layout shift breaks it, and coordinate precision is a genuine weakness of vision models.
Accessibility tree / DOMStructured text of the page's elements."Click the element with id submit-btn."Far more reliable, much cheaper (text not images), but web-only and defeated by badly built pages with no semantic markup.
HybridDOM for structure, screenshot when structure is ambiguous.Either.What the better tools do. More complex.

The current limits, stated plainly

  • Reliability is the problem, not capability. A task that succeeds 90% of the time per step succeeds 35% of the time across ten steps. Multi-step web tasks are exactly that compounding-probability problem, and it is why demos look better than daily use.
  • They are slow. A screenshot per step, a vision model call per step. Seconds per click.
  • Anti-bot defences fight back. CAPTCHAs, rate limits and bot detection are designed to stop exactly this. Do not build evasion; it is a legal and ethical problem, not just a technical one.
  • The blast radius is large. An agent with your logged-in browser session can send email, spend money and delete data as you. This is the level-5 autonomy from 6.1, and it needs approval gates on every consequential action.
  • Prompt injection is at its worst here. Every web page the agent reads can contain instructions, and the agent has real capabilities. Section 3.6's attack, with the safety rails removed.

When to reach for one. When there is no API. That is essentially the whole answer. If a service has an API, use the API — it is faster, cheaper, and does not break when someone redesigns a button. Browser agents are for legacy internal systems, one-off scraping of something you have permission to scrape, and testing. Tooling exists (Playwright-based agents, browser-control frameworks, vendor computer-use APIs) and it changes quickly enough that I would check what is current rather than name versions here.

For the capstone: we do not build one. Our web access is the DuckDuckGo search tool from 6.3's "Try this" — a bounded, read-only, API-shaped capability. That is the right level of ambition for a local-first research assistant, and the difference between the two designs is a good thing to be able to articulate in an interview.

6.15 Part 6 checkpoint

Quiz answer 1: what is the one-sentence test for whether something is an agent?

Does the model decide what happens next, including when to stop? If your code fixes the sequence of steps, it is a chain — however many model calls it makes. Your M5 RAG system makes two model calls and is not an agent; the M8 loop makes an unknown number and is.

Quiz answer 2: your agent typed expresion instead of expression. Why didn't the run crash?

Because call_tool returns (False, "ERROR invalid arguments for calculator: expression: Field required") instead of raising. That string becomes the next observation, the model reads it, and the following step fixes the argument name. Turning failures into messages rather than exceptions is what makes an agent self-correcting — it is the single most important line of design in the tool layer.

Quiz answer 3: an agent invents tool output and answers confidently. What is the mechanical fix?

Add "stop": ["OBSERVATION:"] to your sampling options. The model is completing a document that looks like a transcript, so it happily writes the next observation itself. A stop sequence makes that structurally impossible. Prompt instructions ("never invent tool output") help a little and are free to include, but the mechanism is the fix.

Quiz answer 4: why does approve=None deny rather than allow?

Fail closed. If a caller forgets to wire up the approval handler, the safe behaviour is that nothing gets written, sent or deleted — not that everything does. The same principle appears in ALLOWED_TOOLS_BY_ROLE.get(role, set()), where an unknown role gets no tools, and in the router defaulting to the read-only research path. Defaults are security decisions.

Quiz answer 5: when is multi-agent genuinely justified?

Three legitimate reasons: tool-count pressure (one agent with 25 tools selects badly, so split by domain), different permissions (a read-only researcher that structurally cannot write files, and a writer that can), and different models (a cheap router, an expensive worker). "It seems more organised" is not one. Every split costs twice the calls and loses information at the handoff, since the next agent sees only what the previous one wrote down.

Quiz answer 6: an agent misbehaves. What is the first thing you look at?

The full message list, in order, exactly as printed in 6.2 — not your prompt. The bug is nearly always visible there: a truncated observation, an ERROR the model read as data, the original question buried thousands of tokens back, or a tool description that does not say what you meant. That is why AgentResult.messages is retained and why tracing matters more for agents than for anything else you will build.

You are done with Part 6 when you can

  • Explain the agent loop's five phases and write it from memory in about 60 lines.
  • Read a raw agent trace and say which step went wrong and why.
  • Design a tool schema and predict which malformed calls your validation will catch.
  • Name four independent budget limits and say which runaway each one catches.
  • Say what LangGraph gives you that your loop does not, and what it costs.
  • Explain MCP's client/server split and why exposing your index over it proves your layering is clean.
  • Argue both sides of "should this be multi-agent?"

Part 7

The current market landscape

An honest map of what teams actually use. This is the part of the course with the shortest shelf life, so it is written to be checked rather than trusted: every table says how confident I am, and every row you might build on points at the source.

7.1 How to read this part

Staleness warning, and I mean it. I verified the key claims here against multiple independent sources in September 2026, and I still found sources contradicting each other on basic facts — which model version is current, what a free tier allows, whether two projects had merged. This field moves faster than anyone can document. Treat this part as a map of the terrain and the questions to ask, not a spec sheet. Anything with a ⚠ is something I would check before repeating in a design review or an interview.

The confidence convention used throughout

MarkerMeans
(no marker)Stable for years, unlikely to change: what a vector database is for, why cross-encoders beat bi-encoders, what BM25 does.
⚠I checked it in September 2026 and believe it, but it is version- or date-sensitive. Verify before you depend on it.
⚠⚠Sources actively disagreed, or the thing changed recently enough that I would expect it to change again. Verify first.

The three questions that decide any of these choices

  1. What does it cost me to leave? A library you call from three files is cheap to replace. A framework whose abstractions shape your whole codebase is not. This is why Part 6 built the agent loop by hand before showing you LangGraph.
  2. Can I see what it is doing? When an LLM app misbehaves you need the exact prompt and the exact response. Tools that hide those are tools you cannot debug.
  3. Is the thing it does hard? Adopt dependencies for genuinely hard problems — checkpointing, approximate nearest neighbour search, continuous batching. Do not adopt them for string formatting and HTTP calls.

The single most useful thing I can tell you about this landscape. There is a loud, credible counter-current from senior engineers arguing that most "agentic" projects would be better off as simple prompt chains, and that the heavier framework abstractions cost more than they save. That view is over-stated but not wrong, and holding both ideas at once — knowing the tools and being sceptical about needing them — is what separates an engineer from someone who follows tutorials. Part 6's hand-built loop was 100 lines and does most of what you need.

What to actually do

SituationChoice
Learning, or building something you must be able to debugNo framework. Part 6's loop. You now know it is 100 lines.

A note for interviews. "Which framework do you use?" is often a test of judgement, not recall. A strong answer names one, explains what it buys, and says when you would not use it. "We built the loop ourselves because we needed to see every prompt, and we would move to LangGraph the day we need durable checkpointing" is a better answer than a list of ten names.

7.3 Model families and open-weight status

⚠⚠ Version numbers below are the least reliable content in this course. While checking this section in September 2026 I found sources within weeks of each other naming different current versions of the same families, and disagreeing about licences. The families are stable; the version numbers churn quarterly. Read the model card on Hugging Face for whatever you are about to run — that is the only authoritative source for its size, context length and licence.

Open-weight families

FamilyFromLicenceCharacter
QwenAlibabaApache-2.0 for most sizes ⚠ (a proprietary "Max" tier exists — check the specific model)⚠ The most commonly recommended default open-weight family. Widest range of sizes (0.5B to very large MoE), strong multilingual coverage, good tool calling. The capstone's default for a reason.
LlamaMetaLlama Community Licence — free for you, with conditions above a very large user threshold. Not OSI open source.The most widely deployed open-weight family in enterprises, and the largest ecosystem of fine-tunes and tooling. ⚠ The Llama 4 generation emphasises very long context.
GemmaGoogle⚠⚠ Historically a custom Gemma licence; reported in 2026 to have moved to Apache-2.0. Verify on the model card before assuming either.Strong small and mid-size models, good on a single GPU, several multimodal variants. A common recommendation for laptops and edge.
MistralMistral AI (France)Mixed: Apache-2.0 for several releases, commercial licences for othersEfficient models with clean licensing on the open releases, strong multilingual. Often chosen where licence clarity matters to legal.
DeepSeekDeepSeek (China)MIT on the notable releases ⚠Reasoning and coding strength at the top end, and the family that made "open weights competitive with the closed frontier" a mainstream claim. ⚠ Flagship versions have moved quickly.

GLMZ.ai / TsinghuaPermissive on the open releases ⚠⚠ A family that rose sharply in 2026, particularly cited for coding and agentic work. Worth knowing about; I would verify current status and licence carefully.
KimiMoonshot AI⚠ Check per release⚠ Very large mixture-of-experts models with open weights, cited for coding agents. Far too big to run locally; relevant via hosted providers.
gpt-ossOpenAIApache-2.0 ⚠⚠ OpenAI's first open-weight release since GPT-2. Notable as a signal about the market, and a reasonable Apache-licensed reasoning option.
NemotronNVIDIAPermissive ⚠Models plus unusually open training-data and recipe disclosure; chosen where reproducibility matters.

Closed frontier models — context only

You will not run these, and this course does not use them, but you need to be able to talk about them. The main families are GPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), Gemini (Google), and Grok (xAI). What matters for your purposes:

  • They lead on the hardest reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, and the gap to open weights has narrowed considerably but not closed.
  • They are API-only. No weights, no local running, no fine-tuning beyond what the vendor exposes.
  • Google's is the one with a genuinely usable free tier (Part 4), which is why it appears in this course at all.
  • The architectural lesson: if your system is designed around one provider's API shape, you have taken on a dependency you cannot self-host out of. The ChatBackend Protocol from section 4.1 exists to prevent exactly that.

How to actually choose a model — the durable skill

Version numbers rot; this procedure does not:

  1. Compute your memory budget and pick the largest parameter count that fits at Q4_K_M with your intended context (section 2.9's calculator).
  2. Shortlist two or three current instruct models in that size from different families, using Hugging Face and a leaderboard as a source of candidates — not as a source of truth.
  3. Check the licence on each model card against your actual use.
  4. Run your own eval set from section 5.13 against all of them, on the exact quantised build you will deploy.
  5. Pick on your numbers. A model two places lower on a public benchmark that is three times faster on your hardware is usually the better engineering choice.

7.4 Inference and serving

Two different jobs get confused here: running a model for one person (your laptop) and serving a model to many people (a GPU server). The tools are not interchangeable, and picking the wrong category is a common mistake.

ToolLicenceCategoryBest atNot for
OllamaMITLocal, single userThe default for this course. One command to pull and run, applies chat templates correctly, quantised by default, HTTP API, works offline.Serving many concurrent users. It does not do the batching that makes a GPU efficient.
llama.cppMITLocal, engineThe C++ engine underneath Ollama and LM Studio. Use it directly for fine control: exact quantisation, GPU layer counts, its own server binary, CPU-only performance work.Convenience. You manage GGUF files and flags yourself.
LM StudioFree for personal use ⚠ (check commercial terms)Local, GUIBrowsing and comparing models visually, testing quantisation levels side by side, an OpenAI-compatible local server without a terminal.Automation and headless servers.
vLLMApache-2.0Server, GPUThe standard for serious self-hosted serving. Continuous batching and paged attention mean it keeps a GPU genuinely busy across many requests — the throughput scaling that section 4.5 said Ollama cannot give you.CPU-only machines and casual local use. It wants a real GPU and unquantised or specifically-supported quantised weights.
SGLangApache-2.0Server, GPUA vLLM alternative with strong prefix caching and structured-output performance. Competitive; worth benchmarking against vLLM on your workload rather than assuming either wins.Same as vLLM.
TGI (Text Generation Inference)Apache-2.0 ⚠ (licence terms changed in the past — check)Server, GPUHugging Face's server, tightly integrated with the Hub and their deployment products.⚠ Has lost ground to vLLM in mindshare. Fine if you are in the HF ecosystem.
llamafileApache-2.0Local, distributionPackaging a model and runtime as one executable file. Interesting for shipping a demo to a non-technical person.Anything ongoing.

The decision, in one line. Ollama for your laptop and for the capstone; vLLM the day you need to serve more than one person at once from a GPU you control. That is the whole progression, and the ChatBackend Protocol means switching is a config change — vLLM exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so section 4.4's OpenAICompatBackend already talks to it.

7.6 Observability and tracing

The category you will underestimate and then desperately need. An LLM app has no stack trace: when an agent gives a wrong answer, the evidence is the sequence of prompts and responses, and if you did not record them, the bug is gone.

ToolLicence / free tierBest atWatch out for
LangfuseCore is open source ⚠; self-hosting is genuinely free. Cloud has a free tier with monthly event caps ⚠.The capstone's choice. Self-hostable via Docker, framework-agnostic, traces nested spans (agent step → tool call → model call), tracks cost and latency, and supports prompt management and eval scores.Self-hosting means running Postgres and ClickHouse ⚠ — check the current compose requirements, they have grown.
LangSmithClosed, hosted. Free developer tier with a monthly trace allowance ⚠.The best experience if you are on LangChain/LangGraph. Zero-config tracing, dataset and eval tooling, prompt playground.Not self-hostable on the free tier, and it pulls you further into one ecosystem.
Arize PhoenixOpen source (Apache-2.0 ⚠), runs locally including in a notebook.Fast local inspection with no account at all — you can launch it beside a script and click through traces. Strong on retrieval/embedding visualisation, which is useful for Part 5 debugging.Less of a long-term production store than Langfuse unless you run the paid platform.
OpenTelemetry GenAI conventionsOpen standard (CNCF).The direction of travel. A vendor-neutral semantic convention for LLM spans — model name, token counts, prompts — so your traces are portable between backends. If your company already runs OTel for services, this is how AI traces join the same pipeline.⚠ The GenAI conventions are still evolving; attribute names have changed. Instrument through a library that tracks the spec rather than hand-rolling span attributes.
Plain structured loggingFreeDo not skip this. One JSON line per model call with prompt hash, model, tokens, latency, and trace id gets you 70% of the value on day one.No UI, no aggregation. Fine until it is not.

What to record on every LLM call

Independent of tooling, this is the list. Part 10 wires it up:

  • A trace id shared by every call in one user request, and a span id per call.
  • Model name as returned by the provider, not as requested (section 4.4).
  • The full prompt, or a hash of it plus a prompt-template version (section 3.7).
  • Prompt and completion token counts, latency, and time to first token.
  • For agents: step number, tool name, tool arguments, and whether the tool succeeded.
  • For RAG: retrieved chunk ids, scores, and how many citations verified.
  • Cost, even when it is zero.

Log with care. Prompts contain user data and retrieved documents. Run the redaction from section 6.10 before logging, decide a retention period deliberately, and never log API keys — including in the "full request body" that seems so useful at 2am.

7.7 Evaluation

ToolLicenceBest atHonest limitation
Your own harness—Retrieval metrics (recall@k, MRR) need no LLM, no judge and no library — section 5.13 is 60 lines. Start here; it catches most regressions.Does not measure generation quality.
RAGASApache-2.0The RAG-specific metric set: faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision and recall. Configurable to use a local Ollama model as judge, keeping it free.⚠ API has changed across versions — pin it. And a small local judge is a noisy judge.
DeepEvalApache-2.0Pytest-style assertions for LLM behaviour. Fits naturally into CI, which is where evals belong (Part 10).Same judge-quality caveat. ⚠ Verify current metric names.

GiskardApache-2.0 ⚠Automated scanning for vulnerabilities and quality issues — injection susceptibility, bias, robustness — rather than task accuracy.Different job from the above. Complementary, not a replacement.
Hand-labelling 30 answersFree, costs an hourDo this once, early. It calibrates every automated number you will ever produce, and it is the only way to know whether your judge model agrees with you.Does not scale. That is why the others exist.

The order that works. Golden set of questions → retrieval metrics in CI → hand-label 30 answers → then add judged metrics for the things hand-labelling told you matter. Teams that start with LLM-as-judge dashboards get impressive-looking numbers they cannot act on.

7.9 UI layers — the prototype path and the production path

This is the section that explains the shape of this whole course, so it gets more space than the others.

The two paths

Prototype pathProduction path
StackStreamlit, Gradio, or Chainlit — Python only, no build stepAngular / React / Vue talking to a Python API over HTTP
Time to first chat UI15 minutesA day, then a week to do it properly
Who it is forYou, your team, a demo, a research artefactUsers who did not build it
DeploymentOne Python process; Hugging Face Spaces in a clickStatic files behind nginx, plus an API container
CeilingReal and lowWhatever you can build
ToolLicenceSweet spotWhere it runs out
StreamlitApache-2.0Chat plus charts and dataframes. Unmatched if your AI output sits next to visualisations. Mature and stable.Its execution model re-runs the whole script on every interaction. Session state is a workaround, not a design. Multi-user apps with auth and persistent threads fight the framework.
GradioApache-2.0Fastest possible model demo, and the native citizen of Hugging Face Spaces. Five lines to a shareable link.State management and multi-page layouts are limited. It is a demo tool and does not pretend otherwise.
ChainlitApache-2.0⚠ Purpose-built for conversational AI, and the strongest of the three for agent apps: native streaming, message threads, collapsible step traces, feedback collection, auth and persisted history built in.Still a Python-rendered UI. You get their chat interface, well made; you do not get arbitrary product design. Smaller ecosystem than the other two.
Open WebUI⚠ Check current licence terms — they have changedA ready-made ChatGPT-style front end for Ollama. Not a framework: an application. Excellent if you want a good local chat UI and no code.It is someone else's product. You configure, you do not build.
Vercel AI SDKApache-2.0The TypeScript/React production path, with streaming and UI primitives handled well.React/Next-centric. Relevant as the thing most AI tutorials assume — and the reason Part 9 teaches you to translate them.
Angular / React / Vue + Python APIMITWhat real products ship. Full control over streaming, cancellation, sanitisation, virtual scrolling, routing, auth, accessibility and testing.You write it. All of it. Which is Part 9.

Why real products end up on the second path

Not because the prototype tools are bad — they are excellent at what they do. Because four things converge:

  1. The UI becomes the product. Citations, trace viewers, approval dialogs and document management are not chat decorations; they are the features. Once your interface has opinions, a framework that renders its interface is in the way.
  2. Auth, roles and multi-tenancy. The moment access control matters (section 5.11), you need a real session and route model.
  3. Someone already has a frontend team and a design system. This is the most common reason in practice, and it is why you asked for Angular.
  4. Testing. You cannot meaningfully unit-test a Streamlit script. You can test an Angular component with a mocked AI service, which is the last section of Part 9.

Exactly what the prototype tools hide, and you must now handle yourself

This is the list Part 9 works through. Each of these is one function call in Streamlit or Chainlit, and real work in Angular — and knowing that up front is the difference between "why is this so hard" and "right, that is the job".

ConcernWhat the prototype tool does for youWhat you will write in Angular (Part 9 section)
Token streamingOne call streams tokens into a message widget. You never see the transport.Consume Server-Sent Events from FastAPI, append fragments to a signal, and re-render without thrashing the DOM. Both EventSource and fetch + ReadableStream, because they have different capabilities. (9.7)
CancellationUsually a built-in stop button, or simply absent.An AbortController wired to a Stop button, propagating to the server so generation actually halts — the other half of section 4.5's with block. (9.7)
Markdown renderingRendered automatically, safely, with code highlighting.Choose a markdown library, run it on streaming partial text without breaking on half-open fences, highlight code blocks, and handle tables and lists. (9.8)
SanitisationHandled. You are not tempted to bypass it, because you cannot.The dangerous one. Model output may contain text from a hostile document in your RAG index. Angular's sanitiser protects you until the moment you reach for bypassSecurityTrustHtml to make markdown work — which turns a document-borne injection into script execution in your own UI. (9.8)
Long chat performanceNot really solved, but also not your problem in a demo.Virtual scrolling, so a 500-message history does not render 500 components. (9.9)
AutoscrollAutomatic.Scroll to bottom on new tokens — but not if the user has scrolled up to read something. Deceptively fiddly. (9.9)
Citation displayNothing. You would print a list.A panel linking each claim to its source chunk, with the quote highlighted, clickable back to the document. (9.10, M18)
Agent trace viewerChainlit gives you collapsible steps free; Streamlit and Gradio give you nothing.Render the Step objects from section 6.4 as a collapsible panel with tool names, arguments and observations. (9.10, M18)
Approval dialogNothing.A modal showing the pending tool name and full arguments, pausing the agent and resuming it on the user's decision. (9.10, M18)
Upload with progressOne widget.HttpClient with reportProgress, a progress bar, error states, and per-file status. (9.11)
Error and loading statesSpinners appear by convention.Every state, explicitly: idle, connecting, streaming, cancelled, failed, retryable. (9.9)
CORSDoes not exist — same process.A dev-server proxy plus FastAPI middleware, and the specific ways it goes wrong. (9.12)

The honest recommendation. If your goal is to validate an idea this week, use Streamlit or Chainlit and do not feel bad about it — Chainlit specifically, if it is an agent, since it gives you streaming and step traces for free. Then rebuild on the production path when the UI becomes the product. Because you asked for Angular and because most enterprise teams already run it, this course goes straight to the second path — and now you know precisely what that costs, and what each cost buys.
