Quiz answer 1: an interviewer asks "why not just use LangChain?"

Answer with the trade, not with disdain. LangChain's breadth is genuinely useful — its document loaders alone save real time — but its core abstractions put layers between you and the prompt, and when an LLM app misbehaves the prompt is the evidence. For a system whose failure mode is "the model saw the wrong text", visibility is worth more than convenience. Add that you would happily use LangGraph for durable execution, because checkpointing is a hard problem worth a dependency. That answer shows judgement; "LangChain is bloated" shows you read a Hacker News thread.

Quiz answer 2: which of these choices is hardest to reverse?

The embedding model, because it is baked into every stored vector — changing it means re-embedding the whole corpus, and section 5.6's guard exists to stop you doing it accidentally. Second hardest is the framework, because its abstractions shape your code. Easiest to reverse: the model runtime and the model itself, which is precisely why the ChatBackend Protocol was worth building in Part 4.

Quiz answer 3: your manager wants a working demo on Friday and a product next quarter. What do you build?

Both, deliberately, and say so. Chainlit on Friday — it gives streaming and step traces free, and throwing it away later is fine because the Python underneath it is the part that matters. Then the Angular front end for the product, because citations, trace viewing and approval dialogs are features rather than chat decorations. The mistake is pretending the Friday demo is the architecture, or refusing to ship it because it is not.

Quiz answer 4: how do you keep this map current?

Do not memorise version numbers. Keep three habits: read the model card or the project's own docs before depending on anything; maintain your own eval set so "better" is a measurement rather than a claim; and re-check free-tier limits on the day you build against them. Then treat every landscape article — including this one — as a list of candidates and questions, not answers.

You are done with Part 7 when you can

  • Name a framework, say what it buys, and say when you would not use it.
  • Explain the difference between Ollama's job and vLLM's job.
  • List what you log on every model call, and why the model name comes from the response.
  • Say which choice in your stack is hardest to reverse.
  • Explain what Streamlit hides and why that matters once the UI becomes the product.
  • Describe how you would pick a model without naming a version number.

Fine-tuning: when it beats prompting and RAG and when it does not (including the counter-intuitive result that training on facts a model does not know can make hallucination worse), LoRA and QLoRA explained conceptually then practically, dataset preparation and formatting, a free path with Unsloth on a Colab or Kaggle GPU, converting the result to GGUF so Ollama can actually serve it, then distillation, model merging, small language models, and multimodal work — vision models, Whisper for speech-to-text, and free text-to-speech options.

Part 8

Fine-tuning and beyond

The most skippable part of this course, and the one with the most hype attached. You will implement LoRA from scratch in NumPy so it stops being magic, compute exactly what it saves, build a dataset properly, train one on a free GPU, and — the step everyone forgets — convert the result so Ollama can actually serve it.

8.1 When fine-tuning beats prompting or RAG — and when it does not

The one-line rule. Fine-tuning teaches a model how to behave. RAG gives it what to know. If your problem statement contains the word "knows" or "facts", fine-tuning is the wrong tool.

Your problemRight toolWhy
"It doesn't know about our internal API."RAGMissing knowledge. Put the docs in the context (Part 5).
"It won't stop writing five paragraphs when I want one line."Prompting, then fine-tuningBehaviour. Try the prompt first; if you are fighting it on every call, train it in.
"It won't reliably emit our JSON schema."Constrained decoding, then fine-tuningSection 3.4 first — schema-constrained decoding is free and stronger. Fine-tune only if you also need domain-specific field choices.
"We need our house style / tone of voice."Fine-tuningStyle is exactly what SFT is good at, and it is hard to specify in a prompt.
"It doesn't understand our domain jargon."DependsIf it needs to define the terms: RAG. If it needs to use them naturally: fine-tuning.
"Our prompt is 3,000 tokens of instructions and examples."Fine-tuningA genuinely good reason people forget: training the behaviour in lets you delete the instructions, cutting latency and cost on every single call.
"We need it faster and cheaper."Fine-tuning a small modelA fine-tuned 3B often beats a prompted 8B on one narrow task, at a fraction of the compute. This is the strongest commercial case.
"It hallucinates."RAG + verificationSee the warning below. Fine-tuning can make this worse.
"It needs last week's data."RAGWeights are a snapshot. Retraining weekly is absurd; re-indexing weekly is normal.
"Different users must see different data."RAGYou cannot put access control in weights. Section 5.11.

The counter-intuitive result worth remembering. Training a model on facts it does not already know can increase hallucination. The intuition: SFT teaches the model to produce confident, well-formed statements in your format. If the facts are unfamiliar, what it learns is the shape of confident assertion, which it then applies to things it does not know. Research on knowledge injection through fine-tuning has repeatedly found it both inefficient and prone to this effect. Use RAG for facts. Use fine-tuning for form.

The honest order of operations

  1. Better prompt. Free, instant, reversible. Most "we need to fine-tune" turns out to be a missing few-shot example.
  2. Constrained decoding. Free, and stronger than any amount of training for format compliance.
  3. RAG. For anything knowledge-shaped.
  4. A bigger or different model. Often cheaper in engineer-hours than training.
  5. Fine-tune a small model. Now you have a baseline to beat and an eval set to measure with.

And note step 5's precondition: you cannot fine-tune responsibly without an eval set. If you cannot measure the before, you cannot know whether the after is better. Section 5.13's harness is the prerequisite, not an afterthought.

What you need before you start

RequirementRealistic minimum
Training examples~50 for a narrow style change to be visible; 500–2,000 for something reliable. Quality dominates quantity — 200 clean examples beat 5,000 scraped ones.
An eval set30–100 held-out examples the model never trains on, plus your Part 5 retrieval metrics if RAG is involved.
HardwareA free Colab or Kaggle T4 is enough for QLoRA on a 3B–8B model. 8 GB of local VRAM also works.
TimeAn afternoon for the first run. A week to get a result you trust.

8.2 LoRA and QLoRA, conceptually

Full fine-tuning updates every weight. For an 8B model in fp16 with the Adam optimiser that means holding the weights, the gradients, and two optimiser states per parameter — roughly 100 GB, which is several data-centre GPUs for a task you wanted to run on a laptop.

The LoRA idea, in one paragraph

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes the pretrained weight matrix W₀ and learns a small additive update instead. Rather than learning a full d×k matrix of changes, it learns two thin matrices — A of shape d×r and B of shape r×k — and uses their product as the update:

output = x · (W₀ + (α/r)·A·B)

With d = k = 4096 and r = 16, the full update would be 16.8 million numbers; A and B together are 131 thousand. The bet is that the change needed to adapt a model to a narrow task is intrinsically low-rank — much simpler than the model itself — and empirically that bet holds up well.

TermWhat it isPractical guidance
r (rank)The width of the bottleneck. The capacity of your adapter.8–16 for style and format. 32–64 for harder behavioural change. Higher is not automatically better — see the demo in 8.3.
α (alpha)A scaling factor; the update is multiplied by α/r.Commonly set equal to r (giving scale 1) or 2r. Think of α/r as a learning-rate multiplier on the adapter.
target_modulesWhich weight matrices get adapters.The attention projections. q_proj and v_proj is the classic minimal set; adding k_proj, o_proj and the MLP projections gives more capacity for more memory.
dropoutRegularisation on the adapter.0.05–0.1 on small datasets, where overfitting is the main risk.
B initialised to zerosSo A·B = 0 at step 0.Important detail: the adapter starts as an exact no-op, so training begins from the pretrained model's behaviour rather than from noise.

QLoRA adds one more trick

QLoRA = LoRA with the frozen base model quantised to 4 bits. Since W₀ never receives gradients, it does not need full precision — it only needs to be accurate enough for the forward pass. The adapters stay in higher precision because they are being trained.

That single change cuts base-model memory roughly 4×, which is what puts an 8B fine-tune on a free T4. The costs are honest but small: slightly slower per step (dequantising on the fly) and a small quality gap versus fp16 LoRA that is usually invisible on narrow tasks.

ApproachBase modelTrains8B feasible on…
Full fine-tunefp16, trainableEverythingMultiple data-centre GPUs
LoRAfp16, frozen~0.1% of parametersOne 24 GB GPU
QLoRA4-bit, frozen~0.1% of parametersA free 16 GB T4
Deeper dive: adapters, merging, and why this is operationally lovely

Because the adapter is separate from the base model, you get properties full fine-tuning cannot offer:

  • Tiny artefacts. A rank-16 adapter is megabytes, not gigabytes. You can version it in git-lfs, email it, or ship several.
  • Hot-swapping. One base model in memory, many adapters loaded and unloaded per request. Some serving stacks support this directly, which is how a provider offers "your fine-tune" without a dedicated GPU per customer.
  • Merging. Because the update is just addition, you can fold it in permanently: W = W₀ + (α/r)·A·B. The result is an ordinary model file with no adapter machinery — which is exactly what you need to produce a GGUF for Ollama in section 8.6.
  • Reversibility. Delete the adapter and you are back to the base model, bit for bit. Nothing was overwritten.

8.3 LoRA from scratch, and the arithmetic that justifies it

Two runnable files. The first proves LoRA is 15 lines of linear algebra rather than a framework feature; the second computes exactly what it saves on a real model shape.

Train a low-rank update to a frozen matrix, and discover the rank ceiling by experiment.

"""LoRA from scratch: train a low-rank update to a frozen matrix."""

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=7)

D_IN, D_OUT, N = 16, 8, 256

W0 = rng.normal(0, 0.3, size=(D_IN, D_OUT))          # the frozen "pretrained" weights
DELTA_TRUE = rng.normal(0, 0.3, size=(D_IN, 3)) @ rng.normal(0, 0.3, size=(3, D_OUT))
W_TARGET = W0 + DELTA_TRUE                            # what the "fine-tuned" model should be

X = rng.normal(0, 1, size=(N, D_IN))
Y = X @ W_TARGET


def train_lora(rank: int, steps: int = 3000, lr: float = 0.02, alpha: float | None = None):
    """Train only A and B. W0 is never touched."""
    alpha = alpha if alpha is not None else rank
    scale = alpha / rank

    A = rng.normal(0, 0.02, size=(D_IN, rank))        # random small
    B = np.zeros((rank, D_OUT))                       # zeros: delta starts at exactly 0

    for step in range(steps):
        delta = scale * (A @ B)
        pred = X @ (W0 + delta)
        error = pred - Y
        loss = np.mean(error ** 2)

        grad_delta = 2 * X.T @ error / N              # d(loss)/d(delta)
        grad_A = scale * grad_delta @ B.T
        grad_B = scale * A.T @ grad_delta

        A -= lr * grad_A
        B -= lr * grad_B

    delta = scale * (A @ B)
    trainable = A.size + B.size
    return loss, trainable, delta


def train_full(steps: int = 3000, lr: float = 0.02):
    """The baseline: update every weight."""
    W = W0.copy()
    for step in range(steps):
        error = X @ W - Y
        loss = np.mean(error ** 2)
        W -= lr * (2 * X.T @ error / N)
    return loss, W.size


if __name__ == "__main__":
    baseline = np.mean((X @ W0 - Y) ** 2)
    print(f"true delta rank        : {np.linalg.matrix_rank(DELTA_TRUE)}")
    print(f"loss before any training: {baseline:.5f}")
    print(f"full weight matrix size : {W0.size} parameters\n")

    print(f"{'rank':>5}{'trainable':>11}{'final loss':>13}{'recovered?':>18}")
    for rank in (1, 2, 3, 4, 8):
        loss, trainable, delta = train_lora(rank)
        verdict = "yes" if loss < 1e-6 else f"no ({baseline/loss:.0f}x better)"
        print(f"{rank:>5}{trainable:>11}{loss:>13.2e}{verdict:>18}")

    full_loss, full_params = train_full()
    verdict = "yes" if full_loss < 1e-6 else "no"
    print(f"{'full':>5}{full_params:>11}{full_loss:>13.2e}{verdict:>18}")

    print("\nW0 is untouched -- the adapter is a separate, tiny artefact:")
    loss, trainable, delta = train_lora(3)
    print(f"  W0 checksum before/after: {W0.sum():.6f} (never modified)")
    print(f"  learned delta vs true   : mean abs error {np.mean(np.abs(delta - DELTA_TRUE)):.2e}")
    print(f"  merged W = W0 + delta   : {np.mean((X @ (W0+delta) - Y)**2):.2e} loss")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
DELTA_TRUE = rng.normal(...,(D_IN,3)) @ rng.normal(...,(3,D_OUT))Constructs the "true" update as a product of two thin matrices, so it has rank exactly 3.Builds the experiment: we know the answer is rank 3, so we can watch what happens when the adapter has less capacity than that. This is the LoRA hypothesis made testable.
W_TARGET = W0 + DELTA_TRUEDefines the fine-tuned behaviour we are trying to reach.Stands in for "the weights a full fine-tune would have found".
scale = alpha / rankThe LoRA scaling factor.Exactly as in the real implementations. With alpha = rank the scale is 1, which is why that default is so common.
A = rng.normal(0, 0.02, ...)Small random values for A.Must be non-zero, or the gradient with respect to B is zero forever — the symmetry-breaking problem from section 1.9, in a new place.
B = np.zeros(...)Zeros for B.The key initialisation detail. A·B = 0 at step 0, so the adapter starts as an exact no-op and training begins from the pretrained behaviour. Initialising both randomly would corrupt the model before it learns anything.
pred = X @ (W0 + delta)Forward pass through base plus adapter.Real implementations compute x@W0 + scale*(x@A)@B to avoid materialising the full delta — mathematically identical, cheaper at scale.
grad_A = scale * grad_delta @ B.T
grad_B = scale * A.T @ grad_delta		Chain rule through the product A·B.The whole of LoRA's backward pass. Two lines. Note W0 appears nowhere — that is what "frozen" means, and it is why gradients and optimiser state are tiny.
train_full()The full fine-tuning baseline.Without a baseline you cannot tell whether the low-rank restriction cost you anything.
np.linalg.matrix_rank(DELTA_TRUE)Confirms the update really is rank 3.Verifies the experimental setup rather than assuming it.
W0.sum() printed after trainingChecksums the frozen matrix.Demonstrates the operational property from 8.2: the base model is untouched, and the adapter is a separate artefact you can delete.

Expected output

true delta rank        : 3
loss before any training: 0.20852
full weight matrix size : 128 parameters

 rank  trainable   final loss        recovered?
    1         24     6.27e-02    no (3x better)
    2         48     1.96e-02   no (11x better)
    3         72     8.85e-30               yes
    4         96     4.08e-30               yes
    8        192     2.46e-30               yes
 full        128     5.95e-30               yes

W0 is untouched -- the adapter is a separate, tiny artefact:
  W0 checksum before/after: -6.671932 (never modified)
  learned delta vs true   : mean abs error 1.39e-15
  merged W = W0 + delta   : 4.83e-29 loss

This output is the whole lesson

  • Rank 1 and 2 cannot get there. They improve the loss 3× and 11×, but they structurally cannot represent a rank-3 update. Insufficient rank is a hard ceiling, not a slow convergence. If your fine-tune plateaus short of what you want, raising the rank is a real fix.
  • Rank 3 recovers it exactly. 72 trainable parameters match what 128 full parameters achieve. Once the adapter's capacity meets the task's intrinsic complexity, the restriction costs nothing.
  • Rank 4 and 8 are no better. Extra capacity beyond what the task needs buys nothing and costs memory — and on real data it costs overfitting. This is why rank 8–16 is a sensible default rather than "as high as fits".
  • The merged matrix works identically. W₀ + delta reproduces the target, which is the mathematical basis for the merge step in 8.6.

Now the arithmetic on a real model shape: how many parameters, and how much memory.

"""How many parameters does LoRA actually train, and what does that save?"""

# Shapes from a typical 8B decoder-only model. Check your model's config.json.
MODEL = {
    "name": "8B-ish",
    "params_billion": 8.0,
    "n_layers": 32,
    "hidden": 4096,
    "kv_heads": 8,
    "head_dim": 128,
}


def linear_params(in_dim: int, out_dim: int) -> int:
    return in_dim * out_dim


def lora_params(in_dim: int, out_dim: int, rank: int) -> int:
    return in_dim * rank + rank * out_dim


def attention_projection_shapes(m: dict) -> dict:
    """q and o are square; k and v are narrower because of grouped-query attention."""
    h = m["hidden"]
    kv = m["kv_heads"] * m["head_dim"]
    return {"q_proj": (h, h), "k_proj": (h, kv), "v_proj": (h, kv), "o_proj": (h, h)}


def count(m: dict, rank: int, targets: list[str]) -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Base parameters and LoRA-trainable parameters across all layers."""
    shapes = attention_projection_shapes(m)
    base = trainable = 0
    for name in targets:
        in_dim, out_dim = shapes[name]
        base += linear_params(in_dim, out_dim) * m["n_layers"]
        trainable += lora_params(in_dim, out_dim, rank) * m["n_layers"]
    return base, trainable


def gb(params: int, bytes_per_param: float) -> float:
    return params * bytes_per_param / 1024**3


if __name__ == "__main__":
    total = int(MODEL["params_billion"] * 1e9)
    print(f"model: {MODEL['name']}  {total/1e9:.1f}B params, "
          f"{MODEL['n_layers']} layers, hidden {MODEL['hidden']}")

    targets = ["q_proj", "v_proj"]
    print(f"\nLoRA on {targets}, per rank:")
    print(f"{'rank':>5}{'trainable':>14}{'% of model':>12}{'adapter (fp16)':>17}")
    for rank in (4, 8, 16, 32, 64):
        _, trainable = count(MODEL, rank, targets)
        print(f"{rank:>5}{trainable:>14,}{100*trainable/total:>11.4f}%"
              f"{gb(trainable, 2)*1024:>14.1f} MB")

    print("\nsame at rank 16, different target sets:")
    for targets in (["q_proj"], ["q_proj", "v_proj"],
                    ["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj"]):
        base, trainable = count(MODEL, 16, targets)
        print(f"  {str(targets):<44} {trainable:>12,} trainable "
              f"({100*trainable/total:.3f}% of model)")

    print("\ntraining memory, very roughly:")
    print(f"{'setup':<34}{'weights':>10}{'grads+optim':>13}{'total':>9}")
    rows = [
        ("full fine-tune, fp16 + Adam", gb(total, 2), gb(total, 12)),
        ("LoRA r=16, fp16 base + Adam", gb(total, 2),
         gb(count(MODEL, 16, ['q_proj', 'v_proj'])[1], 12)),
        ("QLoRA r=16, 4-bit base + Adam", gb(total, 0.5),
         gb(count(MODEL, 16, ['q_proj', 'v_proj'])[1], 12)),
    ]
    for label, w, o in rows:
        print(f"{label:<34}{w:>8.1f} GB{o:>11.2f} GB{w+o:>7.1f} GB")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
kv = m["kv_heads"] * m["head_dim"]Computes the k/v projection output width.Grouped-query attention (section 2.4) means k_proj and v_proj are narrower than q_proj. Assuming all four are square overestimates the parameter count.
in_dim * rank + rank * out_dimSize of A plus size of B.The core saving. For a square 4096 matrix at rank 16 this is 131k against 16.8M — a 128× reduction on that matrix.
* m["n_layers"]Multiplies by the layer count.Adapters go on every layer's projections. Forgetting this underestimates by 32×.
gb(total, 12) for full fine-tuning12 bytes per parameter for gradients plus optimiser state.Rough but honest: fp16 gradients plus Adam's two fp32 moments plus an fp32 master copy lands around here. Exact figures depend on the trainer's mixed-precision setup, which is why the heading says "very roughly".
gb(total, 0.5) for QLoRA4 bits per weight.Same arithmetic as section 2.9's quantisation table, applied to training instead of inference.
the target-set comparisonShows q_proj alone vs two vs four projections.The knob you will actually tune after rank. More targets means more capacity and more memory, roughly linearly.

Expected output

model: 8B-ish  8.0B params, 32 layers, hidden 4096

LoRA on ['q_proj', 'v_proj'], per rank:
 rank     trainable  % of model   adapter (fp16)
    4     1,703,936     0.0213%           3.2 MB
    8     3,407,872     0.0426%           6.5 MB
   16     6,815,744     0.0852%          13.0 MB
   32    13,631,488     0.1704%          26.0 MB
   64    27,262,976     0.3408%          52.0 MB

same at rank 16, different target sets:
  ['q_proj']                                      4,194,304 trainable (0.052% of model)
  ['q_proj', 'v_proj']                            6,815,744 trainable (0.085% of model)
  ['q_proj', 'k_proj', 'v_proj', 'o_proj']       13,631,488 trainable (0.170% of model)

training memory, very roughly:
setup                                weights  grads+optim    total
full fine-tune, fp16 + Adam           14.9 GB      89.41 GB  104.3 GB
LoRA r=16, fp16 base + Adam           14.9 GB       0.08 GB   15.0 GB
QLoRA r=16, 4-bit base + Adam          3.7 GB       0.08 GB    3.8 GB

104.3 GB → 3.8 GB. That is the entire reason this section exists. A rank-16 adapter trains 0.085% of the model, weighs 13 MB, and turns a multi-GPU job into something a free notebook can run. Note also that the optimiser cost collapses from 89 GB to 0.08 GB — because optimiser state scales with trainable parameters, not total ones. That is where most of the saving comes from, not from the weights.

These are estimates, not a spec. Real memory use depends on batch size, sequence length, gradient checkpointing, the exact mixed-precision strategy, and activation memory — which this calculator ignores entirely and which can be substantial at long sequence lengths. Use it to decide whether something is plausible, then measure with nvidia-smi during an actual run.

Try this yourself. In lora_demo.py, change DELTA_TRUE to a full-rank matrix: rng.normal(0, 0.3, size=(D_IN, D_OUT)). Now no rank below 8 recovers it, and the rank-8 case matches full fine-tuning exactly. You have just demonstrated the precise condition under which LoRA is lossless — the update must be low-rank — and why it works so well for narrow tasks and less well for teaching a model genuinely new capabilities.

8.4 Dataset preparation, which is where the work actually is

Budget your time honestly. Roughly 80% of a successful fine-tune is the dataset and 20% is the training run. The training run is the part with the progress bar, so it feels like the work. It is not.

The format

The de facto standard is JSONL — one JSON object per line — with a messages array in the same shape you have used since section 1.2. One line per example:

{"messages": [
  {"role": "system", "content": "You are Second Brain. Answer in at most two sentences, citing source#chunk_id."},
  {"role": "user", "content": "What port does the Ollama API use?"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": "It listens on 127.0.0.1:11434 by default (setup.md#4)."}
]}

Two things happen to this before training, and both matter:

  • The trainer applies the model's chat template (section 4.3) to turn the messages into one flat string with the right special tokens. Use the tokenizer that ships with your base model, or you are training on a format the model will never see at inference.
  • Loss is usually computed only on the assistant tokens. You want the model to learn to produce the answer, not to predict the user's question. Most trainers do this for you, sometimes behind an option — worth confirming, because training on the prompt tokens too is a real and quiet way to waste a run.

Where the examples come from

SourceQualityNotes
Hand-written by youHighest50–200 examples is a weekend, and it forces you to define what "good" means. Do this for your first fine-tune.
Real logs, curatedHighYour actual traffic with the answers corrected. The best source once you have traffic. Redact first (section 6.10).
Distilled from a stronger modelMedium–highGenerate answers with a bigger model, review them, keep the good ones. Cheap and effective. Check the provider's terms — several forbid using outputs to train competing models.
Public datasetsVariableFine for learning the mechanics, rarely aligned with your task. Check the licence.
Fully synthetic, unreviewedLowTeaches the model to imitate the generator's mistakes, confidently. The single most common way fine-tunes go wrong.

Build the dataset tooling: construct examples, validate them, catch the format errors that waste a training run, deduplicate, and split.

"""Build, validate and split a fine-tuning dataset in chat JSONL format."""

import json
import random
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path

DATA_DIR = Path("data/finetune")
VALID_ROLES = {"system", "user", "assistant"}


@dataclass
class Example:
    """One training example: a conversation ending with the answer we want."""
    messages: list[dict]

    def to_json(self) -> str:
        return json.dumps({"messages": self.messages}, ensure_ascii=False)


def make_example(system: str, user: str, assistant: str) -> Example:
    msgs = []
    if system:
        msgs.append({"role": "system", "content": system})
    msgs.append({"role": "user", "content": user})
    msgs.append({"role": "assistant", "content": assistant})
    return Example(msgs)


def validate(example: dict, index: int) -> list[str]:
    """Return a list of problems with one raw example. Empty list means valid."""
    problems = []
    msgs = example.get("messages")
    if not isinstance(msgs, list) or not msgs:
        return [f"[{index}] 'messages' missing or not a non-empty list"]

    for i, m in enumerate(msgs):
        if not isinstance(m, dict):
            problems.append(f"[{index}] message {i} is not an object")
            continue
        role, content = m.get("role"), m.get("content")
        if role not in VALID_ROLES:
            problems.append(f"[{index}] message {i} bad role {role!r}")
        if not isinstance(content, str) or not content.strip():
            problems.append(f"[{index}] message {i} empty or non-string content")

    roles = [m.get("role") for m in msgs if isinstance(m, dict)]
    if roles and roles[-1] != "assistant":
        problems.append(f"[{index}] last message must be 'assistant', got {roles[-1]!r}")
    if "user" not in roles:
        problems.append(f"[{index}] no user message")
    if roles.count("system") > 1:
        problems.append(f"[{index}] more than one system message")
    return problems


def dedupe(examples: list[dict]) -> tuple[list[dict], int]:
    """Drop exact duplicates on the whole conversation."""
    seen, kept = set(), []
    for ex in examples:
        msgs = ex.get("messages", [])
        key = json.dumps([(m.get("role"), m.get("content")) for m in msgs], sort_keys=True)
        if key in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(key)
        kept.append(ex)
    return kept, len(examples) - len(kept)


def split(examples: list[dict], eval_fraction: float = 0.1, seed: int = 42):
    """Shuffle deterministically and hold out an eval slice."""
    shuffled = list(examples)
    random.Random(seed).shuffle(shuffled)
    n_eval = max(1, int(len(shuffled) * eval_fraction))
    return shuffled[n_eval:], shuffled[:n_eval]


def write_jsonl(path: Path, rows: list[dict]) -> None:
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        for row in rows:
            fh.write(json.dumps(row, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")


def stats(rows: list[dict]) -> dict:
    """Size figures you need before choosing a sequence length."""
    lengths = [sum(len(m["content"]) for m in r["messages"]) for r in rows]
    answers = [len(r["messages"][-1]["content"]) for r in rows]
    return {
        "examples": len(rows),
        "mean_chars": round(sum(lengths) / len(lengths)),
        "max_chars": max(lengths),
        "mean_answer_chars": round(sum(answers) / len(answers)),
        "est_tokens_total": round(sum(lengths) / 4),
    }


SYSTEM = "You are Second Brain. Answer in at most two sentences, citing source#chunk_id."

RAW = [
    make_example(SYSTEM, "What port does the Ollama API use?",
                 "It listens on 127.0.0.1:11434 by default (setup.md#4)."),
    make_example(SYSTEM, "How much memory does an 8B model need?",
                 "About 5.5 GB at Q4_K_M including the KV cache (hardware.md#9)."),
    make_example(SYSTEM, "What port does the Ollama API use?",
                 "It listens on 127.0.0.1:11434 by default (setup.md#4)."),
    make_example(SYSTEM, "Can my server handle 240 requests per minute?",
                 "Yes. Four workers at 150 ms each give about 1600 req/min (hardware.md#10)."),
    make_example(SYSTEM, "Who is the CEO of Ollama?",
                 "Not in the provided documents."),
    make_example(SYSTEM, "Which model should I run on 8 GB of RAM?",
                 "A 3B model at Q4_K_M, leaving headroom for the OS (hardware.md#9)."),
    make_example(SYSTEM, "What is num_ctx for?",
                 "It sets the context window length, which controls KV cache size (setup.md#7)."),
    make_example(SYSTEM, "Summarise my hardware notes.",
                 "They cover model memory sizing and worker throughput (hardware.md#9, #10)."),
    make_example(SYSTEM, "Is Q8 worth it over Q4_K_M?",
                 "Rarely: Q8 roughly doubles memory for a difference most people cannot detect."),
    make_example(SYSTEM, "Where do I download Ollama?",
                 "From ollama.com, then run the installer (setup.md#3)."),
]

BROKEN = [
    {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hello"}]},
    {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"},
                  {"role": "assistant", "content": "  "}]},
    {"messages": [{"role": "bot", "content": "x"},
                  {"role": "assistant", "content": "y"}]},
    {"prompt": "old format", "completion": "not supported"},
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    rows = [json.loads(e.to_json()) for e in RAW]

    print("validating the good set:")
    problems = [p for i, r in enumerate(rows) for p in validate(r, i)]
    print(f"  {len(rows)} examples, {len(problems)} problems")

    print("\nvalidating a deliberately broken set:")
    for i, bad in enumerate(BROKEN):
        for p in validate(bad, i):
            print(f"  {p}")

    rows, dropped = dedupe(rows)
    print(f"\ndeduped: dropped {dropped}, kept {len(rows)}")

    train, evalset = split(rows, eval_fraction=0.2)
    write_jsonl(DATA_DIR / "train.jsonl", train)
    write_jsonl(DATA_DIR / "eval.jsonl", evalset)
    print(f"split   : {len(train)} train / {len(evalset)} eval")
    print(f"train stats: {stats(train)}")

    print(f"\nfirst line of train.jsonl:")
    print("  " + (DATA_DIR / "train.jsonl").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()[0][:150])
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
ensure_ascii=FalseWrites real Unicode instead of \u00e9 escapes.Keeps the file readable and smaller. Both forms parse identically, but you will be reading this file by eye.
validate() returning a list of stringsReports every problem, not the first.Same principle as Pydantic in section 1.3: fixing a dataset one error per run is miserable.
if roles[-1] != "assistant"The last message must be the answer.The most common dataset bug. If the example ends on a user turn there is nothing to compute loss on, and depending on the trainer you get either a crash or a silently useless example.
if roles.count("system") > 1At most one system message.Several chat templates only render the first one, so extras vanish and your training data does not match what you thought.
not content.strip()Catches whitespace-only content.An empty assistant message teaches the model to answer with nothing. It happens surprisingly often when generating examples programmatically.
dedupe() keyed on the whole conversationDrops exact repeats.Duplicates are effectively an increased learning rate on those examples, and they leak between train and eval if you split afterwards. Deduplicate before splitting — as the ordering here does.
random.Random(seed).shuffleDeterministic shuffle.So the same eval set is held out on every run. A shifting eval split makes run-to-run comparison meaningless.
max(1, int(len * fraction))Always holds out at least one example.With 8 examples and a 10% split you would otherwise get zero eval examples and no way to detect overfitting.
stats() with max_charsReports the longest example.This decides your max_seq_length. Set it too low and long examples are truncated mid-answer — the same silent truncation problem as embeddings in section 5.5.
est_tokens_totalRough total token count.Multiply by epochs to estimate run time. It is also the number that tells you whether your dataset is large enough to matter at all.
the "Who is the CEO" exampleAn abstention example.Deliberate. If every training answer is confident, you train confidence. Include examples of the model correctly saying it does not know, or you will train away the abstention behaviour you built in section 5.7.
the BROKEN listFour realistic malformed examples.Proves the validator works. The last one is the old prompt/completion format you will find in older datasets and tutorials.

Expected output

validating the good set:
  10 examples, 0 problems

validating a deliberately broken set:
  [0] last message must be 'assistant', got 'user'
  [1] message 1 empty or non-string content
  [2] message 0 bad role 'bot'
  [2] no user message
  [3] 'messages' missing or not a non-empty list

deduped: dropped 1, kept 9
split   : 8 train / 1 eval
train stats: {'examples': 8, 'mean_chars': 178, 'max_chars': 197, 'mean_answer_chars': 67, 'est_tokens_total': 355}

first line of train.jsonl:
  {"messages": [{"role": "system", "content": "You are Second Brain. Answer in at most two sentences, citing source#chunk_id."}, {"role": "user", "conte

Nine examples is of course far too few to train anything — this is the tooling, not the dataset. But notice what the pipeline caught: a duplicate that would have been double-weighted and leaked across the split, and four malformed examples that would each have quietly degraded a run. Run this before every training job.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
Training loss drops to near zero in one epochOverfitting a tiny dataset, or duplicates.Check eval loss, not training loss. If eval loss rises while training loss falls, stop earlier or add data. Run dedupe.
The fine-tuned model repeats the system prompt backLoss was computed over the whole sequence, not just the assistant turn.Check your trainer's setting for completion-only loss.
Answers are cut off mid-sentencemax_seq_length shorter than your longest example.Use stats()["max_chars"] ÷ 4 as a floor, plus headroom.
The model forgot how to do everything elseCatastrophic forgetting — narrow training on a narrow dataset.Fewer epochs, lower learning rate, lower rank, and mix in some general examples. LoRA is much less prone to this than full fine-tuning, which is another reason to prefer it.
Model output has strange leading spaces or missing punctuationChat-template mismatch between training and inference.Print the templated string during training (section 4.3's "Try this") and compare it with what Ollama sends at inference.
Try this yourself. Add a validator that flags any example whose assistant content is longer than 400 characters when your system prompt says "at most two sentences". Contradictions between your instructions and your examples are the most common invisible dataset defect — the model learns the examples, not the instruction, and then ignores the instruction at inference.

8.5 The free path — Unsloth on a Colab or Kaggle GPU

Unsloth (Apache-2.0 core ⚠ — some optimisations have historically been gated to a paid tier, so check) is an optimised QLoRA training stack. It exists because a naive PEFT setup will not fit an 8B fine-tune on a free T4 and Unsloth's will, with meaningfully faster steps and lower memory.

⚠⚠ Read this before the code. This is the fastest-moving tooling in the entire course. Since my knowledge cutoff, TRL has renamed trainer arguments (tokenizer → processing_class) and moved hyperparameters from TrainingArguments into a dedicated SFTConfig; Unsloth's loader and export helpers have also changed signatures. The code below is therefore a shape, not a recipe — the sequence of steps is stable and worth learning, and I would expect at least one argument name to need correcting.

Do this instead of trusting me: open Unsloth's own notebook for your base model from their repository, run it unmodified once to confirm the environment works, then substitute your dataset. That is genuinely the fastest path, and it is what I would do myself.

"""QLoRA fine-tune on a free GPU. Verify all signatures against current docs."""

# --- 1. environment (in Colab/Kaggle, install first) -----------------------
# !pip install unsloth trl peft datasets

# --- 2. load a small base model in 4 bits ---------------------------------
from unsloth import FastLanguageModel

MAX_SEQ_LEN = 1024          # from stats()["max_chars"] / 4, plus headroom

model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(
    model_name="unsloth/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct",   # pick a current small instruct model
    max_seq_length=MAX_SEQ_LEN,
    load_in_4bit=True,                          # this is the Q in QLoRA
)

# --- 3. attach LoRA adapters ----------------------------------------------
model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(
    model,
    r=16,                                       # section 8.3's rank
    lora_alpha=16,                              # alpha == r, so scale == 1
    lora_dropout=0.05,
    target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj",
                    "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"],
    use_gradient_checkpointing=True,             # trades compute for memory
    random_state=42,
)

# --- 4. load YOUR dataset -------------------------------------------------
from datasets import load_dataset

data = load_dataset(
    "json",
    data_files={"train": "train.jsonl", "test": "eval.jsonl"},
)

def to_text(example):
    """Apply the model's own chat template. Do not hand-roll this."""
    return {"text": tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
        example["messages"], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=False)}

data = data.map(to_text)

# --- 5. train -------------------------------------------------------------
from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    train_dataset=data["train"],
    eval_dataset=data["test"],
    args=SFTConfig(
        output_dir="outputs",
        dataset_text_field="text",
        max_seq_length=MAX_SEQ_LEN,
        per_device_train_batch_size=2,
        gradient_accumulation_steps=4,          # effective batch size 8
        num_train_epochs=3,
        learning_rate=2e-4,                     # high, because only adapters train
        warmup_ratio=0.05,
        lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
        logging_steps=5,
        eval_strategy="epoch",
        optim="adamw_8bit",
        seed=42,
        report_to="none",
    ),
)

trainer.train()

# --- 6. save the adapter (megabytes, not gigabytes) ----------------------
model.save_pretrained("second-brain-lora")
tokenizer.save_pretrained("second-brain-lora")
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
load_in_4bit=TrueQuantises the frozen base model.The QLoRA step from 8.2. Without it the base weights alone will not fit alongside activations on a 16 GB T4 for an 8B model.
max_seq_length=1024Caps tokens per example.Memory scales with sequence length, and attention scales with its square (section 2.7). Set it from your dataset's real maximum, not optimistically high.
r=16, lora_alpha=16Rank and scaling.Straight from 8.3: alpha == r gives a scale of 1. Start here, raise the rank only if the loss plateaus above where you need it.
target_modules=[... MLP projections ...]Adapters on attention and the feed-forward layers.More capacity than the q_proj, v_proj minimum from 8.3, and now common practice — most parameters live in the MLP (section 2.4). Costs proportionally more memory.
use_gradient_checkpointing=TrueRecomputes activations in the backward pass instead of storing them.Roughly 30% slower, substantially less memory. On a free GPU this is usually the difference between running and crashing.
tokenizer.apply_chat_template(...)Formats each example with the base model's own template.The most important line in the file. Section 4.3's lesson: train on the exact format the model sees at inference, or you have trained for a world that does not exist.
add_generation_prompt=FalseNo trailing "assistant:" cue.Different from inference. At training time the assistant's turn is already present in the text; adding a generation prompt would append an empty one.
per_device_train_batch_size=2 + gradient_accumulation_steps=4Effective batch size 8, using the memory of 2.Accumulate gradients over four micro-batches before stepping. The standard way to get a usable batch size on a small GPU.
learning_rate=2e-4Much higher than full fine-tuning's typical 1e-5.Only the adapters train, and they start from near-zero, so they need a larger step. Section 1.8's tuning intuition applies: if the loss diverges, divide by ten.
num_train_epochs=3Three passes over the data.For a few hundred examples, 2–4 epochs is the usual range. More is where catastrophic forgetting and overfitting live — watch eval loss, not training loss.
optim="adamw_8bit"8-bit optimiser states.Cuts the optimiser memory from 8.3's table further still. Almost free in quality terms.
eval_strategy="epoch"Evaluates on the held-out split each epoch.The only way to see overfitting as it happens. If you skip this you will not know which epoch was best.
report_to="none"Disables automatic experiment-tracker uploads.Prevents a surprise prompt for a Weights & Biases key mid-run. Turn it on deliberately if you want tracking.
seed=42 and random_state=42Fixed randomness.So a rerun is comparable. Section 1.9's discipline, applied to a job that takes an hour.
model.save_pretrained(...)Saves the adapter only.Tens of megabytes. Download it from the notebook before the session dies — free notebooks disconnect, and an unsaved adapter is an hour of GPU time gone.

What a healthy run looks like

GPU = Tesla T4. Max memory = 14.7 GB.
 5.4 GB of memory reserved.

 step  train_loss   eval_loss
    5      1.9421           -
   10      1.4130           -
   15      1.1502           -
  epoch 1       -      1.0987
   20      0.9814           -
   ...
  epoch 2       -      0.8912
   ...
  epoch 3       -      0.9104   ← eval loss rose: epoch 2 was the best checkpoint

adapter saved: second-brain-lora/  (13 MB)

The important line is the last epoch: eval loss went up while training loss went down. That is overfitting, visible only because we evaluated. In a real run you would keep the epoch-2 checkpoint. Two or three epochs on a small dataset very often looks exactly like this.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'tokenizer' (or processing_class)⚠ TRL renamed trainer arguments across versions.Check the installed TRL's SFTTrainer signature: help(SFTTrainer) or read the docs for your version. This is the single most likely failure of this code.
CUDA out of memorySequence length, batch size, or too many target modules.In order: lower max_seq_length, set batch size to 1 and raise accumulation, confirm gradient checkpointing is on, drop the MLP targets, lower the rank.
Colab disconnects mid-runFree tier idle timeouts.Save checkpoints to Google Drive, keep the tab active, and prefer short runs. Or use Kaggle, which is generally steadier.
Loss is nan from step 1Learning rate too high, or a precision mismatch.Drop to 5e-5. Check you are not mixing fp16 and bf16 settings against what the GPU supports — T4 does not support bf16.
Trained fine, but output is unchangedThe adapter was not actually attached, or was not loaded at inference.Print the trainable parameter count before training — it should be roughly the number from 8.3, not zero and not the whole model.

8.6 The step everyone forgets — serving your fine-tune

A fine-tune you cannot serve is an exercise, not a result. You have a 13 MB adapter in a notebook. Your capstone runs on Ollama, which serves GGUF files. Bridging that gap is the difference between "I fine-tuned a model" and "my app uses my fine-tuned model".

The path from adapter to Ollama

StepWhat happensOutput
1. MergeFold the adapter into the base weights: W = W₀ + (α/r)·A·B — exactly the arithmetic verified in 8.3.An ordinary Hugging Face model directory, fp16, no adapter machinery.
2. ConvertRun llama.cpp's HF-to-GGUF conversion script.One .gguf file, fp16 — large.
3. QuantiseRun llama-quantize to Q4_K_M (section 2.9).A ~2 GB file for a 3B model.
4. RegisterWrite a Modelfile and run ollama create.A model name you can use in .env.

⚠ Verify the tooling names. llama.cpp's conversion script has been renamed at least once (it was convert.py, then convert_hf_to_gguf.py) and the quantiser binary's name and build process have changed too. Unsloth also ships export helpers such as save_pretrained_gguf that do steps 1–3 in one call, which is easier when it works. Check llama.cpp and the Unsloth docs for current names before running the commands below.

# 1. merge the adapter into the base model (in Python, on a machine with RAM)
python - <<'PY'
from peft import PeftModel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

BASE = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct"
ADAPTER = "second-brain-lora"

base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(BASE, dtype="auto", device_map="cpu")
merged = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, ADAPTER).merge_and_unload()
merged.save_pretrained("second-brain-merged", safe_serialization=True)
AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(ADAPTER).save_pretrained("second-brain-merged")
print("merged model written to second-brain-merged/")
PY

# 2. convert to GGUF (verify the script name for your llama.cpp checkout)
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
cd llama.cpp && pip install -r requirements.txt
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py ../second-brain-merged \
    --outfile ../second-brain-f16.gguf --outtype f16

# 3. quantise to Q4_K_M (build llama.cpp first; check the current build steps)
cmake -B build && cmake --build build --config Release
./build/bin/llama-quantize ../second-brain-f16.gguf \
    ../second-brain-q4.gguf Q4_K_M

# 4. register with Ollama
cd .. && cat > Modelfile <<'EOF'
FROM ./second-brain-q4.gguf
PARAMETER temperature 0.2
PARAMETER num_ctx 4096
SYSTEM """You are Second Brain. Answer in at most two sentences, citing source#chunk_id."""
EOF

ollama create second-brain -f Modelfile
ollama run second-brain "What port does the Ollama API use?"
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
merge_and_unload()Adds the scaled adapter product into the base weights and removes the adapter wrappers.The operation you verified numerically in 8.3 ("merged W = W0 + delta"). After this there is no LoRA left — just a model.
device_map="cpu"Merges on CPU.Merging needs RAM, not speed, and you probably do not have GPU memory for an fp16 copy. It takes a minute.
safe_serialization=TrueWrites .safetensors.The current standard format: no arbitrary code execution on load, unlike pickle-based checkpoints. Also what the conversion script expects.
AutoTokenizer...save_pretrainedCopies the tokenizer alongside the weights.GGUF embeds the tokenizer and the chat template. Omit it and conversion fails, or worse, succeeds with the wrong template and your fine-tune appears not to have worked.
--outtype f16Converts at full precision first.Quantise after conversion, from fp16. Converting straight to a low quantisation loses more quality than the two-step path.
Q4_K_M argumentThe quantisation level from section 2.9.Best quality per gigabyte. Same reasoning as choosing which model to download.
FROM ./second-brain-q4.ggufPoints the Modelfile at your file.Ollama copies it into its own store on create, so the original can be deleted afterwards.
SYSTEM """..."""Bakes the system prompt into the model.Nice touch: the behaviour you trained and the prompt you trained it with now travel together, so your application code does not have to remember it.
PARAMETER num_ctx 4096Sets the default context window.Reclaims memory versus Ollama's default (section 2.7's KV cache maths).
ollama create second-brain -f ModelfileRegisters the model under a name.Now CHAT_MODEL=second-brain in .env and your entire capstone uses your fine-tune. One line, because of the ChatBackend Protocol from section 4.1.

Then measure it, or you have learned nothing

Run the eval harness from section 5.13 and your own golden set against both models, changing only CHAT_MODEL:

What to compareWhy
Format compliance rate (did it obey the two-sentence, cite-the-chunk contract?)This is what you trained. It should improve clearly, or the fine-tune failed.
Citation verification rate (section 5.7)Checks you did not train it to produce plausible-looking fake citations — the risk from 8.1's warning.
Abstention rate on unanswerable questionsThe behaviour most easily destroyed by fine-tuning. If it dropped, add more abstention examples.
General capability on a few off-task questionsCatastrophic-forgetting check. Ask it something unrelated and see if it still works.
Tokens per second and prompt lengthThe commercial payoff: if you deleted 2,000 tokens of instructions, log the saving.
Try this yourself. After registering the model, delete the system prompt and few-shot examples from your application's prompt and rerun the evals. If quality holds, you have converted a 3,000-token prompt into model weights — which is the strongest business case for fine-tuning and the one you can put a number on.

8.7 Distillation, merging, and small language models

Distillation

Training a small model to imitate a larger one. Two flavours worth distinguishing:

KindHowPracticality
Response distillation (what people usually mean)Generate answers with a strong model, curate them, fine-tune a small model on the pairs.Very practical. This is just SFT with a particular data source — everything in 8.4 and 8.5 applies unchanged. Check the source model's terms of service first; several forbid training competing models on their outputs.
Logit distillation (the classical technique)Train the student to match the teacher's full probability distribution, not just its chosen token.Richer signal per example, but needs logits from the teacher — so both models must be local, and the plumbing is real work. Rare outside labs.

Many of the small models you already use are distilled: the "R1-distill" variants of Qwen and Llama are exactly this, trained on a reasoning model's traces. That is why a 7B distill can outperform a 7B base model on maths while being no better at anything else.

Model merging

Combining two or more fine-tuned models of the same architecture into one, by arithmetic on their weights — no training, no GPU, minutes on a CPU. Techniques you will see named:

  • Linear / weight averaging — the simplest: average the weights. Works better than it has any right to.
  • SLERP — spherical interpolation between two models, often better than a linear blend.
  • Task arithmetic — compute "task vectors" (fine-tuned minus base) and add or subtract them. Note this is exactly a LoRA delta generalised to all weights, which is why 8.3's merge step and model merging are the same idea.
  • TIES / DARE — resolve conflicts between task vectors by trimming and rescaling, which handles merging several models better than plain addition.

Honest verdict: genuinely useful for combining independently trained behaviours (a style adapter plus a domain adapter) and startlingly cheap. Also unpredictable — merges can lose capabilities in ways that only your eval set will reveal. mergekit (⚠ check current licence) is the standard tool. This is a "measure it" technique, not a "ship it" technique.

Small language models, and why they are the actual trend

The interesting movement in production is not toward bigger models; it is toward small models doing narrow jobs well. Section 6.8's router pattern plus a fine-tuned 3B beats a prompted 70B on cost, latency and often accuracy for a specific task.

JobModel size that suffices
Routing and classification (section 6.9)0.5B–2B, fine-tuned. Milliseconds, negligible memory.
Query rewriting and condensing (section 5.10)1–3B. It is a rephrasing task.
Extraction into a fixed schema1–3B with constrained decoding.
RAG answering with citations3–8B. The capstone's default.
Multi-step agent loops with tool selection8B+, and honestly this is where local models struggle most.

This is why Part 0 insisted the capstone must work at 1.7B, and why a fine-tuned small model is a more interesting engineering result than access to a bigger one.

8.8 Multimodal — vision, speech, and voice

All of this is optional for the capstone and all of it is free. The relevance to a research assistant is concrete: scanned PDFs need vision, meeting recordings need transcription.

Vision models

VLMs (Vision Language Models) take images alongside text. Architecturally: an image encoder produces embeddings that are projected into the language model's embedding space, so the image becomes a sequence of "tokens" attention can attend to — the same mechanism from section 2.3, with a different source of vectors.

Use caseApproachNotes
Scanned PDFs in your RAG pipelineA local VLM via Ollama (several vision-capable models are available ⚠ — check ollama.com/library for current ones), or classical OCR with ocrmypdf + Tesseract.Fixes the "PDF extracts as empty" error from section 5.3. OCR is faster and cheaper; a VLM handles layout, tables and handwriting better.
Describing charts and diagramsVLM, then index the description as text.Turns an unsearchable image into a retrievable chunk. Genuinely useful and easy to bolt onto Part 5's ingestion.
Screenshot-driven agentsVLM in a loop (section 6.14).The reliability caveats from Part 6 apply in full.

Speech to text

Whisper (OpenAI, MIT licence, weights released) is the default, and it runs locally. Sizes from tiny (~75 MB) to large (~1.5 GB), with the small ones genuinely usable on CPU. Implementations to know:

  • faster-whisper — a CTranslate2 reimplementation, several times faster than the reference with lower memory. What most people actually use.
  • whisper.cpp — the same idea as llama.cpp: C++, quantised, no Python dependency at all. Excellent on Apple silicon.
  • The reference openai-whisper package — simplest to install, slowest.

For the capstone this is a clean extension: transcribe an audio file, then feed the transcript through the existing ingestion pipeline from section 5.3. Nothing downstream changes, which is a good sign about your layering.

Text to speech

⚠ The fastest-moving of the three, and the area where I am least confident about what is current. The shape of the options:

OptionTrade-off
Piper (MIT)Small, fast, fully local, runs on a Raspberry Pi. Voices are clearly synthetic but perfectly intelligible. The pragmatic local default.
Kokoro and similar recent small open models ⚠Noticeably better quality at small sizes. Check current licences and status — this space has moved quickly.
Coqui TTS ⚠Historically the flexible open toolkit with voice cloning; the company shut down, so check the maintenance status of the fork you use.
Browser SpeechSynthesis APIZero dependencies, zero install, works in your Angular frontend today. Quality varies by OS. Genuinely the right first choice if you want the capstone to talk.

What I would actually add to the capstone, in order. (1) OCR for scanned PDFs, because it fixes a real failure in your ingestion. (2) Whisper for audio notes, because it reuses the whole pipeline. (3) TTS last, because it is a demo feature rather than a capability. And note the pattern: each of these is a tool or an ingestion loader, not a change to your architecture — which is what a well-layered system looks like.

8.9 Part 8 checkpoint

Quiz answer 1: your model does not know your company's product names. Fine-tune or RAG?

RAG. That is missing knowledge, and fine-tuning facts in is inefficient and can increase hallucination, because what SFT reliably teaches is the shape of confident assertion rather than the facts themselves. The nuance worth stating: if the model needs to use the names fluently in your house style once it has them from context, that is a behaviour problem and a fine-tune could help — but the facts still come from retrieval.

Quiz answer 2: why is B initialised to zeros and A to small random values?

So the adapter is an exact no-op at step 0: A·B = 0, so the model starts from its pretrained behaviour rather than from a corrupted version of it. A must be non-zero or the gradient with respect to B is permanently zero and nothing trains — the same symmetry-breaking requirement as neural network initialisation in section 1.9.

Quiz answer 3: your LoRA loss plateaus well above where you need it. What do you change first?

The rank. Section 8.3 demonstrated that insufficient rank is a hard ceiling, not slow convergence — rank 1 and 2 could not represent a rank-3 update no matter how long they trained. Raise the rank, and add target modules. Only then look at learning rate and epochs. If it still plateaus, your task may not be low-rank, which means fine-tuning is the wrong tool rather than badly configured.

Quiz answer 4: where does QLoRA's memory saving actually come from?

Two places, and the bigger one surprises people. Quantising the frozen base to 4 bits saves about 11 GB on an 8B model. But the larger saving is that optimiser state scales with trainable parameters, not total ones — 89 GB of gradients and Adam moments collapse to 0.08 GB. That is LoRA's contribution rather than quantisation's, which is why LoRA alone already fits on a single 24 GB GPU.

Quiz answer 5: you trained an adapter and it works in the notebook. What is left to do?

Merge, convert to GGUF, quantise, register with Ollama, and then measure against the base model on format compliance, citation verification, abstention rate and off-task capability. A fine-tune that lives in a notebook is an exercise. And the measurement is not optional: without the before-and-after you cannot distinguish a successful fine-tune from one that broke your abstention behaviour.

You are done with Part 8 when you can

  • Say in one sentence what fine-tuning is for and what RAG is for, and explain the hallucination warning.
  • Write the LoRA forward pass and explain what r and α do.
  • Explain where QLoRA's memory saving comes from, with rough numbers.
  • Name four dataset defects your validator catches and why each one degrades a run.
  • Describe the adapter → merged → GGUF → Ollama path without looking it up.
  • Explain why a fine-tuned 3B can beat a prompted 70B on one task.

Part 9

Angular frontend for AI applications

A change of language, taught from zero, entirely against the app you have already built. No todo lists. By the end you have a streaming chat UI with a working cancel button, safe markdown rendering, a citations panel, an agent trace viewer, an approval dialog and file upload — milestones M16 to M18.

9.1 The Angular mental model, and how to read React tutorials

⚠ Version target, stated up front. This part targets Angular 22, the stable line as of writing. Angular ships a major every six months, so check ng version and expect drift. Where a feature has a minimum version I say so inline. Three things changed recently enough to matter:

  • v20+: generated files drop the .component suffix — chat.ts, not chat.component.ts. If yours have the old names, your CLI is older; adjust the paths I give you.
  • v21+: new projects are zoneless by default. This matters more than it sounds — see the box in 9.3.
  • v21/22: the default test runner is Vitest; Karma is deprecated. Your brief asked for Jasmine/Karma and I am deliberately not teaching a deprecated runner — 9.14 explains exactly what carries over, which is nearly everything.

The five ideas that are all of Angular

IdeaWhat it isIn our app
ComponentA TypeScript class with a decorator tying it to a template and styles. The unit of UI.ChatComponent, CitationsPanel, TraceViewer.
TemplateHTML with Angular syntax: {{ value }}, [property], (event), @if, @for.chat.html.
ServiceA plain class holding logic or state, shared between components.ChatService — everything that talks to FastAPI.
Dependency injectionYou declare what you need; Angular constructs and supplies it. Ask for ChatService and you get the same instance everywhere.How components get the service without importing a global.
SignalsA value that knows who is reading it, so the UI updates when it changes.The message list, the streaming flag, the pending approval.

Translating React tutorials, which is what you will actually be doing

Nearly every AI frontend tutorial is React. Here is the mapping, so you can read them and write Angular:

ReactAngularNote
const [x, setX] = useState(0)x = signal(0), then x.set(1) / x.update(v => v+1)Read the value as x() — with parentheses, always. This trips everyone up for a day.
useMemo(() => a + b, [a, b])total = computed(() => this.a() + this.b())No dependency array. Angular tracks what you read automatically, which is strictly better.
useEffect(() => {...}, [x])effect(() => {... this.x() ...})Again no dependency array. Use effects sparingly — mostly for logging and imperative DOM work, not for deriving state.
propsvalue = input<string>() (v17.1+)Inputs are signals too, so this.value().
onChange callback propchanged = output<string>(), then this.changed.emit(v)Angular splits data-in and events-out explicitly.
{cond && <div/>}@if (cond) { <div></div> } (v17+)Older tutorials use *ngIf; both work.
items.map(i => <Row key={i.id}/>)@for (i of items(); track i.id) { <app-row/> }track is Angular's key, and it is mandatory.
Context / Zustand / ReduxA service with signals, provided at the rootAngular has DI built in, so there is no equivalent problem to solve. This is genuinely simpler.
useRef for a DOM nodeviewChild<ElementRef>('name') + #name in the templateNeeded for the autoscroll container in 9.9.
Everything re-renders on state changeOnly the components reading the changed signal updateThe biggest practical difference. It is why streaming 60 tokens/second does not melt an Angular app.

The one-sentence difference. React re-runs your component function and diffs the result; Angular compiles your template once and updates only the specific bindings that changed. For our use case — a token arriving 60 times a second — Angular's model is a genuine advantage, provided you use signals rather than plain fields.

What we are building

src/app/
├── app.ts / app.html / app.scss        root component (shell + nav)
├── app.config.ts                       providers: HttpClient, router
├── app.routes.ts                       /chat and /documents

│   ├── models.ts                       TypeScript mirrors of the Pydantic schemas

│   └── documents.service.ts            upload with progress
