10.7 Testing LLM applications

The rule that makes this tractable: unit tests never call a model. Determinism and speed matter more than realism at that level, and everything realistic belongs in the eval suite.

LayerWhat it coversModel?Runs
UnitChunkers, BM25, RRF, citation verification, SSE formatting, guardrails, the agent loop's control flow.No — EchoBackend or a scripted fake.Every commit, milliseconds.
ContractThat the API's JSON matches the TypeScript interfaces, and that the SSE format matches the client parser.No.Every commit.
Retrieval evalrecall@k, MRR against a golden set.Embedder only, no LLM.Every pull request, seconds.
Generation evalFaithfulness, answer relevance, abstention, format validity.Yes, plus a judge.Nightly, or before a release.
SmokeThe whole stack answers one question end to end.Yes.After deploy.
 
"""The agent loop's control flow, tested with no model at all."""

import json

import pytest

from app.agent.loop import run_agent, scripted_model


def action(thought: str, tool: str, args: dict) -> str:
    return json.dumps({"thought": thought, "tool": tool, "args": args})


def final(text: str) -> str:
    return json.dumps({"thought": "done", "final": text})


def test_recovers_from_bad_tool_arguments():
    replies = [
        action("compute", "calculator", {"expresion": "2+2"}),   # typo
        action("retry", "calculator", {"expression": "2+2"}),
        final("The answer is 4."),
    ]
    result = run_agent("what is 2+2", scripted_model(replies), verbose=False)

    assert result.stop_reason == "final"
    assert [s.ok for s in result.steps] == [False, True, True]
    assert "Field required" in (result.steps[0].observation or "")


def test_stops_at_the_step_limit():
    spin = [action("again", "search_notes", {"query": "ollama port"})]
    result = run_agent("x", scripted_model(spin), max_steps=3, verbose=False)

    assert result.stop_reason == "step limit"
    assert result.tool_calls == 3


def test_denied_tool_never_executes():
    replies = [
        action("write", "write_file", {"filename": "a.md", "content": "hi"}),
        final("I did not write the file."),
    ]
    result = run_agent("save it", scripted_model(replies),
                       approve=lambda tool, args: False, verbose=False)

    assert result.tool_calls == 0
    assert "DENIED" in (result.steps[0].observation or "")


def test_approval_defaults_to_deny_when_no_handler():
    replies = [
        action("write", "write_file", {"filename": "a.md", "content": "hi"}),
        final("blocked"),
    ]
    result = run_agent("save it", scripted_model(replies), verbose=False)
    assert result.tool_calls == 0


@pytest.mark.parametrize("garbage", ["not json at all", "{", '{"thought": ""}'])
def test_malformed_replies_become_observations(garbage: str):
    result = run_agent("x", scripted_model([garbage]), max_steps=2, verbose=False)
    assert result.stop_reason == "step limit"
    assert not result.steps[0].ok
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
scripted_model(replies)The fake model from section 6.4.Written then precisely so the loop would be testable. Every branch — malformed JSON, bad arguments, denial, step limit — is reachable deterministically in milliseconds.
action() / final() helpersBuild reply JSON compactly.Keeps each test about the behaviour rather than about JSON literals.
assert [s.ok for s in result.steps] == [False, True, True]Asserts the exact recovery shape.Encodes the most important agent property as a test: a tool error is recoverable. If someone later makes call_tool raise instead of returning a message, this fails and says why.
test_stops_at_the_step_limitA model that never finishes.Tests the limit itself. An agent without a proven termination guarantee is a billing incident waiting to happen.
test_approval_defaults_to_deny_when_no_handlerNo approve argument at all.A security test. Section 6.4's fail-closed default, pinned. If a refactor made the default permissive, this catches it.
assert result.tool_calls == 0Checks the tool never ran.Stronger than checking the observation text. The point of a denial is that nothing happened.
@pytest.mark.parametrizeRuns one test with three garbage inputs.Three tests for the price of one, each reported separately.

The two contract tests worth having

TestHowWhat it prevents
SSE format matches the clientFeed sse() output to a copy of the client's parser, byte by byte — exactly the verified test in 10.2.A change to the wire format silently breaking streaming. This is the highest-value test in the whole project, because the bug only appears over a real network.
API JSON matches the TypeScriptGenerate types from /openapi.json in CI and fail if the committed models.ts differs.The drift section 9.2 warned about: TypeScript interfaces are compile-time only, so a renamed Pydantic field is invisible until runtime.

What not to test. Do not assert on model output text — assert "11434" in answer is flaky and will be deleted by whoever it fails on next. Assert on structure (schema validity, citations verified, abstention when the context is empty) and put quality judgements in the eval suite with thresholds, where noise is expected and handled.

10.8 Security

Five concrete threats, in the order they will actually hurt you.

ThreatWhere it comes fromYour defence
1. Prompt injection through a RAG documentA PDF or web page you ingested, containing instructions.Section 3.6's fencing and scanning, and — the part that actually matters — section 6.3's tool allow-lists plus 6.10's approval gates. Constrain capability, not wording.
2. Secret leakageLogs, error messages returned to the client, and the model repeating its system prompt.10.4's redaction at the formatter; never put secrets in a prompt; return generic messages to the client and detail to the log.
3. Tool abuseModel-generated arguments: path traversal, unbounded loops, code execution.Pydantic validation, the AST allow-list calculator, the resolved-path check, and budgets. All built in Part 6.
4. Resource exhaustionOne user, or a script, sending fifty concurrent questions to a single GPU.Rate limiting, request size caps, and a concurrency semaphore.
5. Cross-tenant leakageRetrieval returning another user's documents.A pre-filter applied last, on the server, that model-supplied filters cannot override.

Build the rate limiter and the tenant filter — the two defences not yet written.

"""Rate limiting and tenant isolation primitives."""

import time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass
class TokenBucket:
    """Allows `capacity` requests, refilling at `rate` per second."""
    capacity: float
    rate: float
    tokens: float = field(init=False)
    updated: float = field(init=False)

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        self.tokens = self.capacity
        self.updated = time.monotonic()

    def allow(self, cost: float = 1.0, now: float | None = None) -> bool:
        now = now if now is not None else time.monotonic()
        elapsed = max(0.0, now - self.updated)   # clamp: injected clocks can go backwards
        self.updated = now
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + elapsed * self.rate)
        if self.tokens >= cost:
            self.tokens -= cost
            return True
        return False

    def retry_after(self, cost: float = 1.0) -> float:
        missing = max(0.0, cost - self.tokens)
        return missing / self.rate if self.rate > 0 else float("inf")


class RateLimiter:
    """One bucket per key. In production use Redis so limits survive restarts."""

    def __init__(self, capacity: float = 5, rate: float = 0.5) -> None:
        self.capacity, self.rate = capacity, rate
        self.buckets: dict[str, TokenBucket] = {}

    def check(self, key: str, cost: float = 1.0, now: float | None = None):
        bucket = self.buckets.setdefault(key, TokenBucket(self.capacity, self.rate))
        allowed = bucket.allow(cost, now)
        return allowed, bucket.retry_after(cost)


def tenant_filter(tenant_id: str, requested: dict | None = None) -> dict:
    """Build the retrieval filter. The tenant clause is applied LAST, always."""
    safe = dict(requested or {})
    safe.pop("tenant_id", None)          # a model-supplied filter cannot forge this
    safe["tenant_id"] = tenant_id
    return safe


if __name__ == "__main__":
    limiter = RateLimiter(capacity=3, rate=0.5)      # 3 burst, 1 every 2s
    t = time.monotonic()
    print("burst of 5 requests from one user:")
    for i in range(1, 6):
        allowed, wait = limiter.check("user-a", now=t)
        print(f"  req {i}: allowed={allowed!s:<5} retry_after={wait:.1f}s")

    print("\na different user is unaffected:")
    allowed, wait = limiter.check("user-b", now=t)
    print(f"  user-b: allowed={allowed}")

    print("\nsame user, 6 seconds later:")
    for i in range(1, 4):
        allowed, wait = limiter.check("user-a", now=t + 6)
        print(f"  req {i}: allowed={allowed!s:<5} retry_after={wait:.1f}s")

    print("\ntenant isolation:")
    print("  clean          ->", tenant_filter("acme", {"kind": "pdf"}))
    print("  forged attempt ->", tenant_filter("acme", {"tenant_id": "globex", "kind": "pdf"}))
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
Token bucket rather than a fixed windowTokens accumulate up to a cap and are spent per request.Allows a short burst (a user asking three questions quickly) while enforcing a sustained rate. A fixed window either forbids legitimate bursts or permits double the rate across a window boundary.
elapsed = max(0.0, now - self.updated)Clamps negative elapsed time.A bug I hit while verifying this. The first version let an injected test clock run backwards, driving the token count deeply negative and denying everything with a 640-second retry. Clamping is both the test fix and correct defensive behaviour against clock adjustments.
now: float | None = NoneInjectable clock.Makes the limiter testable without sleep. Section 4.6's rng parameter, same idea.
retry_after()Computes how long until the next request is allowed.Goes into the HTTP Retry-After header, which section 4.6's client-side backoff honours. Your API should behave the way you want other APIs to.
capacity=5, rate=0.5 defaultsFive burst, one every two seconds.Sensible for an LLM endpoint on one GPU: a human cannot usefully exceed it, and a script hits it immediately.
"In production use Redis"States the limitation.An in-memory dict resets on restart and is per-process, so N workers means N times the limit. Honest, and the fix is a shared store.
safe.pop("tenant_id", None) then safe["tenant_id"] = tenant_idStrips any supplied tenant, then sets the real one.The whole security property, in two lines. Order matters absolutely: the trusted value is written after the untrusted dict is copied, so a self-query filter (section 5.11) or an injected instruction cannot reach another tenant's documents. Merging the other way round is a data breach.

Verified output

burst of 5 requests from one user:
  req 1: allowed=True  retry_after=0.0s
  req 2: allowed=True  retry_after=0.0s
  req 3: allowed=True  retry_after=2.0s
  req 4: allowed=False retry_after=2.0s
  req 5: allowed=False retry_after=2.0s

a different user is unaffected:
  user-b: allowed=True

same user, 6 seconds later:
  req 1: allowed=True  retry_after=0.0s
  req 2: allowed=True  retry_after=0.0s
  req 3: allowed=True  retry_after=2.0s

tenant isolation:
  clean          -> {'kind': 'pdf', 'tenant_id': 'acme'}
  forged attempt -> {'kind': 'pdf', 'tenant_id': 'acme'}

Three through, two refused with an accurate two-second retry, a second user unaffected, and three tokens refilled after six seconds at half a token per second. And the forged tenant_id is overwritten rather than honoured — the attempt produces the same filter as the clean call.

Wiring the limiter and a concurrency cap into FastAPI

import asyncio

from fastapi import Depends, Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse

from app.limits import RateLimiter

limiter = RateLimiter(capacity=5, rate=0.5)

# One GPU means one generation at a time. Queue the rest rather than thrashing.
generation_slots = asyncio.Semaphore(2)


async def rate_limit(request: Request) -> None:
    """Per-caller limit. Use an authenticated user id when you have one."""
    key = request.headers.get("x-user-id") or (request.client.host if request.client else "-")
    allowed, wait = limiter.check(key)
    if not allowed:
        log_event(log, "rate_limited", key=key, retry_after=round(wait, 1))
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=429,
            detail="Too many requests.",
            headers={"Retry-After": str(int(wait) + 1)},
        )


@app.post("/api/chat/stream", dependencies=[Depends(rate_limit)])
async def chat_stream(body: AskRequest, request: Request) -> StreamingResponse:
    async def events():
        async with generation_slots:
            ...   # the generator from section 10.2, unchanged
    return StreamingResponse(events(), media_type="text/event-stream",
                             headers=SSE_HEADERS)
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
dependencies=[Depends(rate_limit)]Runs the check before the handler.FastAPI dependency injection. Declaring it on the route means it cannot be forgotten inside the function, and it applies before any work starts.
request.client.host fallbackKeys by IP when there is no user id.Weak — behind a proxy every request shares an IP, so read X-Forwarded-For if you trust your proxy. Use a real authenticated identity as soon as you have one.
headers={"Retry-After": ...}Tells the client when to come back.Section 4.6's client reads this. Returning 429 without it forces every caller to guess.
asyncio.Semaphore(2)Caps concurrent generations.The lesson from section 4.5: one Ollama instance is one worker, so ten concurrent requests do not go ten times faster — they go ten times slower each and exhaust memory. Two lets one warm up while another finishes. Queuing gives predictable latency; thrashing gives none.
async with generation_slots inside the generatorHolds the slot only while generating.Placed outside, it would be held for the whole request including retrieval. Placed here, the slot is released as soon as generation ends.

The three sentences to remember from this section. Untrusted text reaches your model through documents, not just through the chat box. The only defence that survives a determined attacker is limiting what a successful injection can do — read-only tools, validated arguments, human approval for anything irreversible. And the security filter is always applied last, by your code, over anything the model suggested.

10.9 Latency and cost optimisation

Measure first. Section 4.7's meter and 10.5's spans exist so this section is arithmetic rather than guesswork.

Where the time actually goes

StageTypical share, local modelWhat helps
Embedding the query10–50 msNothing. Already negligible — unless you are reloading the model per request, which the lifespan fix prevents.
Vector search1–20 msNothing, below 50k chunks (section 5.6).
Reranking50–400 msFewer candidates. 20 instead of 50 is a straight linear saving.
Prompt processing (prefill)0.5–5 sShorter prompts. Quadratic in length (section 2.7), so this is where a bloated context hurts most. Prompt caching if your runtime supports it.
Token generation3–30 sSmaller model, fewer output tokens, or streaming so the user does not wait for all of it.

The seven levers, in order of value

LeverEffectCost to you
1. StreamPerceived latency drops from total time to time-to-first-token: section 3.5 measured 4.87 s → 0.41 s. A 12× improvement in what the user feels.Already done (M17). Nothing.
2. Cache deterministic calls401 ms → 0.2 ms on a hit (section 4.8). Enormous during development and evaluation.Forty lines. Remember to include retrieved chunk ids in the key.
3. Route to a smaller modelA 1.7B router deciding whether a question even needs retrieval, then a 4B answering simple ones. Often 3–5× faster on the easy majority.Section 6.9's router. One extra cheap call.
4. Shorten the promptFewer, better chunks (4 not 10), a tighter system prompt, truncated tool observations. Directly attacks the quadratic prefill.Free, and section 2.7 says it may improve quality.
5. Cap output tokens"At most two sentences" plus num_predict. Generation is the biggest cost, so this is the biggest direct saving.Free. Already in the prompt.
6. Prompt cachingA fixed system prompt and stable retrieved context can skip re-processing. Requires a byte-identical prefix at the start.A real design constraint on prompt assembly. ⚠ Support and behaviour vary per runtime and provider — verify.
7. BatchReal throughput scaling for concurrent users.Needs vLLM rather than Ollama (section 7.4). A deployment change, not a code change.

Prompt compression, honestly. Techniques that use a small model to compress the prompt before sending it to a large one exist and can cut tokens substantially. They also add a model call, add latency, and can silently drop the one sentence that mattered. For a local-first app where the saving is compute rather than money, retrieving fewer and better chunks achieves the same thing with no risk. File this under "know it exists"; reach for levers 1 to 5 first.

A worked example

ChangePrompt tokensOutput tokensTotal timeTTFT
Starting point: 10 chunks, verbose prompt, no cap3,40042031 s4.1 s
Rerank to 4 chunks (section 5.9)1,45042022 s1.8 s
"At most three sentences" + num_predict=2001,4501108 s1.8 s
Stream it (M17)1,4501108 s1.8 s felt
Route trivial questions to a 1.7B model1,4501103 s on the easy path0.6 s

Illustrative numbers, but the shape is what recurs: most of the win comes from sending less and generating less, not from clever infrastructure. And note that steps two and three came from decisions made in Parts 5 and 3 for quality reasons — good retrieval and tight prompts are a latency optimisation as a side effect.

Try this yourself. Log prompt_tokens and completion_tokens for twenty real questions using 10.4's record, then compute the mean. If prompt tokens exceed roughly 2,000 on a local model, you are paying quadratic prefill for context the model is probably using poorly anyway (section 2.7). Cut top_k and measure both latency and recall@5 — you will often find you improved both.

10.10 M19 — Docker and one-command startup

Four containers, one docker compose up, and a stack a stranger can run.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.13-slim AS base

ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \
    HF_HOME=/models

WORKDIR /app

# System packages needed by pypdf/torch wheels and healthchecks.
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
        curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Dependencies first, in their own layer, so code changes do not reinstall them.
COPY requirements.txt ./
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY app ./app
COPY evals ./evals

# Run as a non-root user.
RUN useradd --create-home --uid 10001 appuser \
    && mkdir -p /models /app/data \
    && chown -R appuser:appuser /models /app
USER appuser

EXPOSE 8000

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=90s --retries=3 \
    CMD curl -fsS http://localhost:8000/api/health || exit 1

CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
python:3.13-slimA small official base image.slim saves several hundred megabytes over the full image. Avoid alpine for Python: musl means many packages build from source instead of using wheels, so builds are slow and occasionally broken.
PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1Unbuffered stdout.Without it your logs vanish. Python buffers when stdout is not a terminal, so docker logs shows nothing until the buffer fills or the process exits — deeply confusing when debugging a container.
HF_HOME=/modelsRedirects the Hugging Face cache.So the embedding and reranker models land in a mounted volume rather than being re-downloaded on every container start. Several hundred megabytes per start, otherwise.
COPY requirements.txt before COPY appDependencies in an earlier layer.The single most important Docker habit. Docker caches layers; changing one line of Python then rebuilds only from the code copy onward. Copy everything at once and every rebuild reinstalls PyTorch.
--no-install-recommends and rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*Minimal apt install, cleaned in the same layer.Cleaning in a later layer does not shrink the image — the files still exist in the earlier one.
useradd and USER appuserDrops root.A container escape as root is meaningfully worse than as uid 10001. Costs two lines. Note the chown must come before USER.
--start-period=90sGrace period before healthchecks count.Loading a sentence-transformer at startup takes tens of seconds. Without this, the container is marked unhealthy and restarted forever — a genuinely maddening loop.
--host 0.0.0.0Listens on all interfaces.Required in a container. The default 127.0.0.1 is unreachable from outside, which is the classic "the container is running but I can't connect" bug.
no --reloadProduction mode.--reload costs a file watcher and restarts on any change. Use a bind mount and override the command for development.
 
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ---- stage 1: build the Angular app ----
FROM node:24-alpine AS build

WORKDIR /src
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# ---- stage 2: serve the static files ----
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine

COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --from=build /src/dist/frontend/browser /usr/share/nginx/html

EXPOSE 80

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD wget -qO- http://localhost/ >/dev/null || exit 1
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name _;
    root /usr/share/nginx/html;

    gzip on;
    gzip_types text/css application/javascript application/json image/svg+xml;
    gzip_min_length 1024;

    # Hashed build assets never change: cache them hard.
    location ~* \.(js|css|woff2|svg|png)$ {
        expires 1y;
        add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable";
        try_files $uri =404;
    }

    # index.html must never be cached, or users get a stale app shell.
    location = /index.html {
        add_header Cache-Control "no-cache, must-revalidate";
        try_files $uri =404;
    }

    # The API, including SSE.
    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass http://api:8000;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;

        # --- the four lines that make streaming work ---
        proxy_buffering off;
        proxy_cache off;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_read_timeout 600s;

        client_max_body_size 30m;
    }

    # Angular routing: unknown paths return the app shell, not a 404.
    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;
    }
}
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
multi-stage buildBuilds with Node, ships with nginx.The final image contains no Node, no node_modules, no source — tens of megabytes instead of a gigabyte, and a much smaller attack surface. This is what section 9.13 meant by "static files, no Node needed to serve them".
COPY package*.json before COPY . .Same layer-caching trick as the backend.Editing a component does not re-run npm ci.
dist/frontend/browserThe build output path.⚠ Depends on your project name and Angular version — the /browser subdirectory arrived with the application builder. Check what ng build actually produced.
expires 1y; immutable on hashed assetsAggressive caching for fingerprinted files.Safe precisely because the filename contains a content hash: a new build produces new names, so a stale cache is impossible.
no-cache on index.htmlNever cache the shell.The pairing that matters. Cache index.html and users keep loading an old shell that references deleted asset filenames — a blank page after every deploy.
proxy_buffering offStreams the response through.The nginx half of "streaming works in curl but not in the browser". The API's X-Accel-Buffering: no header (10.2) does the same job; both is belt and braces.
proxy_set_header Connection ""Clears the Connection header for keep-alive.With proxy_http_version 1.1, this is what actually enables persistent upstream connections. Both lines are needed.
proxy_read_timeout 600sTen-minute upstream timeout.nginx's 60-second default kills a slow local generation mid-stream. This is the other reason for 10.2's keep-alive comments.
client_max_body_size 30mAllows PDF uploads.nginx's 1 MB default returns 413 before FastAPI is even reached — and section 9.11 already handles that status, which is how you will identify it.
try_files $uri $uri/ /index.htmlServes the app shell for unknown paths.Required for client-side routing. Without it, reloading /documents asks nginx for a file that does not exist and returns 404. Every SPA needs this line.
proxy_pass http://api:8000Uses the compose service name.Docker's internal DNS resolves api. This is why apiBase stays empty and the frontend code is identical in development and production.
 
name: second-brain

services:
  ollama:
    image: ollama/ollama:latest
    container_name: sb-ollama
    ports:
      - "11434:11434"
    volumes:
      - ollama-models:/root/.ollama
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "ollama list >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 30s
    restart: unless-stopped
    # Uncomment for an NVIDIA GPU (needs the container toolkit installed):
    # deploy:
    #   resources:
    #     reservations:
    #       devices:
    #         - driver: nvidia
    #           count: all
    #           capabilities: [gpu]

  api:
    build:
      context: ./backend
    container_name: sb-api
    depends_on:
      ollama:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      - OLLAMA_HOST=http://ollama:11434
      - CHAT_MODEL=${CHAT_MODEL:-qwen3:1.7b}
      - EMBED_MODEL=${EMBED_MODEL:-sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2}
      - LOG_LEVEL=INFO
      - PRODUCTION=true
      - LANGFUSE_ENABLED=${LANGFUSE_ENABLED:-false}
    volumes:
      - ./data:/app/data
      - hf-models:/models
    restart: unless-stopped

  web:
    build:
      context: ./frontend
    container_name: sb-web
    depends_on:
      - api
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  ollama-models:
  hf-models:
Line(s)What it doesWhy we need it
depends_on: ollama: condition: service_healthyWaits for Ollama to be genuinely ready.Not the same as plain depends_on, which only waits for the container to start. Ollama takes seconds to be usable, so the plain form gives you connection-refused errors on every cold start.
OLLAMA_HOST=http://ollama:11434Service name, not localhost.The most common containerisation bug. Inside a container, localhost is that container. Your .env pointing at 127.0.0.1:11434 works natively and fails here — which is exactly why section 1.5 made it configurable.
${CHAT_MODEL:-qwen3:1.7b}Reads from the host environment with a default.Someone with a big GPU sets CHAT_MODEL=qwen3:8b in their shell and nothing else changes. The default keeps it runnable on the tier-A machine from section 0.4.
PRODUCTION=trueDisables the CORS middleware.10.2's flag. Same origin behind nginx, so CORS is unnecessary and its absence is safer.
ollama-models as a named volumePersists downloaded models.Without it, docker compose down deletes several gigabytes you then re-download. Named volumes survive; container filesystems do not.
hf-models:/modelsPersists the Hugging Face cache.Paired with HF_HOME=/models in the Dockerfile. Same reasoning.
./data:/app/data as a bind mountYour documents and index live on the host.Deliberately a bind mount, not a volume: you want to drop PDFs into data/docs with your file manager and see them indexed.
"8080:80"The app on localhost:8080.Avoids needing root for port 80 and avoids clashing with anything already on it.
only ollama and web publish portsThe API is reachable only inside the network.Nothing outside reaches FastAPI except through nginx. Publishing 8000 as well would bypass your rate limiting and caching. (Ollama's port is published purely for convenience during development.)
the commented-out GPU blockOpt-in GPU passthrough.It fails on machines without the NVIDIA container toolkit, so it must not be the default in a course that has to run everywhere.

Bringing it up

docker compose up -d --build

# Pull the model into the Ollama container the first time (it is not in the image):
docker compose exec ollama ollama pull qwen3:1.7b
docker compose exec ollama ollama pull nomic-embed-text   # if using Ollama embeddings

# Build the index from whatever is in ./data/docs:
docker compose exec api python -m app.build_index

docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f api | head -20

# Then open http://localhost:8080
NAME         IMAGE                    STATUS                    PORTS
sb-api       second-brain-api         Up 2 minutes (healthy)
sb-ollama    ollama/ollama:latest     Up 2 minutes (healthy)    0.0.0.0:11434->11434/tcp
sb-web       second-brain-web         Up 2 minutes (healthy)    0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp

{"ts":"2026-09-01T09:31:02","level":"INFO","logger":"secondbrain.api","trace_id":"-","msg":"startup","model":"qwen3:1.7b"}
{"ts":"2026-09-01T09:31:44","level":"INFO","logger":"secondbrain.api","trace_id":"a91f2c04","msg":"request.done","method":"POST","path":"/api/chat/stream","status":200,"ms":4820}

M19 is done. git commit -m "M19: Dockerfiles, nginx and docker-compose for the whole stack". Someone can now clone your repository, run one command, and use your application. That is the difference between a project and a portfolio piece.

Common errors and how to fix them
ErrorCauseFix
Connection refused to Ollama from the APIOLLAMA_HOST still points at localhost or 127.0.0.1.Use the service name http://ollama:11434. On a native-Ollama-plus-containerised-API setup, use http://host.docker.internal:11434 instead.
model "qwen3:1.7b" not foundThe image ships no models.docker compose exec ollama ollama pull .... This is a first-run step, not a bug.
413 on uploadnginx client_max_body_size.Raise it in nginx.conf and check the API's own limit.
Reloading /documents gives a 404Missing try_files ... /index.html.Add the SPA fallback block.
Streaming arrives all at once, only in Dockernginx buffering.proxy_buffering off. Confirm by curling the API container directly.
Container restarts in a loopHealthcheck failing during model load.Raise --start-period. Check docker compose logs api for the real error first.
Blank page after a rebuildCached index.html referencing old asset names.The no-cache block on index.html. Hard-refresh to confirm the diagnosis.
Models re-download on every startMissing named volumes.Keep ollama-models and hf-models, and do not use docker compose down -v casually — -v deletes them.

10.11 Deploying it for free

⚠ Free tiers change constantly. Every figure here needs checking before you rely on it — providers have repeatedly cut, restructured or withdrawn free offerings. Treat this as a map of the options, not a price list.

The problem: nobody gives away GPUs

Your stack has one expensive component, and it is Ollama. A free tier will give you a small container with no GPU and a few hundred megabytes of RAM — nowhere near enough to run even a 1.7B model at usable speed. So the deployment question is really: where does inference happen?

StrategyHowHonest verdict
A. Free API for inference, free tier for the appSet LLM_BACKEND=openai_compat with a Groq or OpenRouter free key (section 4.4). Deploy only the API and the frontend.The best option. Your app becomes small and stateless, and it is fast. Requires accepting a rate limit and a third party seeing your prompts.
B. Everything local, share via a tunnelRun docker compose up at home; expose it with a tunnel service.Free, private, and your GPU. Only up when your machine is. Perfect for a demo call, unsuitable as a product.
C. Frontend hosted, backend localDeploy the built Angular app to any static host; point it at a tunnel to your machine.A pleasant middle ground: the UI is always available and shows an honest error when the backend is not.
D. Rent a GPU by the hourA spot GPU instance running vLLM (section 7.4).Not free, but genuinely cheap for short periods. The right answer when you need to demonstrate a big model.

What changes for strategy A

# .env in production
LLM_BACKEND=openai_compat
OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://api.groq.com/openai/v1     # ⚠ verify the current URL
OPENAI_API_KEY=gsk_...                             # from the platform's secret store
CHAT_MODEL=...                                     # a model the provider currently serves
EMBED_MODEL=sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 # embeddings stay local: small and CPU-fine

Five environment variables. No code changes at all, because section 4.1's ChatBackend Protocol and section 4.5's factory made the backend a configuration concern. That is the payoff for the indirection — it looked like ceremony in Part 4 and it is why deployment is a .env edit now.

Deployment concernWhat to do
SecretsUse the platform's secret store, never a committed .env. Confirm .env is in .gitignore — and if a key ever lands in a commit, rotate it rather than deleting the commit.
The vector indexBake a prebuilt index into the image, or mount persistent storage. Rebuilding on boot on a small free instance is slow and may exceed a start-up timeout.
Cold startsFree tiers sleep. First request after idle can take 30+ seconds — so the frontend's loading and error states (section 9.9) matter more here than anywhere.
EmbeddingsMiniLM on CPU is fine, but the model download plus load can exceed a small instance's memory. Measure, and consider a hosted embedding endpoint if it does not fit.
Rate limitsKeep 10.8's limiter enabled. A public URL with an LLM behind it will be found, and your provider quota is the thing being spent.
Cost ceilingIf you attach a paid key, set a hard spend cap at the provider. Section 6.10's Budget protects one run; only the provider can protect you from a loop you did not anticipate.

What I would actually do for a portfolio. Strategy A, plus a good README with a GIF of the streaming UI, plus the docker compose up path documented for anyone who wants to run it locally with their own model. A reviewer who can try your deployed demo in ten seconds and read how to run it privately learns more about you than any amount of architecture prose.

10.12 Part 10 checkpoint

Quiz answer 1: streaming works with curl but arrives all at once in the browser. Where do you look?

Not your generator — curl proved that works. In order: the text/event-stream media type, the X-Accel-Buffering: no response header, nginx's proxy_buffering off, and in development the ng serve proxy. Curl against the API container directly to isolate which hop is buffering.

Quiz answer 2: your API freezes when two people use it at once. Why?

Blocking code inside an async def route. requests and sentence-transformers block the event loop, so no other request can be served — including the health check. Wrap them in asyncio.to_thread, or declare the route as plain def so FastAPI runs it in a threadpool. Separately, cap concurrent generations with a semaphore: one Ollama instance serving ten requests at once is slower for everyone than a queue.

Quiz answer 3: what makes cancellation real rather than cosmetic?

Two halves. The browser calls AbortController.abort() (section 9.7), and the server checks await request.is_disconnected() inside the token loop and breaks. Breaking closes the async generator, which closes the httpx stream, which makes Ollama stop generating. Without the server half, Stop only hides the output while the GPU keeps working — and you can verify which you have by watching ollama ps after cancelling.

Quiz answer 4: your fine-tuned model is faster, cheaper and scores better on retrieval. Why did CI block it?

Because abstention_correct fell from 0.88 to 0.55 — it lost the ability to say "not in the documents". That is the exact failure section 8.1 warned about, and it is invisible to every metric a developer would naturally check. It is also the argument for having a floor and a drop limit per metric: one catches "not good enough", the other catches "worse than yesterday".

Quiz answer 5: where must the tenant filter be applied, and why does the order matter?

On the server, last, overwriting anything the model or client supplied. The implementation strips any incoming tenant_id from the requested filter and then sets the trusted one. Merge the other way round and a self-query filter or an injected instruction can read another tenant's documents — which is a data breach, not a bug.

Quiz answer 6: one thing to change first when a local RAG answer takes 30 seconds?

Send less. Cut top_k from 10 to 4 with reranking, and cap the output length. Prefill is quadratic in prompt length (section 2.7) and generation is the largest single cost, so those two changes typically halve the time — and section 5.9 showed that fewer, better-ranked chunks often improve quality too. Streaming is already handling the perceived latency.

You are done with Part 10 when you can

  • Write an SSE endpoint from memory, including the headers that stop buffering.
  • Explain why asyncio.to_thread matters in a FastAPI route with a local model.
  • Describe both halves of cancellation and how to verify the server half.
  • Say what belongs on every llm.call log line and why retrieved is on it.
  • Explain the difference between a metric floor and a regression limit.
  • Name the five security threats and the defence for each.
  • Bring the whole stack up on a clean machine with one command.

Part 11

The career part

What the job actually is, what the titles mean, which of your new skills will still be useful in three years, how to turn the capstone into evidence rather than a repository nobody opens, and the interview questions that separate people who built something from people who followed a tutorial. Then the capstone map, and you are done.

11.1 What the job actually is

The gap between how this work is described and how it feels day to day is wider than in most of software. Here is the honest distribution, for an applied role building LLM features on a product team:

ActivityRough share of timeWhat it looks like
Ordinary software engineering~40%APIs, data plumbing, error handling, deployment, code review, someone's PDF parser returning empty strings. Indistinguishable from backend work.
Evaluation and debugging quality~25%"It got worse and nobody knows why." Building golden sets, reading traces, bisecting between a prompt change and a model version. The most distinctive part of the job.
Data work~15%Ingestion, chunking, cleaning, metadata, permissions. Deeply unglamorous and the biggest single determinant of quality.
Prompt and pipeline iteration~10%The part everyone imagines is the whole job. It is real work, but it is a tenth of it.
Explaining limits to stakeholders~10%Why the demo worked and the pilot did not. Why "just make it 100% accurate" is not a task. Why RAG will not fix a knowledge problem you do not have documents for.
Training models~0–2%Most applied engineers never fine-tune anything in production. Part 8 exists so you can judge whether to, which is the actual skill.

The single most useful reframing. This is not a machine-learning job with some software around it. It is a software job with a non-deterministic dependency — one that fails plausibly rather than loudly, cannot be unit-tested in the usual way, and changes underneath you when a vendor ships. Everything unusual about the role follows from that one property.

What surprises people who arrive from normal backend work

  • Your tests cannot tell you if it works. A green suite means nothing broke structurally. Whether answers are good is a separate measurement system you have to build — which is why Part 5's harness and Part 10's CI gate matter more than they look.
  • The bug is often in the data, not the code. "The model is hallucinating" usually resolves to "the chunk containing the answer was never retrieved". Debugging starts at retrieval, not at the prompt.
  • Non-determinism makes reproduction hard. "It did it once" is a real bug report you cannot dismiss, and logging what the model saw (Part 10's retrieved field) is what makes it tractable.
  • Cost is a design constraint, visible per request. Backend engineers rarely think in fractions of a cent per call. Here it drives architecture — routing, caching, prompt length.
  • Stakeholders have calibrated expectations from consumer chatbots and yours will be compared to those, unfavourably, on a much smaller budget.

What surprises people who arrive from data science or ML

  • Nobody wants your notebook. The deliverable is a service with an SLA, error states and a rollback plan.
  • Training is rarely the answer. The instinct to fine-tune is usually wrong; retrieval and prompting solve most of it, faster.
  • Latency is a product requirement, not a footnote in a results table.
  • The frontend matters enormously. Part 9 was not padding — streaming, citations and approval gates are where the trust in an AI product is actually built or lost.

11.2 The titles, and what employers actually mean

⚠⚠ This section is the least reliable in the course, and I want to be explicit about why. I searched for current market data while writing, and the sources disagreed wildly — average salary figures differed by tens of thousands between reports, and the most dramatic supply-and-demand statistics came from staffing firms selling placement services. I have kept only claims that either appeared consistently or come from a methodology I can see, and I have deliberately not given you a single salary number. Check your own market, in your own currency, from postings you can read.

The claims I think are reasonably solid

Entry-level positions are rare. This is usually a second role, not a first one. Which is good news if you already write software: your existing experience is the qualification, and this course is the delta.
Hiring is steady, not cooling. Python is table stakes and breadth is valued. "Prompt engineer" did not become a job. The title "AI engineer" is used vaguely. A Nexus IT Group write-up notes that employers saying "AI engineer" usually mean a specialist in deployment, LLM applications, evaluation, retrieval or production infrastructure, and that vague requisitions attract the wrong candidates on both sides.Self-interested source, but the observation matches every job description I have read.Read the responsibilities, never the title. Two roles with identical titles can be completely different jobs.

One more honest observation from the search. A recent Forbes piece by Bernard Marr noted that demand for AI ethics and governance expertise remains surprisingly low, which the author flags as a concern about industry oversight. I would not advise anyone to specialise there purely for employability today — but I would advise you to be the engineer on the team who raises the question, because that competence is currently scarce and will not stay optional.

11.3 What transfers, and what expires

The genuinely useful question when the tooling churns every six months: which of the things you just learned are worth deep investment?

Durable — invest heavilyWhy it lasts
Evaluation. Golden sets, recall@k, faithfulness, regression gates, thresholds.Every model, framework and vendor change is a question of "did this get better or worse", and that question is answered the same way regardless of what changed. This is the highest-return skill in the entire course.
Retrieval fundamentals. Chunking, embeddings, hybrid search, reranking, why lexical and dense fail differently.Information retrieval predates LLMs by fifty years and will outlast them. The RRF you implemented in 5.9 was published long before transformers.
Verification and grounding. Checking claims against sources, abstention, showing your work.Follows from what a language model is (section 2.8), not from any product. It cannot be patched away.
Debugging non-determinism. Tracing, logging what the model saw, bisecting prompt versus model changes.The core professional skill that distinguishes this work. Purely conceptual, entirely portable.
Cost and latency reasoning. Quadratic prefill, KV cache size, tokens as the unit of everything.Architecture-level facts about transformers. Numbers shift; the shape does not.
Security thinking. Untrusted text reaches the model through documents; constrain capability, not wording.Prompt injection has no known complete fix (section 3.6). The mitigations are the same ones you will use in five years.
Software engineering. Interfaces, dependency inversion, testability, layering.The reason "deploy to a hosted API" was a five-line .env change in section 10.11 rather than a rewrite.
Perishable — learn just enough, expect to relearnEvidence from this course
Specific framework APIs.Section 7.2 documented Microsoft merging Semantic Kernel and AutoGen, and Pydantic AI's v2 breaking redesign — both within a year. Part 8's Unsloth code needed a ⚠⚠ warning about argument renames.
Model names, versions and benchmark rankings.Section 7.3 refused to give you a leaderboard and gave you a selection procedure instead. That was not evasion; it was the durable form of the knowledge.
Free-tier limits and pricing.Every table in 4.4 and 10.11 carries a ⚠. These change without notice, sometimes retroactively.
Vendor SDK surfaces.Langfuse's import paths, the MCP SDK's decorators, TRL's trainer arguments — all flagged, all moved.
Test runners and build tooling.Karma was the Angular default for a decade and is now deprecated (section 9.14). Six months of currency, indefinite conceptual life.
Prompt tricks.Section 3.3 was honest that role prompting is weaker than folklore claims, and newer models are increasingly trained to be robust to phrasing games.

The pattern worth internalising. Every perishable item above is a surface over a durable idea. Frameworks are surfaces over the agent loop you hand-wrote in 6.4. SDKs are surfaces over HTTP. Vector databases are surfaces over the cosine similarity you computed in 1.6. This is exactly why the course made you build the primitive before showing you the tool: when the surface changes, you still understand the thing underneath, and you can read the new API in an afternoon.

11.4 Turning the capstone into evidence

The bar to clear. Almost every AI portfolio project is a RAG chatbot over some PDFs, built from a framework tutorial, with a Streamlit interface and a README that lists the libraries used. Yours has to be visibly not that — and the good news is that it already is, if you present it properly.

The five things that make a reviewer take it seriously

SignalWhere it already exists in your capstoneWhy it lands
1. It runs. One command, on their machine, with no accounts.M19's docker compose up, defaulting to a 1.7B model that fits an 8 GB laptop.Most projects cannot be run by anyone but the author. Being runnable puts you in a small minority before anyone reads a line of code.
2. You measured it. Numbers, a method, and a threshold.Part 5's harness, Part 10's regression gate with a committed baseline.json.Evaluation is the skill most employers say they cannot find. A committed baseline with floors is more convincing than any amount of architecture description.
3. It does not trust the model. Citations verified against source text; abstention when the answer is not there.Section 5.7's verifier, 9.10's panel that flags an unverified quote in red.Demonstrates you understand why models fabricate rather than just that they do.
4. Failure is designed for. Cancellation, timeouts, retries, denials, error states.M17's Stop that reaches the server, 4.6's backoff, 6.10's guards, 9.9's seven UI states.This is the clearest available proxy for production experience.
5. You know its limits. Written down, by you, before anyone asks.Everything the course flagged: single-process approvals, synchronous re-indexing, no conversation history, regex PII redaction being approximate.The strongest signal of the five. A candidate who volunteers the weaknesses of their own system is doing the thing senior engineers do.

The README, which is the actual deliverable

Assume ninety seconds of attention and no willingness to install anything. In order:

## Architecture
[one diagram, five boxes maximum]

## Known limitations
- Approvals are held in process memory: works with one worker, not several.
- Uploading re-indexes synchronously; a large PDF blocks the request.
- No conversation history: each question is independent.
- PII redaction is regex-based and approximate. Not a compliance control.

## What I would do next, and why
Three items, each with the reason it is next rather than a wish list.
SectionWhy it is there
A GIF above the foldStreaming tokens and citations appearing is the whole value proposition, and it is visible in four seconds. Screenshots cannot show streaming, which is precisely the thing that makes your project look built rather than assembled.

Three extensions that add disproportionate signal

ExtensionEffortWhat it demonstrates
An eval report committed to the repository — one markdown file per experiment: what you changed, the before and after numbers, and what you concluded.An hour per experiment, and you already ran them.That you work empirically. Three of these is more persuasive than any additional feature, because almost nobody has them.
A failure gallery — five real cases where your system got it wrong, each with a diagnosis and whether you fixed it.An afternoon.Extremely rare, and it makes you unbluffable in an interview: you have already thought harder about your failures than they will have time to.
A model swap with measurements — run the same eval suite against a 1.7B, an 8B and a hosted model, and publish the table.An evening, mostly waiting.That you can quantify a trade-off rather than assert one. Also produces a genuinely interesting artefact people will want to discuss.

Do not do these. Do not claim a metric you did not measure — you will be asked how, and "I saw it in a blog post" ends the interview. Do not write a README that describes an architecture more impressive than the code (reviewers check). Do not commit a .env with a live key; if you ever have, rotate the key rather than deleting the commit. And do not describe the project as production-ready when it has the limitations you just honestly listed — the list is the strength, the claim is the weakness.

11.5 Interview questions, with real answers

Grouped by what they are testing. The answers are the ones I would give, grounded in what you built — which is the point: every one of these is answerable from your own code rather than from memorised theory.

Questions designed to detect tutorial-following

"Walk me through what happens between the user pressing Enter and the first token appearing."

What it tests: whether you know your own system. This question is fatal to anyone who assembled a framework example, because the framework did the middle for them.

The answer: the POST hits FastAPI, Pydantic validates the body, the rate limiter checks a token bucket, the question is embedded (about 20 ms), BM25 and dense retrieval run and are fused with reciprocal rank fusion, the top ~20 candidates go to a cross-encoder reranker which returns 4, those are rendered into the prompt with source and chunk ids, a citations SSE event goes out immediately so the panel populates, then the model begins prefill — quadratic in prompt length, which is the bulk of the time to first token — and the first generated token is framed as an SSE token event, buffered by the client across chunk boundaries, appended to a signal, and rendered. Time to first token is roughly 0.4 to 1.8 seconds depending on prompt length.

What makes it a good answer: naming where the time goes, and knowing the citations event precedes the tokens deliberately.

"Your RAG system gave a wrong answer. How do you debug it?"

What it tests: whether you debug at the right layer. The tutorial answer is "improve the prompt", which is almost always wrong.

The answer: start at retrieval, because most wrong answers are retrieval failures wearing a generation costume. Pull the trace and look at the retrieved chunk ids. Then ask: (1) is the answer in the corpus at all? If not, the correct behaviour was abstention and the bug is that it did not abstain. (2) Was the right chunk retrieved? If not, is it a lexical miss (an exact identifier the dense retriever missed) or a semantic one — and did chunking split the answer across a boundary? (3) Was it retrieved but ranked below the cutoff? That is a reranking problem. (4) Only if the right chunk was in the prompt and the model still got it wrong is this a generation problem — and then check whether citations verified, because a fabricated quote points at a different failure than a misinterpreted real one.

"How do you know your changes made it better?"

What it tests: the single most common gap. Many candidates have never measured anything.

The answer: a golden set of hand-labelled questions with known correct chunks, scored on recall@k and MRR for retrieval — which needs no LLM, so it runs on every pull request in seconds. Generation quality is measured separately on citation verification rate, correct abstention rate and schema validity. Both an absolute floor and a maximum permitted drop per metric, so CI catches "not good enough" and "worse than yesterday" independently. And a concrete example: a fine-tuned model that was twice as fast and used half the tokens still failed the gate, because correct abstention fell from 0.88 to 0.55.

"What is in your prompt, and why is each part there?"

What it tests: whether the prompt was designed or copied. Copied prompts have parts their owner cannot justify.

The answer: be able to account for every line — the output contract and why it is schema-shaped, the citation format and why it is source#chunk_id, the explicit instruction to abstain and an example of abstaining, the delimiters around retrieved context and why untrusted document text is fenced. And be ready to say which parts you tested and which are there on faith; that honesty is worth more than a confident story.

Foundations

"Why do language models hallucinate?"

The answer: because next-token prediction optimises for plausibility, not truth, and nothing in the objective distinguishes a remembered fact from a fluent guess. Contributing factors: training data is compressed lossily into weights, so rare facts are approximated; sampling deliberately introduces randomness; there is no internal mechanism that says "I do not know this"; and instruction tuning rewards helpful-sounding answers, which pushes towards answering rather than declining. The engineering conclusion is what matters: you cannot prompt it away, so you ground answers in retrieved text and verify the claims against that text rather than trusting them.

"Why does a longer context window cost more than proportionally?"

The answer: attention compares every token with every other token, so the attention work grows with the square of the sequence length. The KV cache grows linearly but gets large fast — around 16 GB for a 128k context on an 8B model, which usually exceeds the weights themselves. So a long prompt costs quadratic prefill time and linear memory, and beyond that there is the practical observation that models often use the middle of a long context poorly. Sending fewer, better chunks is therefore a latency optimisation and a quality optimisation at the same time.

"When would you fine-tune instead of using RAG?"

The answer: fine-tuning teaches behaviour; RAG supplies knowledge. Fine-tune for style, format compliance, domain fluency, or to delete a 3,000-token instruction block from every call — that last one is the strongest commercial case, because it cuts latency and cost on every request. Use RAG for anything factual, anything that changes, and anything with per-user access control, because you cannot put permissions in weights. And the counter-intuitive part: training on facts the model does not know can increase hallucination, because what supervised fine-tuning reliably teaches is the shape of confident assertion.

Retrieval

"Your retrieval misses questions containing exact identifiers, like error codes. Why?"

The answer: dense embeddings capture semantics, and an identifier's meaning is that it is exactly itself — so ERR_4471 and ERR_4472 land close together in vector space while being completely different things. The fix is hybrid retrieval: BM25 handles exact-term matching, dense handles paraphrase, and reciprocal rank fusion combines the rankings without needing the two scoring scales to be comparable. I have a verified example where the keyword search found a chunk by its identifier that dense retrieval ranked outside the top five, and a paraphrased question where the reverse happened.

"How do you choose a chunk size?"

The answer: empirically, against the eval suite, because it depends on the documents. The trade-off: small chunks retrieve precisely but lose the context needed to answer; large chunks carry context but dilute the embedding and waste prompt budget. The failure mode to watch for is an answer split across a boundary, which is why structural chunking on headings beats fixed-size splitting, and why prefixing each chunk with its heading path helps materially. Also check your embedding model's real token limit — MiniLM truncates at 256 tokens, so an 800-token chunk is silently half-embedded, which is a bug that produces no error at all.

"Would you use GraphRAG?"

What it tests: resistance to hype.

The answer: probably not. It is genuinely interesting for questions that require traversing relationships across many documents, but it costs a lot to build and maintain, and most "we need a knowledge graph" situations turn out to be a metadata filtering problem or a chunking problem. I would exhaust hybrid retrieval, reranking and query transformation first, and I would want a specific class of question in the eval set that demonstrably fails without it before taking on the complexity.

Agents

"What makes something an agent rather than a pipeline?"

The answer: the model decides what happens next. In a pipeline you wrote the control flow; in an agent the model chooses the tool, and the loop continues until it says it is done or you cut it off. That single property is where all the difficulty comes from — non-termination, cost blowouts, error cascades — and it is why the first question to ask is whether you need one. Most tasks presented as agentic are better served by a fixed pipeline with one model call at the decision point.

"How do you stop an agent looping forever or costing a fortune?"

The answer: hard limits enforced in code, never in the prompt. A maximum step count, a maximum tool-call count, a wall-clock deadline and a token budget, all checked by the loop rather than requested of the model. Plus thrashing detection — the same tool called with the same arguments three times in a row means it is stuck, so stop and say so. And a clean stop reason recorded on the result, so "step limit" and "finished" are distinguishable in the logs. I test all of this with a scripted fake model, so the limits are verified without spending anything.

"A tool call fails. What should the agent see?"

The answer: a message, not an exception. Tool errors are normal input to the loop, not crashes — the validation error text should go back as the observation so the model can correct itself. In my implementation the model mistyped an argument name, received the Pydantic error, and retried correctly on the next step. If you let the exception propagate, you have thrown away the model's ability to recover from exactly the mistakes it makes most often.

Production and security

"How do you handle prompt injection?"

What it tests: whether you know it is unsolved. Anyone claiming a complete fix is wrong.

The answer: accept that you cannot reliably stop it at the text layer, and constrain what a successful injection can do. In order of value: tool allow-lists so nothing dangerous is reachable, validated and typed arguments so paths and expressions cannot be smuggled, human approval for anything irreversible with the full arguments displayed, and least privilege on every credential the agent can reach. Then the text-layer measures as defence in depth: fence retrieved content in delimiters, neutralise instruction-like patterns at ingestion, and keep the system prompt separate from document text. The crucial point is that untrusted text arrives through your documents, not just the chat box — so a poisoned PDF in the index is the realistic attack, and it is why the frontend sanitises model output before rendering it as HTML.

"Your API becomes unresponsive when a second user connects. What did you do wrong?"

The answer: put blocking code in an async route. A synchronous HTTP client or a sentence-transformer call inside async def blocks the event loop, so nothing else is served — including the health check, which is why the container then gets restarted. Wrap blocking calls in asyncio.to_thread, or declare the route as plain def so the framework uses a threadpool. Separately, cap concurrent generations with a semaphore: one local model instance serving ten simultaneous requests is slower for everyone than a queue of two.

"How do you make a Stop button actually stop generation?"

What it tests: end-to-end thinking. Most people implement half of it.

The answer: two halves. The browser aborts the fetch with an AbortController, and the server checks whether the client has disconnected inside the token loop and breaks out — which closes the async generator, which closes the HTTP stream to the model runtime, which makes it stop. Without the server half you have only hidden the output while the GPU keeps working. You can verify which one you have by cancelling and then watching whether the model is still loaded and busy.

"You are handed a multi-tenant requirement. What changes?"

The answer: retrieval filtering becomes a security boundary rather than a feature. Every chunk carries a tenant id at ingestion, and the retrieval filter is composed on the server with the tenant clause applied last, overwriting anything the client or the model supplied — because a self-query filter or an injected instruction must not be able to forge it. Then: separate caches per tenant, because a cache key that ignores tenancy is a cross-tenant leak; tenant in every log line; per-tenant rate limits; and an eval case that specifically asserts tenant B's documents are never returned for tenant A.

The questions to ask them

These are diagnostic, and asking them signals experience more than any answer you give:

  • "How do you currently measure whether the AI features are working?" If the answer is "users tell us", you would be building the evaluation function as well as the product — which can be a great role, if you go in knowing it.
  • "What happens when a model version changes underneath you?" Tests whether they have been through it.
  • "Who decides what the system is allowed to do autonomously?" Reveals whether anyone owns risk, or whether it will land on you unannounced.
  • "What proportion of the team's time goes on data and permissions versus model work?" The honest answer is usually most of it. An answer of "hardly any" means either they have solved something remarkable or they have not started.
  • "What is in production today, and how long has it been there?" Distinguishes shipped from perpetually piloted.

11.6 Staying current without chasing every release

The tooling churns roughly every six months. Chasing it is a full-time job with no output. A maintainable approach:

CadenceWhat to doWhy
Weekly, 30 minutesRead release notes for the four or five things you actually depend on. Nothing else.Breaking changes in your own dependencies are the only news that is certainly relevant to you.
Monthly, two hoursRun your eval suite against one new model. Record the numbers in the repository.Turns "is the new model better" from an opinion into a measurement, and keeps the habit alive. This is the single highest-value routine on the list.
Quarterly, a dayRebuild one component with a different tool — swap the vector store, try a framework you avoided, replace the reranker.Keeps your knowledge of alternatives real rather than remembered, and occasionally finds a genuine improvement.
YearlyRe-read your own architecture and ask what you would not build again.Most systems accumulate decisions that made sense against constraints that no longer exist.
NeverTry to keep up with benchmark leaderboards, model announcements, or framework release cycles you do not use.Unbounded, and the information decays faster than you can absorb it.

Sources worth the attention, and why

TypeValue
Primary documentation and changelogs for your dependenciesThe only reliably accurate source. Everything else in this course carrying a ⚠ is there because I was working from secondary information.
Model cards and licencesWhere context length, training cutoff, intended use and actual licence terms live. Read these rather than a blog post about the release.
Papers, selectivelyRead the ones that introduced techniques you use — RAG, LoRA, ReAct, RRF, chain of thought. Reading the original of something you have implemented is unusually efficient.
Engineering write-ups from teams running this in productionThe most useful genre by far. Look specifically for post-mortems and "what we got wrong" pieces, which contain information marketing does not.
Your own eval resultsThe only source that is about your system. Weigh it above any external benchmark, always.

The filter I would apply to any new tool or technique. Three questions. What does it replace? What does it cost — in dependencies, in lock-in, in things I can no longer debug? And can I measure whether it helped, on my own eval suite, in an afternoon? If the answer to the third is no, that is not a reason to reject it, but it is a reason to be suspicious of anyone claiming it works.

What "done" means

Not "every milestone has code". These five, all true at once:

  1. A stranger can run it with docker compose up on a laptop with no GPU and no API keys, and ask a question about their own PDF.
  2. You can quote your own numbers — recall@5, citation verification rate, abstention rate — and say exactly how each was measured.
  3. CI fails when you deliberately degrade retrieval quality.
  4. Cancelling stops the model, verifiably, not just the display.
  5. You can list its weaknesses without looking anything up.

Extensions, in the order I would build them

#ExtensionWhy it is next
1Conversation history — session ids, plus the memory compaction from M10 wired into the API.The most obvious missing feature, and it exercises the M10 code you wrote but never connected. Also introduces query condensing (5.10) as a genuine requirement rather than an option.
2Background indexing with a status stream — a job queue, and progress over SSE.Fixes the honest limitation from 10.2, reuses the streaming transport you already built, and completes section 9.11's 'indexing' state.
3OCR for scanned PDFs.Fixes a real ingestion failure, and it is an ingestion loader rather than an architecture change — which is the point.
4Authentication and multi-tenancy.Turns retrieval filtering into a security boundary and makes the project credible for enterprise conversations. Also the answer to a common interview question.
5A model-comparison eval report across three model sizes.Cheap, and it produces the artefact that best demonstrates empirical judgement.
6A fine-tuned small model for the routing or condensing step.Now that you have an eval suite, you can prove whether it helped — which is the only responsible way to fine-tune anything.

11.8 Where this leaves you

You started at Part 0 installing Python. You have since implemented gradient descent by hand, self-attention on four tokens with verified arithmetic, BPE tokenisation, cosine similarity, BM25, reciprocal rank fusion, LoRA, an agent loop, an SSE parser that survives arbitrary chunk boundaries, and a CI gate that blocks a quality regression. You also wrote a frontend that streams tokens and shows its sources, and packaged the lot so a stranger can run it.

The specific value of having done it in that order: you built the primitive before you saw the tool. So when the framework you use is merged into another one, or its API is redesigned, or the model you rely on is deprecated — all three of which happened to things in this course while it was being written — you are reading a new surface over an idea you already implemented.

The five things I would most want you to retain

  1. Measure, or you are guessing. Every quality claim in this course came with a number and a method, and where I could not verify something I said so. Hold your own work to that standard and you will be unusual.
  2. Ground and verify. Models produce plausible text; that is the whole mechanism. Supply the facts, then check the claims against the facts you supplied.
  3. Constrain capability, not wording. Prompt injection is unsolved, so the defence is what a compromised model is able to do — allow-lists, validated arguments, human approval for anything irreversible.
  4. The interesting engineering is around the model, not in it. Retrieval, evaluation, error handling, cancellation, permissions, interface design. The model is a dependency.
  5. Say what you do not know. The ⚠ marks throughout this course were not hedging — they were the most useful thing in it, because they tell you where to check. Doing the same in your own work is the habit that makes people trust you.

A closing note on the ⚠ marks. There are a lot of them, and they are concentrated in exactly the places you would expect: framework APIs, version numbers, free-tier limits, vendor SDKs. That distribution is a finding. The parts of this field that are stable enough to teach without caveat are the fundamentals — attention, retrieval, evaluation, verification — and the parts that need a warning are the surfaces. If you ever find yourself unsure where to invest your learning time, look at which sections needed warnings and which did not.

That is the course. Go and build the thing you actually want to exist, measure whether it works, and be honest about what it cannot do. That combination is rarer than it should be, and it is the whole job.
